chapters.title: First Glimpses
paragraphs: I have hesitated so long before this notebook, because I have not yet managed to discover the exact day when I first met Maitreyi. In my notes from that year, I found nothing. Her name appears there much later, after I had left the sanatorium and had to move into the house of engineer Narendra Sen, in the Bhowanipore district. But that happened in 1929, and I had met Maitreyi at least ten months before that. And if I suffer somewhat as I begin this story, it is precisely because I do not know how to evoke her figure as she was then, and I cannot truly relive my astonishment, uncertainty, and the confusion of those first encounters.

I remember very vaguely that, seeing her once in the car, waiting in front of the "Oxford Book Stationary"—while her father, the engineer, and I were choosing books for the Christmas holidays—I felt a strange start, followed by a very surprising disdain. She seemed ugly to me—with her eyes too large and too black, her fleshy, turned lips, her strong breasts, like those of a Bengali maiden grown too full, like a fruit past its ripeness. When I was introduced to her and she brought her palms to her forehead in greeting, I suddenly saw her whole bare arm, and the color of her skin struck me: matte, brown, a brown unlike any I had ever seen before, as if made of clay and wax.

At that time, I was still living on Wellesley Street, at Ripon Mansion, and my roommate was Harold Carr, an employee at the "Army and Navy Stores," whose company I cultivated because he had a number of friendly families in Calcutta, where I too spent my evenings and with whose daughters I would go out weekly to dances. To this Harold I tried to describe—more for my own clarification than his—Maitreyi’s bare arm and the strangeness of that dark yellow, so disturbing, so little feminine, as if it belonged more to a goddess or a statue than to an Indian woman.

Harold was shaving in the standing mirror on his little table. I can still see the scenes: the teacups, his mauve pajamas stained with shoe polish (he had beaten the boy bloody for this incident, though he himself had dirtied them when he came back drunk one night from the Y.M.C.A. ball), some nickel coins on the unmade bed, and I, trying in vain to unclog my pipe with a twist of paper, rolling it until it thinned like a matchstick.

"Really, Allan, how can you like a Bengali girl? They’re disgusting. I was born here, in India, and I know them better than you. They’re dirty, believe me. And besides, there’s nothing to be done, not even love. That girl will never let you..."

never the hand... I listened to all this with an unspeakable delight, although Harold had not understood a thing of what I had told him and believed that, if I spoke of a girl’s arm, I must be thinking of love. But it is strange how much I enjoy hearing ill spoken of those I love, or to whom I feel close, or who are my friends. When I truly love someone, I like to listen to people gossip about them; it somehow verifies certain obscure processes of my conscience, which I do not understand and which I do not like to recall. It could be said that, parallel to my passion or sincere interest for someone, there also grows a hostile passion, which demands the suppression, alteration, dethronement of the first. I do not know. But catching myself pleasantly impressed by the idiotic criticism Harold—stupid and fanatical like any Eurasian—was making about Bengali women, I immediately realized that something deeper still binds the memory of Maitreyi to my thoughts or desires. This both amused and troubled me at the same time. I went into my room, automatically trying to unclog my pipe. I do not know what else I did after that, for the event is not noted in my journal from that time, and I only remembered it on the occasion of the jasmine garland, whose story I will continue to write here, in this notebook.

At that time, I was at the beginning of my career in India. I had come with a host of superstitions, was a member of the "Rotary Club," very proud of my continental citizenship and descent, read a lot about mathematical physics (although in my adolescence I had dreamed of becoming a missionary), and wrote almost daily in my journal. After I handed over the local representation of the "Noel and Noel" factories and was hired for technical drawing at the new delta drainage company, I became better acquainted with Narendra Sen (who even then was very well known and respected in Calcutta, being the first engineer laureate from Edinburgh), and my life began to change. I earned less now, but I enjoyed the work. I was no longer forced to stew in the offices on Clive Street, to sign and decipher papers and to get drunk every summer evening to ward off neurasthenia. I was away every two or three weeks, had the initiative in the works at Tamluk, and my heart swelled whenever I saw the construction rising each time I had to come from the center and work on site.

Those months were, indeed, happy for me, for I would leave at dawn with the Howrah-Madras express and arrive at the site before noon. I have always loved journeys in the colonies. In India, those in first class are a true holiday. I felt the station was a friend every time I got out of the taxi and hurried lively onto the platform, with my maroon helmet pulled low over my eyes, my servant behind me, five illustrated magazines under my arm, and two tins of "Capstan" tobacco in my hands (for I smoked a lot at Tamluk, and whenever I passed by the tobacconist’s in Howrah,

It seemed to me that I had not bought enough "Capstan," and the memory of a night without pipe tobacco, forced to smoke the workers’ coarse tobacco, made me shudder. I never spoke to my compartment neighbors; I disliked those hara-sahibs with mediocre Oxford educations, the young men with detective novels in their pockets, or the wealthy Indians who had learned to travel first class but had not yet learned how to wear a jacket or how to pick their teeth. I gazed out the window at the bustards of Bengal—never sung, never mourned—and then fell silent before myself, saying nothing, asking nothing of myself.

On the construction site, I was the only master, because I was the only white man. The few Eurasians who supervised the work near the bridge did not enjoy the same prestige; they came to the site in third class, dressed in the usual khaki outfits—shorts and shirts with wide breast pockets—and cursed the workers in flawless Hindusthani. This perfection in language and the richness of their vocabulary of insults lowered them in the eyes of the laborers. I, on the contrary, spoke poorly and without accent, and this impressed them, for it proved my foreign origin, my superiority. Besides, I greatly enjoyed talking with them in the evenings, before retreating to my tent to write and smoke my last pipe, lost in thought. I loved this piece of land near the sea, this plain full of snakes and desolation, where palm trees were rare and the bushes fragrant. I loved the mornings, before sunrise, when the silence made me shout with joy; an almost human solitude, on this field so green and so deserted, awaiting its traveler beneath the most beautiful sky I have ever seen.

The days on the construction site seemed to me true holidays. I worked with appetite, gave orders left and right in high spirits, and if I had had even a single intelligent companion there, I am sure I would have told him wonderful things.

It happened that I met Lucien Metz on one of those days when I was returning—sunburned and ravenous—from Tamluk. I met him on the platform, while I was waiting for my servant to find me a taxi (the Bombay express had just arrived, and there was an unusual crowd). I had met Lucien two years before, in Aden, when I had disembarked there for a few hours—on my way to India—while he was waiting for an Italian steamer to take him back to Egypt. I liked from the start this uncultured and impertinent journalist, full of talent and perspicacity, who wrote an economic report by leafing through price lists on a ship’s deck and comparing them with those in the port, and who could perfectly describe a city after only an hour’s drive through it in a speeding car. When I met him, he had already visited India, China, Malaya, and Japan several times, and he was one of those who spoke ill of Mahatma Gandhi, not for what he did, but for what he did not do.

— Hey, Allan! he called out to me, somewhat surprised to run into me. Still in India, mon vieux? Tell this fellow, please—the one pretending not to understand my English—to take me to the Y.M.C.A., not to the hotel. I’ve come to write a book about India. A bestseller, political and detective. I’ll tell you all about it...

Indeed, Lucien had come to write a book on modern India and had been here for several months, conducting interviews, visiting prisons, taking photographs. He showed me that very evening his album and his collection of autographs. What troubled him somewhat was the chapter on women; he had not yet seen real Indian women. He knew only vaguely about their life in purdah, about their civil rights, and especially about child marriages. He asked me several times:
— Allan, is it true that these people marry girls of eight? I read a book by a fellow, a man who was a magistrate here for thirty years.

We spent a very pleasant evening together on the hostel terrace, but despite my efforts, I couldn’t tell him much, for I myself knew little of the inner life of Indian women and had only seen them, until then, at the cinema or at receptions. However, I thought I might ask Narendra Sen to invite him over for tea and enlighten him. Perhaps I also thought that, on this occasion, I too would be able to see Maitrayi more closely, whom I hadn’t seen since then, as my excellent relations with Sen were limited to our joint work at the office and conversations in the car. He had invited me twice so far to take tea with him, but as I greatly valued my free time, dedicating it entirely to mathematical physics, I had refused.

When I told him that Lucien was writing a book about India, which would be published in Paris, and when I told him specifically which chapter he found difficult to write, Sen asked me to invite him to tea immediately, that very afternoon. My joy, climbing the stairs at the hostel, to share the news with him! Lucien had never been in the house of wealthy Indians before and was preparing to compose a perfect report.
— This Sen of yours, what caste is he? he inquired.

— A true Brahmin, but not at all orthodox. He’s a founding member of the Rotary Club, a member of the Calcutta Club, plays perfect tennis, drives a car, eats fish and meat, invites Europeans to his home and introduces them to his wife. He’ll delight you, I’m sure.

I must confess that my surprise was as great as Lucien’s. I knew the engineer’s house in Bhowanipore, for I had once been there by car to pick up some plans. But never would I have suspected that inside a Bengali house such marvels could be found, so much light filtered through curtains as transparent as shawls, carpets and sofas of Kashmiri wool so sweet to the touch, and little tables with legs like beaten brass trays, on which cups stood...

the tea and the Bengali sweets, brought by Narendra Sen for Lucien’s enlightenment. I sat and looked around the room, as if I had just then fallen into India. I had lived here for two years, and never had I been curious enough to enter a Bengali family, to know their inner life, to admire at least their handiwork, if not their soul. I had lived a colonial life, alone with my work on the construction site or in offices, reading books or attending performances that I could just as easily have found on the white continents. That afternoon I experienced my first doubts, and I remember returning home a little downcast (Lucien was enthusiastic, checking his impressions, asking me here and there if he had understood everything our host had told him) and with a host of thoughts I had never before harbored. Yet I wrote nothing in my journal, and today, when I search those notebooks for any trace that might evoke Maitreyi for me, I find nothing. It is strange how incapable I am of foreseeing essential events, of guessing the people who will later change the course of my life.

Maitreyi seemed to me then much more beautiful, in a sari the color of pale tea, with white slippers embroidered in silver, with a shawl like yellow cherries, and her hair too black, her eyes too large, her lips too red, all seemed to create a life less than human in this wrapped and yet transparent body, which lived, one might say, by wonder rather than by biology. I looked at her with a certain curiosity, for I could not manage to understand what secret this being hid in her soft, silken movements, in her timid smile, on the verge of panic, and especially in her voice, so changed from moment to moment, a voice that seemed to be discovering certain sounds for the first time. She spoke a bland and correct English, textbook English, but whenever she began to speak, both Lucien and I could not help but look at her; it was as if her words summoned us!

The tea was full of surprises. Lucien took notes after tasting each sweet and asked questions incessantly. Because he spoke poor English, and because the engineer had assured him he understood French (he had been twice to Paris, to congresses, and had in his library countless French novels, which, by the way, he did not read), Lucien would sometimes ask questions in his Parisian argot, and then the engineer would reply, smiling, “Oui, oui, c’est ça,” looking at us afterward with extraordinary satisfaction. Lucien begged to be allowed to examine Maitreyi’s costume, her jewelry and ornaments more closely, and the engineer agreed with humor, bringing his daughter by the hand, for Maitreyi had leaned against the window, her lower lip trembling and her shawl slipping onto her forehead. It was an unparalleled scene, that examination of the garments, that weighing of the jewelry in his hands, followed by exclamations and enthusiasm, by questions and answers transcribed in shorthand by Lucien in his notebook, while Maitreyi no longer knew where to look and trembled all over, pale, frightened, until she met my eyes, and I smiled at her, and then it was as if she had found

an island on which to rest, and she fixed her gaze into my eyes, calming herself gently, without spasms, naturally. I do not know how long that gaze lasted, but it resembled no other look I had ever met or embraced until then, and after the examination ended and Maitreyi fled once more to the window, we both shied away from looking at each other again, so clandestine and warm had our communion been.

Because I could no longer look at her, I turned—with different eyes—to the engineer and wondered how such an ugly and inexpressive man could be Maitreyi’s father. Now I could see, more closely and at my leisure, the engineer’s face, which so resembled a frog, with eyes so bulging and a mouth so wide, in a round, swarthy head, with a low forehead and black, frizzy hair; his body was short, his shoulders hunched, his belly misshapen, and his legs stubby. The sympathy and affection radiated by this patron of mine were all the more difficult to understand. At least for me, Narendra Sen was a seductive man, clever and subtle, cultured, full of humor, gentle and just.

As I sat there watching him, in came—bringing with her a strange atmosphere of warmth and panic—the engineer’s wife, Srimati Devi Indira, dressed in a blue sari, with a blue shawl dipped in gold and bare feet, her soles and nails reddened. The lady knew almost no English and smiled constantly. She had probably eaten a lot of pan that afternoon, for her lips were blood-red. When I looked at her, I was astonished; I would not have believed she was Maitreyi’s mother, but rather her elder sister, so young, fresh, and timid did she seem. Along with her came the other girl, Chabù, about ten or eleven years old, her hair cut short and wearing a calico dress, but no stockings or shoes; her bare calves and arms, and her dusky, beautiful face made me, amused, compare her in my mind to a little gypsy girl.

What happened then is beyond my power to recount here. These three women, finding themselves together before us, pressed close to one another, the same panic in their eyes, and the engineer tried in vain to encourage them, to make them speak. The lady wished to serve the tea, but changed her mind and let Maitreyi do it. By someone’s mistake, the teapot was spilled on the tray and on Lucien’s trousers, and then everyone rushed to help him, the engineer lost his composure and began to scold his family harshly in Bengali, while Lucien apologized in French, unable to make himself understood. At last, Narendra Sen spoke:
— Scusez-moi! Ici votre place.
The girls hurried at once to change the silk cover of the armchair, and the engineer continued to scold them, while the two of us did not know what to do with our hands or whom to look at.
Even Lucien was a little embarrassed, although when we left, in the car,
made endless fun of this accident. Only the lady remained with the same smile on her reddened lips and the same warm shyness in her eyes.

The conversation did not last much longer. The engineer showed Lucien the Sanskrit manuscripts from his uncle’s library, his uncle having been the chief pandit of the government, then a series of old paintings and embroideries. I had moved closer to the window and was gazing into the courtyard—a strange courtyard, with high walls, with shrubs and wisteria, and beyond, above the house, rose the trembling bouquet of a coconut tree. I looked on, not knowing whence came that charm, that peace I had never before encountered in Calcutta. And suddenly I heard an unrestrained, contagious laughter, a laughter of woman and child at once, which went straight to the heart and sent a shiver through me. I leaned further out the window and then I saw, sprawled on the two steps in the courtyard, the almost uncovered body of Maitreyi, her hair in her eyes, her arms crossed over her chest, and I saw her moving her feet, shaking with laughter, finally flinging her slippers, with a toss of her ankle, all the way to the other end of the wall.

I could not have enough of watching her, and those few minutes seemed endless to me. I do not know what sacred spectacle her laughter and the wildness of that burning body appeared to me. I had the feeling I was committing a sacrilege by watching her, but I could not find the strength to tear myself away from the window.
As I left, I could still hear her laughter echoing through all the rooms I passed.
chapters.summary: Allan recalls his first encounters with Maitreyi, describing his initial impressions, his life in India.

chapters.title: Solitude by the River
paragraphs: Once, I was in Tamluk and had set out for a walk upstream along the water. That was when I felt how alone I truly was. I remember that only two days before, Norinne had become engaged and we had feasted the whole night; I had drunk heavily, danced until I was dizzy, kissed all the girls, and at dawn we had driven to the Lakes. We had even planned a pajama party, just like the one last March, when I had my conflict and boxing match with Eddy Higgering. I too had loved Norinne once, as we do at twenty-four; I would have held her in my arms, danced with her, and kissed her. That was all. And as I walked slowly, pipe in one hand and riding crop in the other—the sun had not yet set the plain ablaze and the birds were still chirping among those bushes that smelled of incense and cinnamon—I suddenly realized that something unusual was happening to me, that I was left alone and would die alone. This thought did not sadden me; on the contrary, I was calm, serene, at peace with all the plain around me, and if someone had told me then that I must die within the hour, I would not have minded. I would have lain down on the grass, placed my arms under my head, and, gazing at that ocean

the blue above me, I would have waited for the minutes to pass without counting them, without hurrying them, almost without feeling them. I do not know what natural and inhuman grandeur lived within me then. I would have done anything, though I desired nothing anymore. The taste of my solitude in this world of wonders had made me dizzy. I thought of Norinne, of Harold, of all the others, and I wondered how they had entered my life, what place I had among their so peaceful and, yes, mediocre existences. I wandered without understanding anything.

When I returned to the worksite, I came with a mad longing for solitude, for silence, and I rejoiced that I would remain here, in the tent, for another week, during which I would not read newspapers and would not see electric lights. The servant greeted me: — Sahib, you have a telegram from Calcutta. I thought it was about the reception of materials and did not hurry to open it. But when I read it, I remained for a few minutes surprised and disappointed. Narendra Sen was summoning me urgently to headquarters. I had to leave that very evening, and I regretted it as I looked from the carriage window at the plain with its mists, with pale shadows of isolated palm trees, which had received me in the morning so generously into the bosom of its life without beginning and without end. How much I would have wanted then to be free, to remain in my tent with the gasoline lamp and listen to the millions of crickets and grasshoppers around me...

— Allan, I have good news for you, the engineer said to me. We need a capable man in Assam, to inspect the embankments and bridges on the Lumding-Sadyia line. I thought of you at once, and the Council has accepted you, on our responsibility. You have three days to arrange your affairs and hand over Tamluk...

He looked at me with immense goodwill, and his ugly face was lit with a warmth and a love that almost embarrassed me. I learned later that he had had to fight hard with the Council, supporting me—a white man— for the Society was swarajist and was trying to eliminate the last foreign employees, replacing them with Indians. The post was more important and better paid, from 250 to 400 rupees a month, which even surpassed the salary of a representative at "Noel and Noel." I had work in an unhealthy and uncivilized region, of course, yet my love for the jungle—with which I had come to India and which I had not yet fully satisfied—prevailed. I accepted and thanked him warmly. The engineer put his hand on my shoulder.
— We are very fond of you, Allan, both I and my wife, and we often think of you. It is a pity you do not understand our language...

These things did not trouble me then. I wondered, very vaguely, why Sen had preferred me above all his compatriots, and I answered myself, simply, that he had done so for my qualities. I had always been conscious of my constructive spirit, of my energy as a civilizing white man, of my usefulness to India.

When Harold found out, he insisted at once that we celebrate my promotion in rank and salary with a small banquet in "China-Town." We invited the girls and set off in two automobiles, noisy, cheerful, and frivolous. Leaving Park Street and turning onto Chowringhee Road, our cars began to race each other, each of us shouting at the driver (ours was a magnificent Sikh who had fought in the war in France and shouted, "Diable, à table! Vin rouge, vin blanc!"), slapping him on the back, encouraging him.
Geurtie, who had settled herself on my knees, clung to me in alarm (she had just learned of my considerable salary increase) and kept saying to me:
— I'm going to fall! Are you afraid if I fall?

At the intersection with Dhurmtollah Street, our taxi had to wait for the tram to pass. The others had gotten ahead of us, and we were all saddened by this misfortune. Then we crossed paths with the engineer’s car, and I had an unexpected start seeing him beside his wife and Maitreyi. I blushed foolishly as I greeted him, and he smiled at me with contempt, while his wife looked at me with a fear and astonishment I could not understand. Only Maitreyi raised her palms to her forehead and returned my greeting, immensely amused by the company I was keeping and the girl I held in my arms. I tried to imitate that Indian greeting, and in that instant, I felt just how ridiculous the situation was. For a few moments, I was seized by panic, until the car could move on. Turning my head, I caught a last glimpse of Maitreyi’s shawl fluttering, the color of pale tea.
My companions were amused by the respect and embarrassment with which I had greeted “a black man.”
— I’ll soon see you going to bathe in the Ganges, Allan! Geurtie said to me maliciously.
— How can you have relations with a family of blacks? Harold exclaimed, scandalized once again.
The driver, however, who had observed the scene, was delighted. When I paid him in front of the restaurant, he said to me in French, so the others wouldn’t understand:
— Très bien, sahib, jeune fille à vous; bahut achhal.
The next morning, when I met Narendra Sen, he asked me in the most natural tone:
— Who were you with last night, Allan?
— Friends, sir, I replied, annoyingly polite.
— But the girl in your arms? She was very beautiful. Do you like her?

— They’re too cheap for my taste, Mr. Sen. But I had to give my friends a farewell party, and since there were many of us and we wanted to save on cars, each of us took a girl on our lap. Nothing improper, sir, so to speak...
He must have sensed the exaggeration in my tone, for he patted me on the shoulder and said:

"You, Allan, have other paths ahead of you. The life of these Anglo-Indians is not worthy of you. I believe it does you much harm to live in an Anglo-Indian boarding house; you will never come to love India alongside them..."

I was surprised by the interest the engineer took in my private life. Until then, he had only asked whether I got along with the food, whether I had a decent boy, whether I suffered from the heat and the noise, whether I liked tennis.

We had to begin work quickly, I had to sign a multitude of papers, and as I was leaving, Sen invited me to dine with him at the Rotary Club. None of my excuses—that I was not properly dressed, that I felt tired, and so on—could convince him otherwise. I had to accept, and the speech the engineer gave that day, before a select and enthusiastic audience, pleased and flattered me somewhat, for it proved to me once again that I was seated at the table of a remarkable man.
That night I departed for Shillong, with Harold alone accompanying me to the station, giving me his final advice on how to guard myself against snakes, leprosy, malaria, and stomach troubles.
"Drink brandy with soda and whisky with soda!" he shouted to me once more, wishing me a good journey.
chapters.summary: Allan reflects on his solitude by the river, receives a sudden promotion from Narendra Sen, and navigates awkward social encounters.

chapters.title: Jungle Awakening
paragraphs: Today I leafed for a long time through my journal from Assam. With what effort I deciphered the notes of each day and transcribed them into the notebook I had begun with my new life. I was seized by a strange feeling: that I was living the existence of a pioneer, that my work building railways in the jungle was far more effective for India than a dozen books about her, that this world so ancient and our work together so new still awaited its novelist; for a different India than that of travel reports and novels was revealing itself to me then, among the tribes, beside people known until then only to ethnologists, beside that poisonous flora of Assam, in the endless rain, in the humid and dizzying heat. I wanted to give life to these places drowned in ferns and lianas, with their people so fierce and innocent. I wanted to discover their aesthetics and their morals, and each day I gathered anecdotes, took photographs, sketched genealogies.
The deeper I ventured into the wilderness, the more a hidden dignity and an unsuspected pride grew within me. I was good and just in the jungle, more honest and calmer than in the cities.

But the rains... What nights of struggle with neurasthenia, listening to that unforgettable rhythm of water on the roof, endless downpours, days on end, interrupted only by hours of hot, misty drizzle, through which I passed as through a greenhouse, for those invisibly tiny drops carried the most exhausting perfumes, and

I could scarcely bear to keep my head bowed; I had to throw it back on my shoulders and run with flared nostrils and parted lips. In the evenings I would sit in my comfortable, cool room or pace the veranda of the bungalow, trying to recapture the taste of tobacco (which not even my most exaggerated precautions had saved from the damp), and sometimes I felt I could not endure any longer. I would feel the urge to clench my fists and strike the wooden balustrade, to howl and rush out into the rain, into the darkness, anywhere, to a land where the sky did not pour down eternally and the grass was not so tall, so wet, so fleshy. I longed to see flowers again, to walk through fields like those in Tamluk, to feel the salty breeze or the dry wind of the desert, for those vapors and vegetal scents had driven me mad.

I was alone with the three servants and the bungalow watchman, and when a traveler happened by—an inspector from some jute plantation or a department agent, or a tea merchant on his way to China—we would share a bottle of whisky. I drank every evening, as soon as I finished my inspection and returned to the bungalow for my bath. It was an hour when I could scarcely feel my own flesh; if I scratched myself then, I felt no pain. And yet I felt my nerves like a web of quicksilver, I trembled, my breath was hot, I grew dizzy whenever I had to rise from my chair, and I stared into emptiness, without will, without time. The boy would bring the whisky bottle and the soda siphon to my little table, and I would drink slowly, my chin resting on my chest, in pajamas, sprawled limply on the portable chaise-longue, until I felt a gentle warmth loosening my body; then I would leap up, press my temples, get dressed, and go out to walk in the rain.

Breathing that air, thick with warm, misted drops, I yearned for a modest, happy life, a farm near a city, where I could drive each day by car. Those wanderings through the rain were my hours of weakness. I would stay out until the urge to work or to sleep seized me. I slept long and heavily, especially during those three weeks I worked forty miles north of Sadyia. I would come to the bungalow by car, sometimes even after midnight, for we had to avoid the low roads and chose only those on the slopes. I would fall asleep dressed and unwashed, after swallowing a cup of tea with much rum and quinine, for the next day, before nine, we had to be on the road again. I had grown ever more neglectful of my appearance. There was not a single white man in the whole region during those peak monsoon months; only a few Eurasian families, whom I sometimes visited out of boredom, just to hear English spoken and to drink together.

On Sundays, while my servants took the train to Shillong for provisions, I would sleep until noon, wake with a heavy head and a sticky mouth, and spend the entire day in bed, transcribing my notes into my journal. I wanted to publish, later, a book about the true life of the white man in Assam, and I
I analyzed as precisely as I could: my days of lethargy and neurasthenia, alongside the more numerous days, of course, of pioneering, of proud effort, of growth.

Throughout July, I went to Shillong only once, and there I basked in the sun, watched films again, repaired my gramophone, and bought detective novels—the only ones I was still able to read since coming to Assam. Still, I knew my work was well appreciated at headquarters, and this not through our agent in Shillong—a conceited Irishman who had once tried to make me wait at the door—but directly by Narendra Sen, who wrote me almost weekly a few lines dictated to his typist, warm and friendly. In October, I was to have a month’s leave. But I could come to Calcutta even in mid-August, if I submitted my report and finished the inspection and repair of those difficult points near Sadyia.

But something happened that I had feared in my hours of utter depression. At the beginning of August, I fell ill with malaria—a severe malaria, accompanied by nervous exhaustion. I had come back to the bungalow a few hours earlier than usual and found the tea tasteless. I had a fever and was shivering. I went to bed after swallowing three glasses of brandy, remembering Harold’s advice. But the next day I began to rave, and when a Eurasian, Mr. Frank, was called, he understood it was malaria, and they took me that very afternoon to Sadyia. The sun was blazing, and I saw flowers and birds, and at the station I was shaken by the presence of a woman; I hadn’t seen a white woman in four months.

From then on, I remember nothing. I know I was taken to Shillong and put in the European hospital there, that a telegram was sent to Calcutta, and before my replacement arrived, Mr. Sen came to see me at the hospital. Five days later, in a first-class compartment, with two nurses and Harold, I was on my way to Calcutta, where I was admitted directly to the hospital for tropical medicine.

…I awoke one morning and looked around in surprise at that white room—smelling of burnt sugar and ammonia—and at the lady reading comfortably in an armchair near the window. For a few minutes I listened to the whir of the fan, trying to recall who had just spoken to me about Lord Jim by Joseph Conrad. I had heard him, I knew his voice, and how I wished I could get out of bed and tell him that the novel was mediocre, that I could not compare it at all to my favorite book, Almayer’s Folly, written by Conrad in his youth.
“Whoever hasn’t read Almayer’s Folly does not yet know Conrad’s talent,” I said aloud to the lady, who continued her reading with her face turned toward the window.
“My God! So you’re not deaf?!” exclaimed the lady, utterly surprised, coming closer to me and smiling. “Do you want something?”

"I want to shave," I said calmly, stroking my cheeks, which I felt shriveled and cold beneath the beard that had grown unchecked. "Please forgive me for presenting myself like this before you. I believe I was brought here while I was delirious. I beg your pardon once again."
The woman laughed heartily. Then, suddenly serious:
"Good thing you've come to your senses. I was beginning to despair. I should call Mr. Carr. The poor boy has asked about you every day..."

The thought that Harold had inquired after me moved me so deeply that tears welled up in my eyes. I felt as if I were alone, abandoned somewhere without friends or acquaintances, and I was afraid of death. I saw myself dying here, five weeks away from my homeland, and the thought paralyzed me, fear freezing my cheeks.
"What is it?" the lady asked, strangely.
"Nothing; I just want to shave," I lied, for it seemed to me she would not understand.
But the tears would not stop, and so I whispered to her:
"Do you think I’ll get better, that I’ll see New York and Paris again? Will I ever be healthy once more?"

I do not remember what she answered, though the day of my awakening remains vividly fixed in my mind. Several doctors came, Europeans, then Harold entered, who squeezed my hand for two or three minutes on end.
"All right, man?! All right, man?!" he asked, looking at me.

He told me a host of things that amused me: Geurtie is now flirting with a manager from the 'Middle Bank,' a slender fellow who only dares to kiss her and takes her to the cinema in seats that cost three rupees and eight annas. Norinne, now married, is less beautiful. In my room on Wellesley Street, a poor Anglo-Indian family has moved in; the husband, young, brings schoolgirls into the room and fondles them in front of his wife, who is in her last month of pregnancy, and she says to him:
"Jack, you’re going to get yourself worked up again..."
While we were talking nonsense, the engineer came in, who shook my hand warmly and stroked my forehead, gazing at me for a long moment. I introduced him to Harold, who said cheekily:
"Delighted to meet you, Mr. Sen."
"Allan, you overdid it with work. That’s why you fell ill," the engineer consoled me. "Don’t worry about a thing, I’ve arranged everything."
I could see he was embarrassed by Harold and would have told me more if we had been alone. He promised to return the next evening, after finishing work.
"That fellow is dreadful," Harold remarked. "I wonder why he takes such an interest in you. Could it be he wants you to marry his daughter?"
"You're absurd, Harold," I protested hypocritically, blushing.
The image of Maitreyi, from whom I had long been parted, appeared before my eyes again, this time warmer, more human,

almost mocking, with her painted smile (for, curiously enough, her face and Mrs. Sen’s face seemed to complete each other in my memory, and the mother’s lips reddened by pan passed alongside the large eyes and black hair, gathered at the nape, of the daughter). I remained for a few moments contemplating her, a wonder and a sweet suffering tempting my soul (was it her absence, was it the fear that soon I would have to see her and perhaps speak to her?). Harold’s presence suddenly struck me as a kind of desecration, and I could not explain to myself this strange feeling; it was not love, certainly, nor was it respect, for until then Maitreyi had seemed to me a haughty and strange Bengali girl, who despised the whites and yet was drawn to them. Everything Harold told me ceased to interest me. I wished he would leave, so I could remain alone. Too much was happening in a single day.

Among those many things I could sense all too well that there was also the image of Maitreyi, which had suddenly arisen in a consciousness freed from fever, an image I did not know where to place or what to say to it when it would become presence.

I had never been ill before, and this convalescence, which promised to be long, made me uneasy. I wanted to throw off the sheet, to search for my clothes somewhere and set off wandering through Calcutta, for whose lights I longed. I wanted to reach the "Chinese City" and eat chiao—those noodles boiled in butter, with leeks and many vegetables, with lobster and egg yolks—and to stop on the way back at "Firpos," to listen to jazz with a good cocktail before me. All my proud white man’s health rebelled against the dull regime of the sanatorium. I could do nothing, not even smoke.
I complained the next day to the girls—Geurtie and Clara—who had come with chocolate, cigarettes, and fruit: “I wish I could run away from here and have some fun.”

Harold was planning a monstrous party, with an extension to the Lakes, on the night I would leave the sanatorium. Geurtie, ever precise, searched for a piece of paper and a pencil to make a guest list. The two Simpsons would not be invited, because Isaac hides in corners and drinks whisky neat, while Gerald steals cigarettes; she had seen him herself at Norinne’s engagement. We must, absolutely, invite Catherine, who had asked about me all the time and was so sorry when she found out I was ill in the sanatorium. As for the Huber brothers, with the beautiful Ivy, we would talk more. The others were known.
Listening to her as she ticked off names and decided for me, I did not know whether I should be saddened or amused. I watched her, and my eyes often slipped from her face into emptiness.
“Mr. Sen,” announced the nurse.

Then I felt the same confusion I always do when I must bring face to face an Indian whom I respect with young Eurasian men or women. The girls turned their heads curiously toward the door. In came Narendra Sen, with the same smile widening his mouth; and after him, with hesitations and soft steps, Maitreyi. I felt how

my heart stops and I immediately realize that I am unshaven for a day, that I am wearing a foreign pajama that does not suit me, that, in short, I am ridiculous. I shook the engineer’s hand, pretending to be unwell (to cover up any possible foolishness), and brought my palms to my forehead, greeting Maitreyi with a comical seriousness. But how surprised I was when, after introducing her to the girls, she turned decisively toward them and shook their hands, asking politely:
“How do you do?...”

“My daughter knows two codes of elegance,” laughed the engineer (casting a glance at Geurtie, whom he then spied on the whole time, especially after she said something witty). “This code, the Western one, she applies only to ladies and young women.”

I sat on pins and needles. The girls began to talk among themselves, calling Harold over as well, while the engineer explained something in Bengali to his daughter, who looked around with a curiosity at once keen and mocking. Then I noticed that, whenever she listens attentively to something said to her in earnest, an imperceptible smile of irony, of wild sarcasm, flutters on Maitreyi’s lips—a smile you would hardly believe real on that face so innocent and frightened. I wondered then, a little annoyed by my own awkwardness, what it was that disturbed me in the presence of this girl, who has nothing fascinating about her, whom I could never love, with whom I would meet only sporadically and to no purpose.
“When will you come to our house, Mr. Allan?”
Her voice sounded strange, and the three turned their heads to look at her.

“As soon as I get well...” (And I hesitated, for I did not know how to address her: “miss” did not fit, “devi” I did not dare; the confusion made me blush and I began to apologize.) “Forgive me if you found me unshaven and the room as it is, untidy. I felt so ill today” (and I mimed again that same false gesture of exhaustion, praying inwardly that they would leave at last and put an end to a situation that seemed unbearable to me).

“You know, Allan, I’ve decided to invite you to stay at my house,” said the engineer. “My wife gave me the idea. You are not used to our food here, and if you have to remain in Calcutta, I fear that life here, as weakened as you are by illness, will ruin you. And then, there’s another thing: you would save a considerable sum of money, and after a year or two, you could go visit your family. As for us, your presence—I think there’s no need to tell you...”

He finished his speech with the same long, moist, frog-like smile. Maitreyi looked me straight in the eyes, without saying anything, without asking, just waiting. How I regret now that I did not note down immediately after their departure the very disturbing state of soul brought on by Narendra Sen’s words. I remember vaguely (and this vagueness is due not so much to the distance in time as to the countless

feelings and rebellions I have experienced since then, which have almost neutralized, have blurred into grayness and banality the preliminaries), I remember that two souls were crying out within me; one urged me toward a new life, one that, to my knowledge, no white man had ever truly known at its source, a life that Lucien’s visit had revealed to me as a marvel, which Maitreyi’s presence made more mysterious and fascinating than any legend, toward which I felt drawn and disarmed; and the other soul rebelled against this shadowy conspiracy of my chief to paralyze my freedom and involve me in an existence of rigors and mysteries, where my youthful pleasures would have to be sacrificed, drinks excluded, cinema visits rarefied. I felt both urges just as organically, just as much “my own.” But I could not delay my answer and thanks for too long.

“I am so much in your debt, Mr. Sen. But I am afraid I might disturb you,” I murmured, glancing at the girls, who savored my captivity with a certain spite (the engineer and Maitreyi were right by the bed, Harold and the girls near the window).

“Don’t talk nonsense,” laughed Narendra Sen. “There are so many free rooms downstairs, next to the library. And besides, your presence will be yet another ferment in the civilizing mission of my family, believe me.” (Did he say that ironically? I wondered.)

I remember that, once, speaking with the girls about the engineer and his beautiful daughter, I jokingly told them I needed their help, and here’s how: if we should meet— with the engineer, the girls, and myself all present—Geurtie should innocently ask me, “Allan, how is your sweetheart?” I would pretend to be embarrassed, try to make signs, but Geurtie would speak first: “Come on, don’t pretend you don’t know who I mean! I’m asking how Norinne is (or Isabel, or Lilian, whatever girl’s name comes to mind)?”
I had almost forgotten this joke when Geurtie turned to me and asked, blinking slyly:
“Allan, how is your sweetheart?!”
And without waiting for an answer (the Engineer remained with a frozen smile on his thick lips, Maitreyi lifted her head slightly to look at me), Geurtie continued, apparently in very good spirits:
“Come on, don’t pretend! You must ask her permission before moving in with Mr. Sen, isn’t that right?”
“Without a doubt,” agreed the engineer, trying to grin.
Maitreyi looked at her in genuine astonishment, then fixed her gaze on her father’s eyes.

“I’ve brought you something to read, Allan,” the engineer said quickly, to cut the scene short. “My daughter picked out Lafcadio Hearn’s Out of the East. But now it’s too late for her to read to you.”
“I won’t be able to read at all, babà,” said Maitreyi. “The English—”
mine is incomprehensible (she said the word with a clear care for pronunciation and accent).
"But Allan, you haven’t told me anything about your sweetheart," Geurtie insisted, dissatisfied that her intervention hadn’t met her expectations.
"Oh, leave me alone, I don’t have any sweetheart!" I shouted, furious both at my own stupidity and at hers.
"He’s lying," she said more quietly, almost confidentially, to the engineer. "He’s a great womanizer..."

A scene. The engineer looked at his daughter, bewildered and confused. Maitreyi gazed at everyone with her absent, inhuman eyes. Harold thought the battle had been won and was making signs to me from near the window. To me, everything seemed utterly ridiculous; and, as in any ridiculous situation I am incapable of making any decision, but wait for some miracle to intervene and put an end to it, I fixed my eyes on a single point and rubbed my forehead, as if to extract myself from the situation through a feigned headache.
"It’s time to let Allan rest," said Mr. Sen, shaking my hand.
"We’re leaving too," added Harold, saying goodbye to the engineer and to Maitreyi (whom, in fact, he didn’t know how to greet).
After they left, the girls came over to my bed, snorting, and began to congratulate me ironically.
"Hey, Allan, you’re lost, boy!" said Geurtie.
"But she’s not ugly," Clara remarked in passing, "only she seems dirty to me, like any Indian girl. What does she put in her hair?"

Suddenly, cowardice took hold of me. I began to gossip about both the engineer and Maitreyi, without believing a word I said, but amusedly listening to what the girls and Harold were saying. Any trace of fascination or respect vanished from my consciousness. Especially since I understood nothing of what had just happened.

"Let’s look over the list again," Geurtie remembered. "I think it would be good to invite the Huber brothers too. The elder, David, has a car... By the way, what do you think of my presence of mind with the 'sweetheart'? I saved you, Allan, you know..."
chapters.summary: Allan battles isolation, monsoon rains, and illness while working on railway construction in Assam, eventually falling seriously ill and being hospitalized.

chapters.title: Strange New Rituals
paragraphs: I woke up every morning with a new sense of wonder. My camp bed was right next to the door, and my first glances would discover a strange room, with a tall, barred window, walls painted green, a vast wicker armchair and two stools, beside a work table, a few Bengali lithographs, nailed to the right side of the bookcase. It took me a few minutes

to remind myself where I was, to make sense of those muffled noises that drifted in from outside, through the open window, or from the corridor, through the wide door, which I barred at night with a wooden beam. I would push aside the foamy canopy that hung above the bed and go out to wash in the courtyard, in a tin cabin that sheltered the cement tub, into which the servants poured, the evening before, several dozen buckets of water. This improvised shower in the middle of the courtyard was a new and invigorating ritual. I would scoop the water with a jug and fling it over my body, shivering all over, for it was winter and the courtyard was paved with stone. But I was proud of this courage of mine; the others brought with them a bucket of hot water, and when they found out that I always took a cold shower, they could not hide their astonishment and admiration. For several days, the whole house spoke of nothing but my morning bath, without hot water. I waited for Maitreyi to say something as well, whom I met very early, at tea, in a simple white sari, barefoot. And one day she spoke to me (her first unofficial words): — In your country it must be very cold. That is why you are white... She pronounced the word "white" with a certain envy and melancholy, her gaze lingering, almost involuntarily, for a few moments longer on my arm, as it rested on the table, half bare in my work shirt. I was both surprised and delighted to sense this envy, but in vain did I try to continue the conversation. Maitreyi finished her tea listening to us, to me and to the engineer, and agreed with me whenever I addressed her directly. We almost never spoke together. I would catch a glimpse of her passing in the corridor, hear her singing, knew of her that she spent a good part of the day shut away in her room or on the terrace, and it vexed me terribly, this being so close to me and yet so utterly foreign. It seemed to me, moreover, that I was being watched all the time, not out of any particular suspicion, but because they were all afraid I might feel uncomfortable in my new lodgings. When I was alone, laughing at all that seemed strange and incomprehensible to me, I would receive, every hour, cakes and fruit, tea with milk or coconuts, carefully peeled. A servant would bring them, bare-chested and hairy, the only one with whom I could exchange a few words in Hindusthani. I had noticed how greedily he looked at my things, as he sat cross-legged by the door and devoured me with his eyes, unable to bring himself to leave, asking me if the bed was good enough, if the cover protected me well from mosquitoes, if I liked raw milk, if I had brothers and sisters, if I missed my country, and I knew that in an upstairs room Mrs. Sen and the other women (whom I had not yet met) were waiting for him, and he would repeat to them, word for word, everything I had said. Maitreyi seemed to me proud and disdainful. Often, at table, I would catch a distant and slightly malicious smile on her lips. She always left earlier, to eat pan, and as she passed into a neighboring room, she would begin to laugh and talk

Bengali. She never spoke to me when there were several of us together; and if I happened to meet her alone, I did not dare to speak. I was afraid of breaking some rule of that unknown ceremonial of Indian good manners. That is why I often pretended not to see her and withdrew to my room. Sometimes I wondered what she thought of me, what kind of soul she hid beneath that ever-changing expression of her face (for there were days when she grew almost ugly, and days when she was so beautiful I could not tire of gazing at her). I wondered, above all, whether she was as stupid as all the other girls, or whether she was truly as simple as a primitive, as I imagined Indian women to be. And then, so as not to let myself be carried away by useless thoughts, I would shake the ash from my pipe and return to my reading. The engineer’s library occupied two rooms on the ground floor, and every day I brought new books to my table.

Once—only a few weeks had passed since my arrival in Bhowanipore—I met Maitreyi in the hallway. I greeted her almost automatically, joining my palms before my forehead, for I do not know why it seemed stupid to me to raise my colonial cap before an Indian woman (perhaps I thought I might offend her with a greeting foreign to her race; or perhaps I greeted her thus to win her trust).
“Who taught you our greeting?” she asked, smiling at me unexpectedly, almost as a friend.
“You did.” (I remembered the awkward scene of our meeting in the car.)

She looked at me for a moment, her face crumpling with a fear almost physical, her lip trembled, and she fled down the corridor without another word. I entered my room, embarrassed. I decided to tell the engineer all this, to confess how confused I was, to ask him to teach me something.
A few days later, when I had returned from the office and was lying sprawled on my bed, tired and thoughtless, Maitreyi knocked at my door.
“Please tell me when Father will be back,” she said, leaning shyly against the door.
I jumped up, bewildered (I confess I did not know how to behave with this girl), and told her all I knew, in more words than were necessary and without daring to invite her in, to sit down.

“Mother sent me to ask you,” she added timidly, yet fixing her gaze in my eyes. “You do not amuse yourself enough in our house, and that is why you spend hours alone here in your room. Mother says that if you work by the sun’s word, you will fall ill.”
“What else could I do?” I asked her.
“If you wish, you can talk with me… Or go for a walk.”
“I have no more friends,” I told her honestly, moving closer to the door, “I have no one else to visit. I walk enough when I return from work.”
“You amuse yourself much better there, on Wellesley Street,” she said
She smiled. Then, as if she had suddenly remembered something, she turned toward the veranda. “I’m going to see if any letters have arrived.”

I remained leaning against the door, waiting for her. She was humming a tuneless song, just as I heard her do in the evenings, before falling asleep, from her room. I knew that upstairs, with its windows opening onto the narrow lane that crossed the maidan, and a door leading to the balcony thickly draped in red-flowered wisteria, was her room. I would hear her singing and scolding her little sister, I would vaguely sense her when she stepped out onto the balcony, and from there would come her short, birdlike voice, startled, when she answered some call from below: “Giacè!”

She returned with a few letters and stopped in front of me, trying to tie the key to the corner of her sari. “I’m in charge of the mailbox,” she said proudly. “But no one writes to me,” she added, a little saddened, looking at the names on the envelopes. “Who should write to you?” “People. Why is there a post, if I never get letters from people I don’t see?”

I looked at her without understanding. She too stood there for a few moments, thinking fearfully of something, closing her eyes. “I thought I made a grammatical mistake,” she confessed, troubled. “There was no mistake.” “Then why were you looking at me like that?” “I didn’t quite understand. How could strangers write to you?” “They can’t, can they? Father says the same thing. Father says you’re very intelligent, is that true?”
I smiled foolishly and tried to make a joke, but she continued: “Would you like to see the terrace?”

I accepted with delight, for I longed to stretch out there, on the rooftop, to gaze at the sky at my leisure, at the clusters of coconut palms and the garden, to see from above this neighborhood of nothing but parks and villas, in which I had gotten lost almost every day at first. “Can I come as I am?”
She looked at me, surprised. I explained: “I’m wearing tennis shoes, no socks, no collar, no jacket.”

She kept looking at me. Then suddenly, with a strangely curious air, she asked: “How do people go up to the terrace in your country?” “We don’t have terraces.” “Not at all, not at all?” “Not at all.” “That must be sad. How do you see the sun, then?” “In the street, in the fields, as one sees the sun.”
She thought for a moment. “That’s why you’re white. You’re very beautiful. I wish I could be white too, but that’s not possible, is it?”
"I don't know, but I suspect not. Powder."
She gave me a look of disdain.
"Powder washes off. Did you use powder when you were little?"
"No, no one uses powder when they're little..."
She looked at me, delighted.
"If you use powder, you'll get sick. Tolstoy says so too."
Again I was surprised, and I must have been looking at her quite amused, for she suddenly became serious.

"You don't know Count Lew Tolstoy" (she pronounced 'Lew' in the English way: 'Liu'), "the great Russian writer? He writes beautifully; and he was rich, but in his old age he gave up everything and withdrew to the forest; as if he had been an Indian..."

She remembered the terrace and invited me. We both climbed the stairs, I a little intimidated, because I had to pass by the women's room, and she tried to speak loudly so her mother could hear—and, as she later confessed to me, so she would know that I was being 'entertained.' (My host had spent several sleepless nights worrying about how hard it would be for me without 'entertainment': without music, without friends, without a gramophone.) When I reached the top, I was suddenly seized by an immense joy. Never would I have guessed how different the world looks from the rooftop of a house, how peaceful the city appears, how green our neighborhood is. I passed every day by the trees in Bhowanipore, but never would I have believed there were so many. I leaned against the parapet and looked down into the courtyard. I remembered the day I had seen Maitreyi sprawled on the steps, laughing. It seemed to me that years had passed since then. Years had also passed since Maitreyi had come, timid, to my door to ask, "Please tell me when father will return..." I hadn't understood her; she seemed a child to me, a primitive. Her words attracted me, her incoherent thoughts delighted me, her naiveties, and for a long time afterward, I liked to think of myself as a complete man beside this barbarian.
"My sister doesn't speak English well," she said, coming with Chabù by the hand, "but she understands everything. She asks you to tell her a story... And I like stories too."

Once again I was left dry and inert before these girls, who stood hand in hand under a sky at the beginning of evening such as I had never seen. I had a strange sensation of dreaming, of the scenery changing in an instant. As if a curtain had been lifted from somewhere. Or perhaps I had changed; I don't know.
"I haven't read stories in a long time," I replied after a rather long pause. "And besides, there's something else: I don't know how to tell stories. It's a gift, storytelling. Not everyone has it."

They both grew sad, so spontaneously and sincerely that I felt guilty and began to wonder whether I might still remember something from all the stories I had read in childhood. None came to mind. I felt foolish, and the awareness of my own dullness paralyzed me. I quickly ran through them in my mind: Perrault, Grimm, Andersen, Lafcadio Hearn. It seemed to me...

they all seemed familiar. It seemed to me I would be ridiculous to tell them the story of Little Red Riding Hood, or the Sleeping Princess, or the enchanted treasure. I wished I knew a marvelous story, full of adventures and many complications, one that Maitreyi would also like. One that would, at last, be worthy of an intelligent and well-read young man; something original, impressive, symbolic. And yet, not a single such symbolic story came to my mind.
“Tell me a story with a tree,” said Chabù, looking at her sister to see if she had expressed herself correctly.
I thought I could improvise something and began:
“Once upon a time there was a tree, and at the root of the tree, a treasure was hidden. A knight...”
“What is a knight?” asked Chabù.
Her sister explained in Bengali, while I tried to guess what I would say next.

“One night, a knight dreamed that a fairy showed him the place of the treasure.” (What I had just said seemed so ridiculous to me that I was ashamed to look at the girls and bent down to tie my shoelaces.) “With the help of a magic mirror, the knight found the treasure.” (It was impossible for me to go on. I felt as if Maitreyi understood my embarrassment. But when I raised my eyes, I saw her listening very attentively and, apparently, very interested in what would come next.) “But imagine his surprise when, above the treasure, he discovered a living dragon, with eyes like embers and a mouth of fire.” (I blushed as I pronounced the last words.) “Then...”
“But the tree?” interrupted Chabù. “What did the tree say?”
“That was not an enchanted tree and did not have the gift of speech, so it said nothing.”
“But why does it have to be enchanted to be able to speak?” asked Chabù.
I felt a little confused and said to myself: pantheism.
“Well, that’s how the story goes; not all trees have souls, only the enchanted ones.”

Chabù spoke very passionately with Maitreyi, and for the first time I regretted that I did not understand their language at all. The sounds were sweet, Italianate, and the vowels prolonged, as if at any moment they might break into song.
“What is she saying?” I asked Maitreyi.
“She’s asking me if her tree has a soul. I told her that all trees have souls.”
“But does she have a tree of her own?”
“It’s not exactly a tree. It’s the shrub in the yard, the one with branches on the veranda railing. Chabù feeds it every day: cakes and pastries, and crumbs from everything she eats.”
I was happy and repeated to myself: pantheism, pantheism. I thought what rare documents I had before me.
“But Chabù, the tree doesn’t eat cakes.”
“But I do!” she replied, very surprised by my observation.

It seemed to me that this discovery should not be lost, and, under the pretext of going to smoke a pipe, I went down to my room. I locked the door with the bar and wrote in my journal: “First conversation with Maitreyi. Worth noting the primitiveness of her thinking. A child who has read too much. Today, on the terrace, an embarrassing incident with storytelling. I am incapable of telling stories; probably, my awkwardness with all that is innocent and naive. The revelation was Chabù, a pantheist soul. She makes no distinction between her feelings and those of objects; for example, she gives cakes to a tree because she eats cakes, though she knows the tree cannot eat. Very interesting.”

After jotting down those few lines in my journal, I stretched out on the bed and let myself drift into thought. I do not know what doubts crossed my mind then, for after a few minutes I got up, reopened the journal, and added: “Perhaps I am mistaken…”
In the evening I worked with the engineer in his study. Before we parted, he rested his hand on my shoulder and said:

“My wife is very fond of you, Allan. I want you to feel here as if you were at home. You may go freely through all the rooms. We are not orthodox and do not have a women’s quarters. If you need anything, please tell my wife or Maitreyi. I believe you are good friends enough…”
The events of the day tempted me to say “yes.” Yet I confessed to him my difficulties.
“Any Indian girl behaves like this with a stranger…”

He then began to tell me a story. Once, when he had to take tea at the Italian legation, the consul wished to help Maitreyi cross an inner courtyard—it was raining and they had only one umbrella—and took her arm. This gesture from a stranger so frightened Maitreyi that she broke into a run through the rain, dashed into the street, jumped into the car, and did not stop crying until they reached Bhowanipore, after she had thrown herself into her mother’s arms. And this had happened only a year before, when Maitreyi was nearly fifteen and had passed the matriculation exam for the University, preparing for her Bachelor of Arts. Another time, when a European family had invited them to their box at the opera and a young gentleman tried to take her hand in the darkness, Maitreyi whispered in his ear, loud enough for the neighbors to hear: “I’ll hit you with my slipper on the mouth!” Panic. The box, on its feet. Mrs. X (her name is too well known in Calcutta to mention here) intervened. Discussions, explanations, apologies.
“Did I make a grammatical mistake?” Maitreyi asked.

This made me laugh heartily, though I wondered whether this girl concealed innocence or a perfect refinement, cultivating humor and amusing herself at our expense. This thought came to me often whenever, later on, I listened to her speak or heard her laughter from the other rooms.
“Don’t you know that Maitreyi writes poetry?” the engineer asked me, very proudly.
“I was only imagining it,” I replied.

This discovery made her somewhat unsympathetic to me. All girls write poetry, and all child prodigies do as well. I understood that the engineer wanted to present his daughter as a sort of child prodigy, and this disgusted me. How many times before had he told me: “Maitreyi has genius!” and in those days I looked at her with a certain resentment. Perhaps that was why she was so conceited, I reflected. “She writes philosophical poems, which Tagore likes very much,” he added, watching me. “Really?” (I feigned as much indifference as possible.) As I was descending the stairs, I met Maitreyi coming out of the library. “I didn’t know you were a poet,” I said, in a tone I intended to be ironic. She blushed and leaned against the wall. This sickly sensibility of hers was beginning to annoy me. “In the end, there’s nothing wrong with writing poetry,” I added. “The only thing is to write it beautifully.” “How do you know they aren’t beautiful?” she asked, playing with the volume she had brought from the library. “I don’t doubt it. I was only wondering what you could possibly know of life to write philosophical poems.” She thought for a moment, then began to laugh. She laughed more and more sincerely, pressing her arms to her chest in a strange gesture of modesty. “Why are you laughing?” She stopped suddenly. “Shouldn’t I laugh?” “I don’t know. I don’t understand anything. In the end, everyone does what they like. I asked you why you were laughing; I thought you could tell me.” “Father says you are very intelligent.” (I made a gesture of impatience.) “That’s why I always ask you questions; I’m afraid of making mistakes, of offending you.” She had an expression that made me happy. “And why don’t you want to offend me?” “Because you are our guest. A guest is sent by God...” “And if the guest is a bad man?” I asked her, as one would ask a child, although her face had grown serious, almost frowning. “God calls him back,” she answered promptly. “Which God?” “His God.” “What, does every man have his own god?” I emphasized the last words. She looked at me, thought for a moment, closed her eyes, and opened them again with a new, moist, gentle gaze. “I was wrong, wasn’t I?” “How should I know?” I said, to hide my embarrassment. I am not a philosopher. “I am,” she said quickly, without blinking. “I like to think, to write verses, to dream.”
I said to myself: “She has no idea about philosophy!” and I smiled.
“I wish I were old,” she began suddenly, in a warm, melancholy voice that pierced me. “Old like Robi Thakkur.”
“Who is Robi Thakkur?” I asked, confused without understanding why.
“Tagore. I wish I were old like him. When you are old, you love more and suffer less.”

Then she blushed at her own words and made a gesture as if to flee. She stopped and composed herself, for she had looked at me and probably understood how embarrassed I was, standing there, leaning against the stairs, not knowing how I ought to behave with her.
“Mother was very upset: she read in a book that in Europe people have soup every evening. Here, you never had soup, that’s why you’ve lost weight. We never keep that broth, we give it to the birds.”
“I don’t like soup either,” I tried to reassure her.
“I wish you did!” she said, and her eyes sparkled for a moment.
“In the end, what difference would it have made?”
“For mother…”
She wanted to say something more, but stopped. I too was uneasy at this interruption and did not know what to make of that angry gleam in her eyes. “Perhaps I’ve offended her,” I thought to myself.
“Please forgive me if I have done something wrong,” I said gently. “I don’t know how to behave with Indians…”

As I spoke, she was already preparing to climb the stairs, but she stopped to listen to me. She looked at me again, this time so strangely (ah! how shall I ever suggest her glances, never the same, never), that I too stood wide-eyed, drinking her in.
“Why did you ask my forgiveness? Why do you want to make me suffer?”
“Not at all,” I stammered, confused. “It seemed to me that I had upset you and so…”
“How can a man ask a girl for forgiveness?”
“When you do something wrong, you must… Well, that’s the custom…”
“To a girl?”
“And to a child,” I boasted. “At least…”
“Do all Europeans do that?”
I hesitated.
“True Europeans, yes.”
She thought for a moment and closed her eyes, but only for a moment, for she burst out laughing and again crossed her arms over her chest, shyly.
“Perhaps they only ask forgiveness among themselves, whites among whites. Would anyone ask me for forgiveness?”
“Of course.”
“And Chabù?”
“Her too.”
“Chabù is darker than I am.”

“It’s not true.” Her eyes sparkled again. “Yes, it is. Mother and I are lighter-skinned than Chabù, and than Father. Didn’t you notice?” “So what? What does it matter?” “How, is that unimportant? Chabù will have a harder time getting married, because she’s darker, and she’ll need a bigger dowry…” As she said this, she blushed and grew flustered. In truth, I was rather embarrassed myself, for by now I knew much more about Indian marriage than I had during Lucien’s visit, and I understood how awkward it must be for an Indian girl to speak of such bargains. Fortunately, Mrs. Sen called for Maitreyi from upstairs, and she ran off happily, the book under her arm, calling: “Giacè!” I returned to my room, utterly delighted by all I had discovered that day. I washed up, for dinner was approaching (we ate very late, around ten or eleven, according to Bengali custom, and after dinner everyone went straight to bed), and I opened my journal to jot something down. I waited a few seconds, pen poised in the air, then closed the notebook, telling myself: “Nonsense…”
chapters.summary: In Chapter 4, the narrator navigates the unfamiliar rituals of his new Bengali household, sharing awkward yet meaningful encounters with Maitreyi.

chapters.title: Lessons in Bengali
paragraphs: I want to confess from the very beginning, and plainly, that never did I think of love in those first months spent in Maitreyi’s company. What tempted me more was her being, what was sealed and fascinating in her life. If I often thought of Maitreyi, if in my journal from those days there are recorded a number of her words and incidents, if, above all, she troubled and unsettled me, it was due to the strangeness and mystery in her eyes, in her answers, in her laughter. It is true that I felt drawn to this girl. I do not know what charm and what call even her footsteps held for me. But I would be lying if I did not say that my entire life in Bhowanipore—not just the girl—seemed miraculous and unreal to me. I had entered so quickly and without reserve into a house where everything seemed to me incomprehensible and dubious, that sometimes I would wake from this Indian dream, my thoughts returning to my own life, to our life, and I would feel like smiling. Something had changed, certainly. Almost nothing from my old world interested me anymore; I saw no one except the guests of the Sen family, and I had even begun to change my reading habits. Gradually, my interest in mathematical physics waned, I began to read novels and politics, then more and more history. But something else happened. One day, Maitreyi asked me if…

I wanted to learn Bengali; she would give me lessons. I had already bought, in the very first week, a simple manual for Bengali conversation, from which I read in secret, struggling to grasp the meaning of those words Maitreyi would shout when she was called or when she was upset. Thus, I learned that giacè means “I’m coming now”; and ki vishan!—which I heard in every conversation—a kind of exclamation and wonder, something like “how extraordinary!” My manual didn’t teach me much, and when Maitreyi suggested we take lessons together, I accepted. In exchange, I was to give her French lessons.

That very day, immediately after lunch, we sat down to work in my room. At first, I was shy about having the lessons in my room and suggested the library, but the engineer advised me to stay in my own quarters, where it was quieter. (The visible efforts Sen made to befriend me with Maitreyi, and the excessive tolerance of Mrs. Sen, embarrassed me more and more, made me suspicious, even malicious. Sometimes I even wondered if they hadn’t set their minds on marrying me to their daughter, although, logically, such a thing was impossible, and they would all have lost their caste and name if they had allowed such a marriage.)

We both sat at the table, I quite far from her, and Maitreyi began her lessons. I understood at once that I would only be able to learn Bengali on my own. She explained everything so beautifully and looked at me from so close that I listened to her without retaining anything. I only said, from time to time, “Yes!”...

I watched her and let myself be caught by my own gaze, by that fluid will which has nothing to do with the eyes, though it passes through them. I have never seen a more insurgent face, refusing, with greater stubbornness, to be captured by any plastic form. I still keep three photographs of Maitreyi, but when I take them out of the drawer and look at them, I do not recognize her in any of them.
After that, as we had agreed, came the French lesson. I began to explain the pronouns and the pronunciation of the alphabet, but Maitreyi interrupted me.
“How do you say: ‘I am a young girl’?”
I told her how to say it, and she repeated happily:
“Je suis jeune fille, je suis jeune fille!”
She pronounced it with astonishing precision. But my lesson was in vain, for she kept interrupting me to have me say in French a series of sentences and words without any purpose.
“Say something, translate it for me, and I’ll repeat it,” she found the best method.
So I began a series of very strange conversations, because Maitreyi kept asking if I was translating exactly what I had first said in French.
“I would say something and translate something else,” she confessed to me.

After a few lessons, she no longer looked at me, but played with her pencil on the notebook while I spoke to her. She wrote dozens of times: Robi Thakkur, Robi Thakkur. Then she signed her name, drew a flower, calligraphed
“Calcutta,” “I’m sorry,” “Why?” or she would improvise verses in Bengali. And I, when I could not look into her eyes, spoke as if I were facing a stranger. Yet I did not dare to ask her to stop.
“Why won’t you tell me that you don’t like me writing while you’re speaking?” she suddenly asked, looking me straight in the eyes, her voice carrying a femininity that surprised me.
I answered something in passing and continued, embarrassed, it’s true, but also a little irritated. She lowered her eyes to her notebook again and wrote: “It is late, too late, but it is not late.”
“What does that mean?” I asked her, unable to resist glancing at her notebook.

“I was just playing,” she replied, erasing what she had written, letter by letter, and drawing a flower above each word. An idea struck her: she would give French lessons to Chabù. I remember I burst into wild laughter, which cheered her as well.
“Do you think I couldn’t? I’d be a better teacher than you, even in French…”

She spoke with a playful seriousness, glancing at me furtively, in a way I had never seen before, and this made me start and rejoice, for she seemed much more feminine, more mine, thus. I understood her better when she played at being womanly than when she remained a barbarian without beginning or end, a “pantheist,” as I called her. I don’t know what I said to her in French, and I refused to translate it. This animated her; she blushed and begged me to repeat the sentence once more. She memorized it perfectly and took the English-French dictionary from the table, beginning to leaf through it for the words she thought were in that mysterious phrase I refused to translate. (In truth, it was nothing; I had told her some banal remark.) She did not find any of those words from my sentence, and this greatly displeased her.
“You don’t know how to play,” she told me.
“Nor do I want to play during the lesson,” I replied, trying to sound much drier than I really was.
This made her thoughtful, and she closed her eyes for a moment, as was her habit. Her eyelids were paler, with a very faint and charming violet shadow.
“I’m going to see if any letters have arrived,” she said, and quickly rose from the table.

I waited for her, a little bored, for I saw she was learning nothing, and I was afraid the engineer would think it was my fault she wasn’t studying. She returned very quickly, quite downcast, with two flowers plucked from the wisteria on the veranda. She sat down and asked me:
“Shall we resume the lesson? Je suis jeune fille…”
“All right, I see you know that, but what next?...”
“J’apprends le français…”
“That’s from last week.”
“That girl in the car—did you teach her French?” she asked me.
she asked suddenly, looking at me again, somewhat frightened.
I understood that she was thinking of Geurtie, whom she had seen sitting in my arms, and I blushed.
“It would have been very difficult,” I defended myself. “That girl was very stupid. Even if I had taught her for five years…”
“How old would you be in five years?” Maitreyi interrupted me.
“Thirty or thirty-one,” I replied, flattered.
“Not even half his age,” she whispered, more to herself.

She lowered her eyes to her notebook and began to write “Robi Thakkur,” both in Bengali characters and in European script. This irritated me for several reasons; first, because her passion for a seventy-year-old man intrigued me; second, because the conversation had drifted away from Geurtie (through whom, I believed for a moment, I might have made her a little jealous); and finally, because I suspected she was making fun of me and pretending to be more naive than she really was. I would not have tolerated, for anything in the world, being mocked by a sixteen-year-old girl for whom I felt no love, only intellectual delight. That is why, for a long time, I paid no attention to a series of very skillful and discreet gestures by which she might have tried to catch me in her net and make me look ridiculous. After all, I thought, I am the first young man whom Maitreyi has come to know more closely, I live next to her, I am white, and she would have so many reasons to like me. This thought gave me courage. I liked to nurture it, because I knew myself immune, I felt I could remain above the game, involved in her possible passion, yet free with respect to myself. The journal of those weeks proves this well enough. I watched Maitreyi’s game with great lucidity.
