For indeed, ever since her initial shyness had faded and she had begun to speak openly with me, Maitreyi gave me the impression that she was playing. She stood up, gathering her books, and took a flower in her hand.
“I chose the reddest ones,” she said, looking at the cluster of wisteria.
She was getting ready to leave.
“Take them both,” I called her attention, stuffing tobacco into my pipe to show her how little I cared for her flowers.

She turned back and took the other one as well, thanked me for the lesson, and left. But she quickly returned to the door, tossed a flower onto my table (the other she had already put in her hair), and ran off. I heard her climbing the stairs, four at a time. I didn’t know what to think: a declaration? I opened my journal and recorded the scene with a foolish comment.
The next day, at morning tea and before leaving for the office, Maitreyi asked me in passing what I had done with the flower.
“I pressed it,” I lied, to make her suspect some budding idyll in my soul.
“I lost mine on the stairs,” she confessed sadly.
I thought about this scene all day and imagined a series of utterly absurd events. When I returned from

At the office, I looked at myself in the mirror and, for the first time in my life, I wished to be more handsome. But I have a remnant of humor that never abandons me, and, catching sight of myself in the mirror, the way I was making faces like a cinema actor, I began to laugh heartily and threw myself on the bed, happy that I was, after all, a young man both intelligent and lucid.
Then Maitreyi entered, books in her arms.
“Shall we have our lesson today?” she asked me, very timidly.

We began with Bengali, in which I was making great progress, because I studied alone in the evenings and spoke all the time with Chabù only in Bengali. She gave me a translation exercise, and while I was writing, she asked:
“Where did you put the flower?”
“I pressed it.”
“Show it to me.”
I was rather embarrassed, for in truth, I had thrown the flower out the window.
“I can’t,” I pretended.
“You keep it in a very secret place?” she asked, extremely interested.

I kept silent, letting her believe so, and we continued the lesson. After she left, I went out onto the veranda, picked a flower that seemed to me most like the one I had received, and pressed it, wilting it a little with pipe ash, as if it had been picked the day before.
I met Maitreyi at dinner. Her eyes shone strangely, she kept wanting to laugh.
“Mother says we’re up to nonsense…”

I looked at her, frozen, and then fixed my gaze on Mrs. Sen, who was smiling very generously. The thought that even our sentimental jokes were being encouraged disgusted me. It seemed to me there was a general conspiracy at play, to make me fall in love with Maitreyi. That, I told myself, explained why we were always left alone, why the engineer always withdrew to his room to read detective novels, why none of the women upstairs ever came down to spy on us. I felt like running away from the house that very moment, for nothing repulses me more deeply than a matrimonial conspiracy. I lowered my eyes and ate in silence. There were only the three of us: Maitreyi, Mrs. Sen, and myself. The engineer was dining with friends.

Maitreyi talked the whole time during dinner. In fact, I had long noticed that she only fell silent when her father or a strange man was present. With us, the rest of the household, she was very talkative.
“You should take a walk in the evenings,” said Maitreyi. “Mother says you’ve lost weight again…”

I replied something indifferent and in a distant tone, which Mrs. Sen noticed at once. She began to ask Maitreyi something in Bengali, and Maitreyi answered sulkily, tapping her feet under the table. I pretended not to notice anything, but it hurt me to see Mrs. Sen saddened, for I loved her like a mother, though she seemed so young and shy.
When I left, Maitreyi followed me into the corridor. This had never happened before, for her to
approached my room at night.
“Please give me back the flower.”

I noticed at once that she was agitated. She had even made a very serious grammatical mistake. I didn’t dare invite her inside, but she entered directly, without waiting. I showed her the pressed flower and begged her to return it to me, for I still wanted to keep it (or something of the sort; in any case, I uttered some stupidity meant to sound mysterious and somewhat sentimental).
She took it, her hand trembling, looked at it for a moment, and then began to laugh with such delight that she had to lean against the door.
“That’s not my flower,” she said, very happily.
I must have turned a little pale, for she looked at me triumphantly.
“How can you say that?” I pretended to be indignant.
“The flower I gave you had, woven into it, a strand of my hair…”
She looked at me once more, apparently very amused, and ran off. I heard her, long past midnight, singing in her room.
chapters.summary: During their language lessons, Allan becomes increasingly captivated by Maitreyi's playful spirit and enigmatic gestures.

chapters.title: Essence of Beauty
paragraphs: One day, Mr. Sen knocked at my door. I stepped onto the threshold and saw him ready to leave, while Maitreyi was dressed in the most beautiful sari she owned, the color of raw coffee, with a brown shawl and golden slippers.
“My daughter is giving a lecture on the essence of beauty,” he told me.

I looked at them, surprised, and smiled with feigned wonder and delight. Maitreyi played indifferently with her shawl. She held a roll of manuscript in her hand and her hair was carefully arranged. Without a doubt, she had perfumed herself with “Keora atar,” for that dizzying fragrance reached me even there.
“I wish her all the success from my heart. Only, let her not be intimidated,” I added, looking at her.
“It’s not the first time she’s spoken,” Mr. Sen clarified, proudly. “It’s a pity you don’t understand Bengali well enough to listen to her yourself…”

I went back into my room, somewhat intimidated, with a vague disappointment in my soul. I resumed my reading with difficulty, for the image of Maitreyi lecturing on beauty obsessed me. Either this is a joke, or I am a fool, I told myself. I never would have believed that this girl could think about such responsible matters. I kept repeating, stupidly: the essence of beauty…
When I heard the car stopping in front of the house, about two hours later, I deliberately went out onto the veranda to meet them. Maitreyi seemed a little sad to me.
“How was it?” I asked, addressing them both.
“Not everyone understood her,” the engineer replied. “She was too
Deeply, she had spoken of things too intimate: about creation and emotion, about the internalization of beauty, and the audience could not always follow her.

For a moment, I thought Maitreyi would stop and no longer speak with me, but she passed before the door without looking at me and ran upstairs. I heard her closing the windows in her room. I could not settle myself, so I took my cap and set out to walk in the park. As I descended the steps of the veranda, I heard myself called from the balcony.
"Where are you going?"
Maitreyi was leaning over the balustrade, in a white sari, for the house, her hair loose on her shoulders and her arms bare. I told her I was going to walk in the park and to buy some tobacco.
"You can send a servant to buy tobacco."
"And what should I do?" I asked.
"If you wish, come upstairs and let us talk..."

This invitation disturbed me greatly, for although I could move freely throughout the house, I had never yet been in Maitreyi’s room. I arrived there in an instant. She awaited me at the door, with a tired face, pleading eyes, and lips strangely red.
(This detail struck me: I learned later that whenever she went out in the city, she painted her lips with pan, following the ceremonial of Bengali elegance.)
"Please leave your shoes here," she told me.

I remained in my socks, and this made me feel ridiculous, confusing me even more. She invited me to sit near the door that opened onto the balcony, on a cushion. The room seemed more like a cell. Though it was as large as mine, it had only a bed, a chair, and two cushions. On the balcony there was a small writing table, which probably also belonged to the room. No pictures on the walls, no wardrobe, no mirror.
"Chabù sleeps in the bed," she said, smiling.
"And you?"
"On this mat."

She showed it to me from under the bed; a mat as thin as cloth, made from bamboo straw. I was moved; it was as if I suddenly found myself before a saint. I almost adored her in that moment. But she gave a hidden laugh and whispered close to my ear:
"Many times I sleep on the balcony: the breeze blows and I hear the street below."
A street where no one passed after one o’clock at night, more a corner of the park than a street.
"I like to hear the street," she said, looking over the balustrade. "Who knows where that road down there leads?"
"To Clive Street," I said, thinking I was making a joke.
"And from Clive Street?"
"To the Ganges."
"And then?"
"To the sea."
She started and came close to me again.

“When I was very little, even smaller than Chabù, I used to go every summer to Puri, by the seaside. My grandfather had a hotel there. Waves like those at Puri, I don’t think exist in any other sea. As big as this house…”
I can imagine! Waves as big as the house, and beside them, Maitreyi lecturing on the essence of beauty. I couldn’t suppress a superior, lucid smile.
“Why are you laughing?” she asked me sadly.
“It seemed to me you were exaggerating.”
“And so you had to laugh? My grandfather exaggerated more than I did: he had eleven children…”
She turned again to the balcony. I thought I had offended her and muttered some sort of apology.
“It’s useless, now you don’t ask for forgiveness as you did the first time,” she said, smiling coldly. “You don’t even believe what you’re saying. Do you like Swinburne?”

I was used to her disordered way of speaking, and I answered that I liked Swinburne well enough. She brought me a worn volume from the little table and pointed out a passage in *Anactoria*, underlined in pencil. I read it aloud. After a few verses, she took the book from my hand.
“Perhaps you like another poet, for Swinburne does not please you enough.”

I was offended, and began to excuse myself, pretending that the entire romantic poetry was not worth a single poem by Valéry. She listened very attentively, looking me in the eyes, as she had during the first French lessons, and nodding her head in submissive agreement.
“Would you like a cup of tea?” she interrupted me just as I was criticizing the “philosophical poem” as such, calling it hybrid and ineffective.
I fell silent, a little bored by the interruption. She went out into the corridor and called down into the courtyard to the cook, telling him to prepare tea.
“I hope you won’t spill it on my trousers, as you did last year on Lucien’s!”

I thought she would laugh, but she suddenly froze in the middle of the room, exclaimed something in Bengali, and immediately ran off. From her footsteps, I guessed she had gone to the engineer’s office, which was next to the reception room. She returned with two books.
“I received them this morning from Paris, and I was so absorbed in that conference of mine that I forgot about them.”
They were two copies of Lucien’s *L’Inde avec les Anglais*, and, being sent by the publisher, they bore no dedication.
“One is yours,” said Maitreyi.
“Do you know what we’ll do? I’ll give you my copy with a dedication, and you, also with a dedication, will give me yours.”

She clapped her hands. She brought me ink and could hardly contain her impatience while I wrote: “To my friend Maitreyi Devi, from a student and teacher, in memory of etc.” That “etc.” intrigued her. On her copy she wrote only this:
“To my friend.”
— And if this book is stolen by someone? — What does it matter, he too may be my friend.

She sat down on the mat, her chin resting on her knees, and watched me for a moment as I drank my tea. Dusk had settled in. Down in the street, the lantern had been lit, and the shadow of the coconut tree had grown strangely large and blue. I wondered what the other souls in this house might be doing, why I never heard their voices or their footsteps, whether, perhaps, there was a conspiracy to always leave us alone, this time even in her own room, the only light the blue breath of the lantern.
— Today our friendship begins, doesn’t it? Maitreyi asked me very sweetly, taking my empty cup.
— Why today? We have been friends for some time, since we first began to speak seriously together.
She sat down again on the mat and told me that, if we were truly good friends, she would have confided her sadness to me. I begged her, and she remained silent, looking at me. I too fell silent.
— Robi Thakkur did not come to the conference today, she said.
This confession made me suffer. I would have liked to say something to wound her, to tell her she was mistaken if she considered me a friend, that she was ridiculous and in love.
— You love him, I insinuated maliciously.
I was preparing to begin something that would upset her. But she suddenly turned her face away from me and asked abruptly:
— Do you like sitting in the dark with girls?
— I never have, I replied at random.
— I would like to be alone, she said after a pause, exhausted, finished, going to lie down on the mat in the balcony.
I left, struggled to put on my shoes in the darkness, and tiptoed down the stairs, with a strange sadness and fury in my soul. I was very moved to see lamps lit everywhere.
From the journal of that month:

“She does not have a regular beauty, but one beyond all canons, expressive to the point of rebellion, enchanting in the magical sense of the word. I admit I could not get her out of my mind all night. And now, instead of working, I think of her, a pale image in a dark blue silk sari with golden flowers. And her hair… The Persians were right, in their poems, to liken it to serpents. What will be, I do not know. I will probably forget…”
“When will I find peace, my emulator, my God, my friend?”

“Chabù has written a story, and today Maitreyi is translating it for me on the terrace, laughing. It could be summarized thus: ‘A king had a son named Phul. One day, he rode his horse into a forest…’”

the sea. Immediately, everything in the forest turned into flowers; only the prince and his horse remained the same. Returning to the palace, the son recounted the event to the king, but the latter did not believe him and reproached him for telling lies. He summoned the royal pandit and ordered him to read the prince parables and advice about lying. Yet, since the prince still refused to admit, the king gathered the entire army and went into the forest. At once, they all turned into flowers. A day passed. Then came Phul, the king’s son, bringing with him the books containing parables and advice about lying. He took the books and began to scatter the pages to the wind. And as the pages were scattered, so the king’s soldiers and the king himself came back to life...”

“I observe a few unsavory traits in the engineer’s character. He is full of himself, it is unbelievable how superior he considers himself. Last night, on the terrace, he discreetly asked me for details about the courtesans of Paris. He would like to leave for a few months in France, to take care of his blood pressure. He suffers, from time to time, from a kind of ‘mouches volantes’ because of his blood.”

“The engineer’s cousin, Mantu, has now come from Delhi, where he was a secondary school teacher, to take up a post as lecturer at the Government Commercial School. He seems to be about thirty years old, is short and thin, and lives in a room next to mine. We became friends very quickly. He confides that he has come to get married. He does not want to, but Mr. Sen wants him to. He senses some kind of misfortune and is afraid. He is a good boy, who speaks English with his eyes closed. He laughs a lot.”

“Mantu’s wedding ceremony, which began four days ago, ended last night. There were feasts both at the bride’s house (dark-skinned, ordinary, but very likeable), and at the engineer’s house. I note Sen’s attitude in this marriage; in fact, he arranged everything and complains to me that Mantu ‘suggests’ too much and rushes things. Mantu respects him so much that he would have given him even the bride’s virginity, as is the custom in certain parts of India, for the disciple to grant the first night to his guru (Mantu always tells me that the engineer is not only his cousin, but also his guru). I have been everywhere, I have seen all the details, always at the forefront, in an Indian silk costume (I confess it suits me very well, and my sincere, spontaneous appearance, forcing myself to speak Bengali all the time, has made me very popular). I admit that Indian ‘society’ delights me, Indian friends are gems. Sometimes I am strangely in love, in the divine sense of the word (as in India), considering every woman a ‘mother.’ Never have I felt a more devoted, purer, and more soothing filial love than for Mrs. Sen, whom—as is the custom

here—everyone calls her “mother.” When I glimpse blue saris on the street (like Mrs. Sen’s), even without seeing the women’s faces, I feel the same emotion. I feel that I am a “son,” that nowhere else will I find a more selfless, purer, and higher maternal passion than in India.

I liked to imagine myself married to Maitreyi. I cannot lie: I was happy. I dreamed of her the whole time Mantu’s wedding lasted; fiancée, lover. But I never lost my head. (Note: That is, I wanted to convince myself she was not so beautiful, I criticized her hips as too wide for her too slender waist, I invented all sorts of physical flaws, believing that this way I would distance myself from her. In reality, as often happens, it was precisely these flaws that drew me closer to her.)

I do not know whether all the insinuations the family friends make are mere jokes or whether they come from a sure source, seriously oriented toward my marriage by the engineer. Once, at the table, I understood that Mrs. Sen would also wish for the same thing. I cannot say it is a conspiracy (note: although for a long time I believed so), because they consider marriage a happiness and a duty, they love me much and sincerely, and then Maitreyi is so well known in the Bengali elite that she could easily find a husband superior to me.

I wonder: what would I become, married to Maitreyi? Is it possible that I might lose my lucidity so much that, caught in the trap, I would accept? Without a doubt, she is the most talented and enigmatic girl I have ever known, but I simply cannot be married. What would become of my freedom? I imagine myself as Maitreyi’s husband; I would be too happy. Where would be my journeys to places I can hardly believe exist, and the books I buy in every city only to sell them in the next?

But until then, how happy I feel. And how much I have seen. Last night—the first nox—in the chamber flooded with flowers, the girls singing on the balcony, Maitreyi reciting her poem, written especially for this ceremony.

An observation I have repeated to the point of exhaustion in recent days: every time I understand that they are speaking of a possible marriage between me and Maitreyi, or every time I suspect it, a sudden and violent emotion sweeps through me. The basis is sexual: excessive nervousness, prolonged abstinence, a purely genital restlessness, inner unease, and dread of fate. I am more and more afraid, but the dangerous situation fascinates me and I cannot bring myself to explain, to say plainly that I will not marry. Nor can I run away. It would be stupid to flee. I am irredeemably a moral man, although my demon tempts me to the contrary. (Note: The diary is almost always a poor psychologist, as this story will confirm. That is why I extract these notes; to realize once more how absurdly I floated in imagination.)

Mantu confessed today to the women what I had told him: that I will not marry and that I will never marry. Maitreyi is now angry and contemptuous; she no longer comes to lessons, she no longer seeks me out when I return from work so that we might talk. Mrs. Sen no longer shows me the same affection. I felt ill at ease because of this change, though I had wished for it and feared that earlier, interested affection. Maitreyi laughed tremendously this evening, listening to Khokha’s jokes. (Note: A young man, a poor relative of the engineer, who had drifted into Bhowanipore on the occasion of Mantu’s wedding and who slept in the corridor.) I was writing in my room. I had a painful fit of jealousy, of which I am ashamed. (Note: In truth, I was not very much in love at that time. Still, I was jealous of anyone who could make Maitreyi laugh.)

Maitreyi was indifferent to me as long as I knew I was sought after with affection by the whole family; I was afraid when I suspected a matrimonial trap; but as soon as my decision to remain a bachelor became known and Maitreyi changed completely towards me, she began to be dear to me (note: this is not true), and I suffer a little from jealousy, from loneliness, from my fate. Much has changed; I eat only with the engineer and Mantu, the women eat after us. There is no longer any joy at our meals without Maitreyi. I would very much like to leave on some inspection through the south of Bengal and, upon returning, to find some pretext and move elsewhere. The experience is beginning to last too long.

For two days it has been dark and raining. Today, true torrents. I went out onto the veranda to see the flooded streets. I met Maitreyi, splendidly dressed (velvet maroon with black silk), also watching. (I knew she had written poems about the rain, perhaps even today, upstairs in her room.) We spoke little and coldly. She looked at me indifferent, distracted. Would I ever have guessed that there was in her so much feminine experience and that she could intuit so precisely all the attitudes required by the new situation? I feel a stranger in this house, where I have known the most sincere and most Indian affection. Suddenly, everything has frozen around me, and my spontaneity has vanished. At table I am sullen and silent, in my room I feel almost ill. It is true, at times I have fits of joy, panic, and I dance humming (something that happens to me so very rarely).
Since yesterday, my relations with Maitreyi and the family have been restored to

the old theme of intense affection. Perhaps because I explained to the engineer—as we were returning by car from the office—Mantu’s indiscretion; who did not quite understand my conception of marriage, I add. (Note. It seems to me that the coldness, which the journal attributed to the paralysis of marriage plans with Maitreyi, was in fact due to a misunderstanding; Mantu had said that I made a mockery of marriage, and since Indians can conceive of no duty more sacred than this, naturally they reacted, perhaps involuntarily.)

With Maitreyi I laughed a great deal yesterday; today we talked at length in the library, we read Shakuntala together, on the carpet, for her private tutor had come and I had asked to be allowed to attend the lesson as well. At night, on the terrace, she recited endlessly from Tagore’s Mahuya. Afterwards she withdrew without our noticing, for poetry is her final word, and, having spoken it beautifully, she grows somber.
Do I love her?
chapters.summary: Maitreyi delivers a lecture on beauty, leaving the narrator both fascinated and unsettled as their friendship deepens through intimate conversations, shared poetry.

chapters.title: Passion and Illusion
paragraphs: From the journal of the following month: “The two of us, alone, discussing virility; Walt Whitman, Papini, and the others. She has read little, but listens to me. I know she likes me. She tells me so. She confesses that she would give herself as in a poem by Tagore, on the beach, at the onset of a storm. Literature.”

“Passion grows, a delicious and natural mixture of idyll, sexuality, friendship, devotion. When I sit beside her on the carpet, reading together, if she touches me, I am aroused and become wildly agitated. I know she is agitated too. (Note. Not true. Maitreyi never felt passion at that time.) We say much to each other through literature. Sometimes we both sense that we desire each other. (Note. Inaccurate; Maitreyi was captivated only by the game, by the voluptuousness of illusion, not by temptation. She could not then imagine what passion might mean.)”

“The first evening and night (until eleven) spent alone with Maitreyi, translating Tagore’s Vallaka and talking. The engineer, returning from a dinner in the city, surprised us in her room, chatting. I, calm, continued to speak. Maitreyi became flustered, grabbed the volume of poems and opened it; and when Mr. Sen entered the room, she said: — We are learning Bengali... So, she lies too?! (Note. This journal is exasperating.

Why must I suffer so much just to understand a single person? For I confess, I understood nothing of Maitreyi at the time, though I believed I loved her and that I was loved in return. She did not lie, she merely forgot. She had forgotten that I had come to her for Vallaka, and when the engineer entered, she remembered, naturally. Had it been someone else, she would have continued the conversation, but in front of her father she never spoke, and so she returned to her book.

Today I brought her lotuses, so many that, as she took them in her arms and thanked me, her face was entirely hidden. I am certain that Maitreyi loves me. (Note. How long it took me to understand!) She writes poems for me and recites verses to me all day long. I do not love her. I admire her immensely and she excites me: everything, her flesh as much as her soul. I have discovered something new in her. I was talking with Lilu and told her that I would repeat certain things, things I had heard from her, to her husband.
“And what could he do to me?” Lilu asked insinuatingly.
“I don’t know, I’m not versed in marital quarrels,” I replied.
“He will punish her, in one way or another,” Maitreyi emphasized, and repeated the words, laughing, when we were alone.

So, she knows as well?... Besides, she confessed to me that she would like to fall into madness, intoxicated by love or by passion. I discover sincerities inaccessible to others, which I would never have suspected in the early days of our friendship. (Note. The truth was that Maitreyi was simply playing, and even after Lilu had confided to her what conjugal love meant, she understood nothing and repeated certain things only because they delighted her.)

Our escapade—Maitreyi, Lilu, Mantu, and I—to a neighborhood cinema, where an Indian film starring Himansural Ray was showing. How much we spoke, so close together, and how much we laughed. But as we were leaving, she had a fit and lost consciousness. I could not explain it: the darkness, the subject of the film, or a sexual spasm brought on by my nearness? I know she is unimaginably sensual, though pure as a saint. In fact, this is the miracle of the Indian woman (confirmed by the confessions of my Bengali friends): a virgin who becomes the perfect lover on the very first night.

Maitreyi hints at an idyll with a superb young man, a Bengali studying in England. So, she follows the itinerary of all sentimental mediocrities... (Note. She only wished to confess to me her decision to renounce everything that had happened before me.)
Again I bring flowers. She is upset that I gave some to the other girls as well,
and Mrs. Sen. I think Mantu has noticed our familiarity, for he promptly intervenes whenever we are alone, and although Maitreyi tells him it is a private talk, he still remains.

I went to the cinema with the engineer, who spoke to me sadly about the postponement of his journey to France. Was it just my impression, or did he insinuate a possible union between me and Maitreyi? When I return, I ask myself if, indeed, she is dear to me, although the whole time, in the car, I was intoxicated by the image of our nuptial bed.

I continue a strategy that amuses me. I avoid meeting Maitreyi, pretending that I am afraid, that I am madly in love, and so on. She spoke to me this morning, almost forcing me to receive her in my room. This intimacy with an Indian girl is something extraordinary. Even I do not know how it will end. It disturbs me, it fascinates me, but I am not in love. I am only amused.

An unexpected volte-face from Maitreyi. I had gone too far, simulating a childlike devotion (I believed this was the path to the heart of any Indian woman). But Maitreyi is not only an Indian maiden, but also an original soul, with a strange will. She is disgusted by devotion, by the adoration of men, she tells me (including me among her other platonic admirers). It is common, banal, childish. She hates or despises admirers. She dreams of an exceptional man, above feelings and sentimentality. My attitude irritates her.

Good! If what she says is true, I will change my tactics. Already the sensual charm that overwhelmed me during our conversations disappeared as soon as she confessed these things. Now I am much freer, more liberated. I burn with impatience to meet her again in my room, to see how she will react. I will show Maitreyi that I do not care for her love. I know that she loves me. She cannot hide it. I know she is bound to me. And if we were to remain alone for twenty-four hours, she would give herself to me without hesitation.
But why does she insult me, for God's sake? Why does she tell me that common love repulses her? Is there anything better?

No woman has ever disturbed me so much. My sensual suffering is a curse, in this arid month, with so much work on my mind. Could it be, perhaps, the mystery of her body? I doubt it; any conversation that insinuates the danger, that is, my union with Maitreyi, which is being plotted, disturbs me. I know I am in this danger. I have so many daily proofs. Mrs. Sen, especially, overwhelms me with her maternal sympathy. The engineer calls me his "child." (Note. Of course, I understood nothing at the time!)

In the evening, at dinner, Mrs. Sen complains that I still call her “madam” instead of “mother,” as is the custom in India. She possesses a saintly and communicative gentleness, a disarming innocence. I love her.
There are insinuating remarks. Mantu insists that I call him “uncle,” and Lilu “auntie,” though she is only seventeen. I am amused.

The problem of Maitreyi. Over a trifle we quarreled (in fact, this happens to us twice a day), and she tried all sorts of sentimental and erotic gestures to make peace. I worked sullenly the whole time, shut away in my room. Yet I was happy, for I hoped that our overly familiar friendship and our unspoken passion would be spoiled. I was afraid I had gone too far, and clung to any pretext to draw back. But no; she apologized, and the game began anew. I feel I shall not be able to restrain myself much longer.

This afternoon, I almost kissed her, the two of us alone in the room. I struggled not to embrace her, so excited was she, and so maddened was I. I contented myself with squeezing and biting her arm. I would go no further. I am afraid, I am terrified of myself. (Note: Maitreyi was not, for a moment, excited, as I had thought. She was only disturbed by my attitude. She had wanted to play, while I had gone much further.)
Maitreyi is a rare girl; but as a wife, will she not be just as mediocre as any other?

She came later, toward evening, in that admirable scarlet shawl, which leaves her almost naked and reveals her dusky breasts in a pallor that is fatally disturbing. I know she put on this obscene and enchanting costume for me; the engineer is absent, otherwise she would not have dared to wear it. (Note: In fact, it was only a Rajputana costume, which is worn directly on the body, not over a bodice, as is customary in Bengal.)

Maitreyi comes constantly into my room, comes for no reason at all, and always insinuates or provokes. Passion makes her beautiful. Sensual, carnal, she is beyond measure tempting. I make efforts to see her as hideous, fat, foul-smelling, so that I might restrain myself. It is a kind of “meditation through contrary images” that I attempt. The truth is that my nerves are needlessly consumed, and, in fact, I still understand nothing clearly. What do they want from me?

In the morning, a quarrel with Maitreyi. She feels offended over every trifle and threatens not to speak to me for a week. Today I told her I did not care, whatever she might do. This calmed me and helped me to work. Lilu came to intervene, telling me that “the poetess is unspeakably depressed.” I replied that I was not upset, but if this would...

amuses me... How banal all women are, I understood. The same melody, the same in Europe or in Asia, with intelligent women, stupid, perverse or virgins. In the evening I went to the cinema alone, having a wonderful time. At dinner, Maitreyi sat next to me, in a superb sari, a hundred years old. She had been crying, silent; she barely ate.

"Mother" understood everything. She thanked me for speaking with her. After dinner we had a little "explanation." Maitreyi tells me that I did not understand her when I thought she despised love, sympathy...

The struggle lasted a quarter of an hour. I crushed her hands. She was enchanting as she struggled; her face contorted, she wept, she prayed in her mind to Tagore. She tried to free her hands, caught at the wrists in my fist; for that was the struggle. I was calm, detached from physical pain and pride. At last, she had to admit it, she was defeated. This gave her a joy mixed with bitter sensuality. I know she was happy that I had conquered her. But she suffered because her spiritual master, her guru, had not helped her. Etc. When we went toward her room, the two of us, alone, she whispered to me: — You have broken my hands! I took them without thinking and, caressing them, I kissed them. This is extraordinary for India. If anyone knew, they would kill her! (Note. I exaggerate.) After the meal, without speaking to me, she threw a flower into my room...

Cinema with Maitreyi and the others. She sat next to me, of course. In the darkness she told me that important things needed to be clarified. Then, when she found out that I was playing, that I cared little for her "feelings," that I hated her (I lied), she lost her queenly calm (Cleopatra?) and began to cry. I was not moved. She cried a second time, at the exit, violently. I said to her:

"Maitreyi!" and then fell into an awkward silence. That same evening she cried again in my room, nervously, covering her face with her shawl. Always without any explanation. But she had the strength to laugh when the others came in.

Unexpected "explanations" with Maitreyi. She was stronger today. She cried only once. I showed myself nervous, desperate, hinting at an urgent departure. The ending was violent; I begged her to leave my room. I threw myself on the bed, feigning a crisis greater than my mere confusion. I was ridiculous. I promised Maitreyi that we would become "friends" again. How stupid! Through an idiotic tactic I "confessed" a hundred...

lies that make me feel banal to the point of nausea, I made “scenes” etc., etc... and she was admirably calm. She told me that she, too, bears some guilt for our sentimental “jokes.” For this, she suffers, because she has fallen in my esteem. But things must end here; we should be friends again.
Night.

Oh! But things are not so simple. I love her deeply, fiercely, and I am afraid of Maitreyi. She told me she suffers from the harm she has done me. I am afraid, but I am glad. My soul is not yet dried up by new and unresolved thoughts. I can still be a passionate lover, though not sentimental. But, in fact, what do I care whether I am sentimental or not?

Intoxication? Am I falling victim to my own farce? Today, from morning till late at night, I was “happy,” by which I mean, with this dull word, an irrational flood of major, vital feelings, restoring my appetite for existence and play. I was ready to say to Maitreyi: “Will you be my wife?” and I am ready even now. I would be so happy to be her husband! So purified, so serene...

In the afternoon, a conversation with Maitreyi about marriage. I think about it a lot and imagine myself as her husband, head of the family, and an ethical miracle. Satisfaction, tranquility. In the evening she tells me she is desperate because Tagore has not written to her. The poet is for her more than a guru; he is a friend, confidant, fiancé, god, perhaps lover. She confides that no one suspects their connection. An Indian love. Am I jealous? I have decided to tell her that our love is useless; from now on, she knows everything, whether I confessed it, suggested it, or she understood on her own (note: yet, she knew nothing, understood nothing precisely), because I will not accept that my wife should have loved another before me. She noticed my displeasure, somewhat severe and emphatic. After dinner, we did not speak. She sent word through Khokha, telling me I had offended her. I did not reply. Sometimes, this whole affair irritates me, other times it amuses me. In general, I am intoxicated by love, I dream of marriage and children. It makes me waste a lot of time. Mental concentration is difficult. But I will not give up on love.
The night was shaken by an earthquake. I had a fever the whole time. This morning, when I met Maitreyi, I gave her an expensive book.

A day of extraordinary emotion, which I find impossible to record here. In short, Maitreyi scolded me, asking where I intended to go with all this, for my persistence was compromising her, and that Mantu and Khokha had begun to suspect something, and so on. She wept with spasms. I did not utter a word. I was saddened; I had offended her. But I was also posing, immensely.

Unfortunately, Khokha was on the veranda, next to my room, and heard everything. When Maitreyi found this out, she began to cry even more desperately. She wrote to me on the edge of an envelope that she wished she could die. For an Indian girl, what Khokha now knows is dishonor.
Yet, when she calmed down, she tidied up my room and arranged the flowers on my table. I did not speak.
Maitreyi has begun to write a book of poems about “beautiful illusions and mirages.”

Today, as I was telling her about the debaucheries of girls in Europe, she asked me if I was pure, and just the thought that I might not be terrified her so much that she began to cry. This violent, mystical thirst for purity moved me deeply.

In the evening, as we came again to speak of her marriage—with a stranger, a young Bengali who, as Maitreyi herself admits, will surely not make her happy—I confessed to her that my great sin is to have been born white (I believe little in this confession), that if I had been Indian, I would have had other chances, and so on. This puzzled her again, and I asked her the great question: why can’t we be married? Why is our union not permitted? She looked at me, petrified, and searched with her eyes in all directions, to see if anyone had overheard me.

She began to say that it is so decreed by fate or by God (I had asked her whether God had decreed this or prejudice, but she replied that God manifests His will through prejudice), that perhaps my love is only a fleeting illusion, and so on. The fact is that this love—which at first I had considered impossible, minor, fanciful—and Maitreyi’s attitude, whom I had for so long believed to be in love with me—while in truth she is in love with no one—now possess me and carry me far away; into a part of my soul unknown until now, into a corner of thought where I feel happy and splendid. I do not know how to express all these revealed feelings. I am seriously thinking of union...
From that day on, I saw her only with difficulty. She remained all the time in her room, writing and singing. I sent her a few innocent notes
through Lilu, to which she did not reply. I believed a great many things the first night, then fewer, and finally I believed nothing at all. I noticed that I could live very well without Maitreyi.
chapters.summary: In Chapter 7, the narrator navigates his passionate, confusing relationship with Maitreyi, exploring their emotional games, cultural barriers, and misunderstandings.

chapters.title: Rumors and Doubt
paragraphs: Not long after that, one afternoon, I met Harold. He seemed colder, more spiteful.
"Is it true that you’re marrying the engineer’s daughter?" he asked me, among other things.

I blushed and began to make fun, as I always do when I’m embarrassed, especially if I have to defend someone dear to me. Harold quickly brushed aside my jokes and told me he had heard this at the office, where he had once looked for me to invite me to a picnic. He had also learned then that I wanted to renounce my own faith and convert to Hinduism. And although he himself is a great sinner and only goes to church for Iris, this news horrified him enough. He told me that Sen was a monster, that I had been bewitched, that I should give five rupees to the "Sisters of the Poor" so they would pray for me.
"How are the girls?" I asked.

"They miss you," he confessed. "You’re probably saving a lot there, in Bhowanipore," he began again after a moment. "You don’t pay for house, you don’t pay for food, and you never go out in the city. What do you do all day?"
"I’m learning Bengali so I can take my Provincial-Manager exam," I lied. "And besides, it’s a new world, I don’t even know how the time passes..."
He asked to borrow five rupees, so he could go that evening to the Y.M.C.A. ball.
"Doesn’t it tempt you?" he probed.

In truth, it did not tempt me. I thought without melancholy of those years of waste and error spent on Wellesley Street, on Ripon Street. I looked at Harold, and his lanky body, his dark face with beautiful, shadowed eyes, evoked nothing for me. A stranger, this comrade of mine, with whom I had chased after so many girls and wasted so many nights. The life I had begun seemed so sacred to me that I did not even dare to confide it to him. He promised to visit me one day and carefully wrote down my address. ("For some possible large loan," I thought.)

At home I found everyone in the drawing room, having tea. Mantu was there, and his wife, Lilu, and Khokha, and Khokha’s sisters (two of those shadow-women whom I hardly ever saw). I told them all, with great sincerity, about my meeting with Harold and my disgust for the life led by the Europeans and Eurasians in this city, a life I myself had led for so long.

This confession of mine delighted them. The women drank me in with their eyes and kept praising me in their incomprehensible argot, while Mantu squeezed my hands and closed his eyes, as was his habit. Only the engineer, after warning me about my overzealous enthusiasm, withdrew to read his indispensable detective novel.

I went upstairs to the terrace with Maitreyi, Khokha, and Lilu. We waited for evening, stretched out on carpets, speaking rarely and each seeking the most comfortable position, with a pillow under our heads. I had come in sandals and my feet dangled in the air, trying to rest decently and somewhat by chance against the parapet. In these last months, I had learned an entire ceremonial of the feet; I knew, for example, that whenever I accidentally touched someone with my foot, I had to bend down and touch their foot with my right hand; that I must never, not even in jest, make the gesture of kicking someone, and many other such things. That is why I hesitated before resting comfortably against the parapet.
Then I heard Lilu whispering something to Maitreyi.
“She says you have a very beautiful foot, a white, alabaster foot,” Maitreyi explained, unable to hide a look of incomprehensible envy and annoyance.

I blushed, both with pleasure (for, being ugly, any praise of my physical being delighted me beyond measure) and with shyness; I did not know how to interpret Maitreyi’s glances. She fixed her gaze on my feet with a scornful, spiteful, humiliated smile. I began to speak nonsense to break the silence, saying that it did not matter at all, since one never sees the feet, at least among us, the whites.

“With us it’s different,” Maitreyi interrupted, softened. “Among us, friends show their affection by touching each other’s bare feet. Whenever I talk with my friends, I squeeze their foot. Like this…”

Blushing, she slipped her foot out of her sari and brought it close to Lilu. Then something strange happened. I had the impression I was witnessing a love scene of the most intimate kind. Lilu squeezed the lower part of Maitreyi’s calf between her ankles, shivering and smiling as if released from a kiss. Those lazy caresses along the calf, with fingers clenched, heel bent, and then the squeeze, in which the flesh was pressed warm and trembling, were true caresses. I suffered terribly, both from jealousy and from revolt, against this absurd love between the flesh of two women. Maitreyi abruptly withdrew her foot from the embrace and passed it over Khokha’s instep. I felt like biting my lips, like fleeing, for I had suddenly seen how Khokha’s black and dirty foot, cracked from heat and pavements, received the warm approach, as an offering, of Maitreyi’s body. Khokha wore the smile of a caressed dog, and I regretted that I could not see Maitreyi’s eyes, to guess in them the voluptuousness betrayed by her calf in the nearness of the boy’s flesh.
I thought then that Maitreyi’s laughter—which that ugly clown provoked—betrayed the same abandonment, the same possession.

I wondered, later on, whether there might not exist other kinds of possession than those we know—more refined and more ineffable ones, obtained furtively, with a touch or a jest, when a woman surrenders herself completely to the warmth or spirit of another, and is taken wholly, in a way that we ourselves can never take her, not even in the most final and mad hours of love. For a long time after that, I was jealous not of the handsome young men, the poets and musicians who gathered in the Sen household and with whom Maitreyi spoke, gazing at them intently, smiling at them, loving their books, but of anyone who could make her laugh until she wept—of Khokha and Mantu, especially the latter, who, being her uncle, could allow himself to squeeze her arm while speaking to her, or pat her on the shoulder and shake her by the hair.

These gestures of innocent abandon tormented me more than any rival could. It seemed to me that Maitreyi was unaware of the secret violation committed upon her by a foreign flesh or spirit. And, to confess everything, it was above all the spiritual possessions that made me suffer: a young poet, Acintya, whom Maitreyi had seen only once and spoke to only by telephone, when he sent poems for the magazine Prabuddha Bharatta; a mathematician who came very rarely and about whom Maitreyi had spoken to me with enthusiasm, confessing that she liked tall men; and above all, her guru, Robi Thakkur. With great skill I tried to insinuate that she abandoned herself too much, whether in spirit or in flesh. But she looked at me with such innocence, such astonishment and sincerity, that I gave up. Besides, all this happened after the events I have just recounted, at a time when I had received enough proof that I had nothing to fear from anyone.

…I remained pensive and disgusted, secretly biting my lips and gazing at the first stars in a sky still pale. The conversation continued in a colloquial Bengali, of which I understood very little; in any case, I did not even try to understand, and I started only at Maitreyi’s laughter, which Khokha kept alive with endless puns and grimaces. She must have noticed my shyness, for she asked me in English whether I was too tired and if I would like to amuse myself by helping her, in my free hours, to finish the catalog of Mr. Sen’s library. This, she said, would be a pleasant recreation for me after my office work, and we could spend more time talking. (For, in truth, in the last few days I had hardly seen Maitreyi at all.) I knew nothing about the catalog and learned that Mr. Sen, who had by now collected some four thousand volumes—some inherited, some purchased—intended to have the library catalog printed in a deluxe brochure, so that it could be donated, in case of his death, to a local college. All this seemed rather ridiculous to me, but I accepted.
“Father did not dare to ask you to help me,” Maitreyi confessed. “He was afraid you would lose too much time. I am small, I have nothing to do all day, and I like to copy out the book titles…”
I remember that evening, left alone, I cursed myself for having too hastily accepted a proposal that would…

makes me waste almost all my free time. (As far as I had understood, the titles had to be copied onto small slips of paper, then arranged alphabetically with their respective shelf numbers, and transcribed again into a file to be sent to print. This work repulsed me.) And I was also afraid that our game might begin again at a time when I had managed to calm myself.
I met Maitreyi the next afternoon, before tea, on the threshold of the library, waiting for me.
"Come, let me show you what I've done," she called to me. She had brought about fifty volumes onto a table and arranged them with their spines up, so that they could be read one after another.

"You start from this end of the table, and I'll start from the other. Let's see at which volume we meet, shall we?" She seemed very emotional, her lip was trembling, and she looked at me, blinking rapidly, as if she were trying to forget something, to dissolve an image from before her eyes. I sat down to write with a strange premonition that something new was about to happen, and I wondered whether perhaps I was waiting for Maitreyi's love, whether the surprise I sensed was not a possible sharing, an illumination of the hidden corners of her soul. But I found myself little shaken by these possible events. Writing, I asked myself: do I still love her? No; it seemed to me that I loved her, nothing more. For the hundredth time I understood that something else attracted me to Maitreyi: her irrationality, her barbaric virginity, and, above all, her fascination. I understood this perfectly; that I was bewitched, not in love. And, strangely, I understood not in my hours of lucidity—few or many as I still had—but in the moments on the threshold of decisive experiences, in the real moments, when I began to live. Reflection had never revealed anything to me. I put my hand on a volume and met Maitreyi’s hand. I started.

"Which volume have you reached?" she asked me. I showed her. It was the same one she had reached: Tales of the Unexpected by Wells. She blushed suddenly, with joy, with delight, I don’t know, but she said to me in a faint voice:

"Do you see what ‘unexpected’ lies before us?" I smiled, a little influenced myself by this coincidence, although most of the volumes on the table had characteristic titles: The Dream, Take Me With You, Help!, Nothing New? and others. I was searching for an answer with many meanings, but Chabù came to call us to tea, and we both rose from the table very happy, continuing to look at each other. During tea, I spoke with great exuberance about my latest readings, all related to

Krishna and the Vaishnav cult, and I recounted with such enthusiasm and sincerity scenes from the life of Chaitanya, that Mrs. Sen could no longer contain herself and approached me with two large tears in her eyes, saying:
— It is as if you were a Vaishnav...

I was happy that she had spoken to me so. I confessed that I considered Vaishnavism to be one of the most elevated religions, and from there a discussion on religions began, sustained mainly by Mantu and me, which Maitreyi listened to with vacant eyes, without saying a word.
— What do you know about religion? she burst out suddenly, blushing, then turning pale, on the verge of tears.

I was taken aback, not knowing whether I should apologize or explain myself. Mantu tried to comfort her, but she broke away and fled to the library. I finished my cup of tea, intimidated. No one spoke anymore. I withdrew to my room to answer letters, with an unease and impatience unknown to me until then. But as I was writing, I suddenly felt the need to see Maitreyi and I went.

That day holds great significance in the present story. I transcribe from my journal: “I found her dejected, almost in tears. I told her I had come because she called me, and this surprised her. We parted then for five minutes, so I could finish my letter. When I returned, she was sleeping on the couch in front of the table.

I woke her. She started; her eyes were wide. I began to look at her intently; she drank in my gaze, eye to eye, asking me at intervals, in a whisper: ‘What?’ Then she could no longer speak, nor could I question her; instead, we stared fixedly at each other, enchanted, possessed by the same supernatural sweetness, incapable of resisting, of shaking off the spell, of awakening. It is hard for me to describe the emotion. A calm and yet violent happiness, before which the soul offered no resistance; a beatitude of the senses that surpassed sensuality, as if it partook of a heavenly happiness, a state of grace. At first, the state was sustained only by our gazes. Then we began to touch each other’s hands, without breaking eye contact. Barbaric squeezes, devoted caresses. (Note: I had recently read about the mystical love of Chaitanya and thus expressed my experiences in mystical terms.) Naturally, kisses on the hands followed. She was so lost, biting her lips so passionately (and yet chastely), that I could have kissed her on the lips, I could have done anything. I restrained myself with great difficulty. The situation was truly risky. We could have been seen by anyone coming down the stairs. She is of a mystical emotionality. (Note: In my journal from that time, influenced by certain Vaishnav readings, I used the term ‘mystical’ very often. Moreover, the commentary on this event, as I find it in a stray notebook, is pervaded from beginning to end by

“‘Mystical experience.’ I was ridiculous.) I asked her, once again, why the two of us could not be united. She shuddered. To test her, I asked her to recite twice that mantra which Tagore had taught her, to protect herself from dangers threatening her purity. Yet, after she repeated them, the enchantment persisted. With this, I proved to her—as I believed myself—that our experience had no sexual roots, but was love, though manifested in carnal sincerities.

I felt and verified this human miracle: contact with the supernatural, through touch, through the eyes, through flesh. The experience lasted two hours, exhausting us. We could repeat it whenever our gazes met and fixed upon each other.

She asked me to take off my sandals and bring my foot close to hers. The emotion of that first touch I shall never forget. It avenged me for all the jealousies I had endured until then. I knew that Maitreyi gave herself to me wholly in that abandonment of her ankle and thigh, as she had never given herself before. The scene on the terrace was forgotten. No one could lie so divinely as to deceive me with such a touch, I told myself. Unwittingly, I raised my foot higher onto her thigh, up to that joint of the knee which I sensed to be deliriously sweet, burning, which I imagined to be dusky and virginal, for, without a doubt, no human body had ever ventured so far into her flesh. In those two hours of embrace (were the caresses of our ankles and thighs anything else?)—which my journal sketches so briefly, so faintly, that for a long time afterward I wondered whether I should continue recording the stages of our journey—I lived more and understood the being of Maitreyi more deeply than I had managed in six months of effort, of friendship, of the beginnings of love. Never had I known more precisely than then that I possessed something, that I possessed absolutely.

I had not yet told her plainly that I loved her. We had both guessed it; or so it seemed to me. And I had interpreted, for a long time, every gesture of hers as a sign of sympathy or love. I did not doubt for a moment that she loved me, and I did not doubt that she knew this just as well about me. That is why her rebellions saddened and troubled me (that frightened silence, those panic-stricken eyes, the hands with which she covered her face) whenever I had spoken to her of a union between us. I did not understand; for it seemed to me that she, and her parents, continually favored this.

I told her then that I loved her. I do not know how my words sounded, for she covered her eyes and did not answer. I drew closer and repeated, more warmly, more sincerely, those few words of love I could say in Bengali. She wished to rise.
“Let me go,” she said to me in a distant, foreign voice. “You see, you have not understood my love. I love you as a friend, a very dear friend. Otherwise I cannot, otherwise I do not wish…”
“But this is not friendship, it is love,” I replied, unexpectedly regaining both my humor and my lucidity.
“How many kinds of love does the soul not know?” she added, looking at me.
“But you love me, it’s useless to hide it,” I insisted. “We can no longer live without each other, we have tormented ourselves enough until now, hiding. I love you, Maitreyi, I love you…”
I spoke to her, mixing the words, one phrase in Bengali and five in English.
“Tell me that in your own language,” she pleaded. I told her everything that came to my mind. Night had fallen, the lamps were lit everywhere. I wanted to turn on the light in the library.
“Leave it as it is,” Maitreyi said.
“What if someone comes and finds us in the dark?”
“What does it matter? Here we are brother and sister…”
I pretended not to understand, but I turned closer to her and took her hands, caressing them.
“Why do you not hear certain words?” she asked, and I could tell from her voice that she was about to laugh.
“Because you’re talking nonsense,” I replied, very sure of myself and of Maitreyi’s love.

Then something unexpected happened. Maitreyi began to cry and tore herself from my hands. She wanted to run away. I caught her in my arms and brought my head close to her hair, whispering to her, trying to charm her, begging her not to cry, to forgive me. But I could not resist the fragrance and warmth, and the temptations of that body untouched by anyone, and I kissed her. Maitreyi struggled and cried out, turning her mouth away. I was afraid someone might hear us and let her go. She fled from my arms with a sob that humbled me, but she did not head for the door, but toward the window. There, in the light of the street lantern, I could see her. I shuddered. She had a strange, desperate, tear-stained look, her hair disheveled over her shoulders, her lips bitten. She looked at me as if I were a spirit or a madman. She pointed with her finger to the place where I had kissed her, on her cheek. She could not speak, could not defend herself. I approached, took her in my arms and kissed her again, maddened by confusion, darkened by passion. I kissed her on the mouth and met her lips, moist, tender, and fragrant, as I never would have believed would be given to me to kiss. In the first moment they pressed together under my mouth, trying to defend themselves, but she was so weak that she opened them and let them be kissed, bitten, sucked. I felt her breasts, I felt her whole being, and she abandoned herself so completely to my body that I even felt a trace of melancholy that she had given herself so quickly. I do not know how long this first embrace lasted. I sensed that she was suffocating, struggling, and I let her go. She collapsed suddenly at my feet. I thought she had fainted and bent down, pale, to help her, but she embraced my feet, weeping and begging me not to touch her again, imploring me in the name of my God, in the name of my mother, in the name of Mrs. Sen. I trembled and fell silent. I let her rise on her own. She wiped her tears hurriedly, fixed her hair, looked at me, without really seeing me, for I was standing in the pale light of the lantern,
and she left into the darkness, sighing.

I returned to my room, agitated, a hundred feelings passing through me, tormented both by the joy that she was mine, and by pride, remorse, fear. I could do nothing until dinner. I wondered if I would have the courage to look at her during the meal. I wondered especially what she would think of me, whether she would say something to Mrs. Sen or to Lilu. I knew nothing, believed nothing. She did not come to dinner, but immediately afterward, Lilu approached me and said:
— The Poetess sends you this note.
I opened it, holding my breath. So that no one would understand, it was written in French: "Vous venir matin six heures en bibliothèque."
