chapters.title: Morning Uncertainties
paragraphs: I went to the office only at ten, and we all had tea at eight in the morning. So we could talk undisturbed for two hours. That night I fell asleep with difficulty, feverish and haunted by atrocious dreams; it seemed to me I was losing Maitreyi, that an angel with a white beard was casting me out of this house, that Sen was watching me absently from the terrace. I kept waking, trembling, my forehead cold and damp. It was as if I had committed a great sin.

I found Maitreyi in the office, in a white sari, a gray shawl over her shoulders, writing catalog cards. I wished her good morning, extremely embarrassed, not knowing whether I should kiss her or only smile, or behave as if nothing had happened between us recently. The first meeting after a decisive episode in love has always required from me an effort of attention and imagination. I never know how to behave, what “attitude” to assume; I do not know whether I should be rigid or gentle, I do not know above all what she thinks and how she would like me to be. This indecision makes me hesitate before any gesture, contradict myself, apologize, and, in general, be ridiculous.

Maitreyi, on the contrary, seemed calm, resigned, determined, though the dark circles and pallor of her face betrayed a night of prayer and meditation. (Was it my imagination, or had I heard her voice toward morning, murmuring on the balcony a monotonous prayer, interrupted and resumed several times, then suddenly stilled, as in weeping?)
I sat down across from her, at the same desk, on the chair she had prepared for me beforehand. I began to write mechanically, copying book titles, without lifting my eyes from the cards.
— Did you sleep well? I asked after a few minutes, to break the silence.
— I did not sleep at all, she answered calmly. I thought it was...
…it is time for you to leave our house. That is why I called you…

I tried to interrupt her, but Maitreyi made a desperate, imploring gesture, and I let her speak, growing ever more troubled and surprised by what I was hearing. She spoke while playing with a pen on a sheet of paper, without looking at me, drawing and erasing, writing lines I could not read, making marks and figures I could not understand. This game reminded me of the beginnings of our friendship and those first French lessons. I wanted to interrupt her, to tell her how many mistakes she had made in last night’s note, but I caught myself in the pettiness of this humor and kept silent. There was no time for melancholy reflections. Maitreyi was telling me things I did not know how to believe. They disturbed and surprised me, wounding both my pride and my certainty. Never before had I listened to her speak so much on her own, without changing the subject, without asking me anything, without waiting for a reply or comment. It was as if she were speaking into an empty room. I was no longer there.

I was mistaken, she said, to think that she loved me as I loved her. Her soul had long been given to another, to Robi Thakkur. She had loved him since she was thirteen, since she first read his books. She used to spend her summers, until just last year, at Shantiniketan, she and her family hosted in the poet’s own house. How many nights had the two of them spent on the terrace, alone, Maitreyi at the old man’s feet, listening to him, her hair caressed! At first, she did not know what this Feeling was that made her live almost without waking, as if in an unbelievably beautiful dream; she thought it was veneration and filial love for her guru. Until one evening, the poet told her that this was love. She fainted then, on the terrace. She awoke, she did not know how much later, in his room, lying on the bed, her face wet. The room was filled with the fresh scent of jasmine. His mouth continued to caress her, and he gave her then that mantra, the protector from sin.

To remain pure her whole life, that is what he told her. To write verses, to love, to dream, and never to forget him. And she has not forgotten. She has a whole box of letters from him, sent from all over the world wherever he traveled. The box is of scented wood and was given to her by the poet two years ago, together with a lock of his hair… (What a disgusting charlatan, I thought, burning with jealousy, with fury, with helplessness. What a corrupter, what carnal mysticism, what a hideous mixture of devotion and fraud. How could I have believed that this maiden was pure? How could I have believed that I was the first to touch her body?)

Yet, he had never kissed her, nor caressed her except on the hair, Maitreyi added, as if she had guessed my thought. Besides, she had not seen him for a long time, since he was always traveling; and then (her hesitation, at this moment!), it seems that Mrs. Sen noticed certain sentimental excesses toward the guru and no longer allowed her to see him. But she had not forgotten him for a moment. She would have liked us to become good friends, to share all this with me, to…

we love together. To me, she has been nothing but a friend, she loved me as a friend, never did she think of any other kind of love, and our game was meant to remain a game, without embraces and without kisses. (She blushed and whispered these words with many mistakes, both of grammar and pronunciation. That is why she repeated the sentence in Bengali.) Her gestures were sincere and warm, for, in a way, she loves me very much and likes to be with me, to joke, to look into each other's eyes and to touch hands, but all these are nothing more than friendship. If I believed otherwise, it is her fault, for she hid many things from me and led me to believe anything else, even to believe that she loves me.

When she finished, exhausted and pale, I rose from my place (I hardly knew what I was doing, so dazed was I) and went to her. She looked at me with panic and pity; I took her head between my hands and, knowing she could not cry out, could not call for help, I kissed her on the mouth. We both knew that at any moment someone could come down from upstairs and see us from the stairs, but that only made me prolong the kiss even more, almost suffocating her.

“Why are you doing this?” she said. “I am weak, you know I cannot resist, but I feel nothing when you kiss me. I feel your lips as if they were Chabù’s, a child’s. They do not make me tremble! I do not love you!...”

I let her go and went into my room. I went straight to work, without waiting for tea, somewhat lightened by Maitreyi’s confession, though jealous and furious. It seemed to me that everything this girl did was against nature.

That day I did not see her and did not seek her out. In the evening, at dinner, she was again at my right. I was among the first to come down. Only Mantu, Lilu, and Maitreyi had arrived. We began to discuss politics: the arrest of the city’s mayor, Sarojini Naidu’s speech, the number of prisoners in the civil revolution. I had promised myself not to look at Maitreyi and not to touch her, not even by accident. But suddenly I felt her warm, bare foot under the table, trembling as it settled over mine. The shiver that passed through me then betrayed me. Maitreyi, without being noticed, lifted the edge of her sari, and I ran my foot along her thighs, with no attempt to resist the charm, the warmth, the sensuality. She was pale, her lips red, looking at me with deep, frightened eyes, but her flesh called to me, beckoned me, and I had to dig my nails into my chest to awaken myself for a moment. I think the others noticed our distraction.

From then on, the embrace of our thighs beneath the table became one of our daily joys. For only there could I caress her thighs, her knees, in this way. If I had touched her with my hand, Maitreyi would have considered such an attempt an act of disgusting lewdness and would have immediately doubted the purity of my feelings.
After dinner, Maitreyi stopped me in the doorway.
“Do you want to see what I have been working on so far?”

She turned on the light in the library, but instead of approaching the table where the index cards lay, she headed toward the other room, the one without a lamp. She glanced to the right and left, as if afraid someone might surprise her, then stretched out her arm to me, bare up to the shoulder.
“Try whatever you want with it, kiss it, caress it; you’ll see that I feel nothing…”

Long before, we had once talked together about sensual pleasure, and I had told her that someone who truly knows how to love can experience voluptuousness from even the slightest touch of the other’s body. I had explained then that, for me, possession is much more mysterious and complicated than it seems. It is very difficult to truly have something, to obtain it or to conquer it. More often we imagine we possess than actually possess. These banalities, which I had told her in passing, certain that she would not be able to retain anything more serious, had troubled Maitreyi enough. Now she was trying to test her feelings through that essential “voluptuousness” I had spoken of.

I took her arm and gazed at it for a moment, fascinated. It was no longer a woman’s arm. It had acquired a transparency and an autonomous warmth, as if all passion had concentrated beneath that brown, matte skin, and all the will to victory alongside it. It lived by itself; it no longer belonged to the girl who had stretched it out over the embers to test her love. I held it in my hands like a living offering, myself bewildered by the intensity with which it throbbed and by the strangeness of what was to follow. I began to squeeze it, to caress it, to kiss it, certain that I was embracing the whole being of Maitreyi, that it was her I was caressing, her in her entirety I was rejoicing in. I felt how she bent under the pleasure, how she yielded, agonizing, I felt that she was awakening to a new day, for amid the kisses I saw her face growing ever paler, her eyes ever more aflame, her will ever more lost. In that call of my love, wandering over the flesh of her bare arm, I was calling to her. The gliding of my fingers toward her shoulders was directed at her, all of her. And I sensed then how she wavered and leaned more and more upon me, until she wrapped her other arm around my shoulders and began to hold me tightly, weeping, breathless. After a few moments I had her in my arms, she giving herself to me (for I made no move to hasten her surrender, determined only to torment her arm), and when I kissed her mouth this time, I understood that it was no longer a kiss of violence, for her lips opened to drink me in, her teeth tried to pierce me, the embrace was no longer resistance nor abandonment, but a coincidence with my longing, with my blood. I understood then that whatever might have happened before in Maitreyi’s emotions and thoughts, whoever might have stirred them before me, those traces had been erased, burned away by this new day at whose dawn the maiden was being born. An indescribable beatitude invaded me then through every gate of my soul and body. I felt my being fully and continuously, an ineffable wave

I was rising out of nothingness, yet without being separated from myself, without losing my way. Never have I lived more fully and more immediately than in those moments, which seemed to me to be without duration. That embrace at Maitreyi’s breast was more than love. She awoke, her palms turned inward, covering her eyes. She moved away from me slowly, glancing at me now and then with a start, then covering her face again. She passed by the table with the books and said mechanically, pointing them out to me: — This is what I worked on today... Her words were an unnatural premonition. For at that very moment Khokha entered and told her that Mrs. Sen was calling her upstairs, to her room. I turned off the lights, trying to compose myself; for I was dazed and happy, and I almost felt like telling Khokha what happiness had been given to me out of the blue, without my deserving it. In my room I could not find my place. I looked out through the barred window, threw myself on the bed, got up and paced the room. I longed to see Maitreyi once more, to fall asleep with her image, with the memory of her lips undisturbed by Khokha’s appearance. It seemed to me that we had not parted as we should have, in the intimacy we had discovered today. We could only part with an embrace, and Khokha’s arrival had prevented it. I am sure Maitreyi felt the same, for I could hear her stepping lightly above, in her room, going out onto the balcony, returning. On the wall opposite I could see her shadow whenever she approached the window. But then the light went out, and a strange regret petrified me by the bars. Then I heard a whistling, in which a melody might have been guessed, but I guessed something else. I went to the window and whistled too; there was no reply. She must be on the balcony, I thought; and, opening very carefully the door of my room and then the heavier door of the corridor, I stepped out onto the veranda. I did not dare go down into the street, for the lamp’s light was too strong. I whistled again. — Allan, Allan! I heard myself called from the balcony. She was saying my name for the first time. I went down and saw her leaning against the balustrade, only a shawl over her shoulders, her black hair falling over her arms, among the wisteria. She was a legendary apparition, from an oriental fairy tale, her form almost naked among the clusters of flowers, in a balcony faintly lit by a street lantern. I looked at her without saying a word. From the languor of her arms abandoned over the balustrade and the resignation with which she rested her head on her shoulder, I understood that she too no longer had the strength to say anything. We only looked at each other. Then, she searched under her shawl, at her breast, and threw me something white with a lazy glide. Through the air—a garland of jasmine flowers. I did not see her the next moment. Nor could I thank her. I returned to my room happy and at peace, after closing the doors with the same care. I met Khokha in the corridor. — I went to drink a little fresh water, he told me awkwardly, before I could say a word.

I did not wonder then why he was always around us, or whether he might be spying on us. I wore the jasmine crown with too much tenderness and joy to think of anything else. I understood later that this was the sign of betrothal, that the maiden who gives such a crown to a young man is considered his forever, for this exchange of flowers held the value of a vow beyond circumstances and death. But at that time I did not yet know its symbol, and I held it in my hands and kissed it, because it had belonged to Maitreyi, had touched her breast, and from there she had tossed it to me, priceless to me. And as I sat on the bed, gazing at the jasmine flowers, my thoughts suddenly wandered to the beginnings of the beginning, when I had barely seen Maitreyi and had not liked her; when I believed that nothing would ever bind me to her, and I understood that, in fact, I had loved her from then, though I did not clarify this to myself and did not wish to clarify it.

It was a night of rocking between dream and memory, with the scent of jasmine tempting my lips with Maitreyi’s, a night in which it seemed to me that I heard for the first time the cranes of Bengal, their cries above the flooded fields at the edge of the gulf. I saw then, through that gateway of happiness open to the world, a legendary life, on a land of serpents and tam-tams, where I walked beside Maitreyi, two lovers of the road.

The next day I had much work at the office and returned late after lunch. Maitreyi was waiting for me with the meal in the dining room. She had brought her index cards and was sorting them alphabetically, in a box with as many dividers and letters. She turned pale when she saw me and immediately brought me food. Then she sat down close to me, her shawl drawn over her head almost to her forehead, watching me! How I suffered then, not knowing what to say to her, afraid of seeming vulgar (for I was tired and ate greedily), pausing in my hunger to cast her a glance in which to confess that I had not forgotten her, that she was as dear to me as the night before.
“Did you think of me today?” I asked her, remembering that lovers ask each other such sweet questions.
She closed her eyes, and I saw two tears, or rather glimmers, for the drops had not grown enough to fall from her lashes.

“Why are you crying?” I asked abruptly, trying to seem more moved than I was. (And yet, I loved her, God, I loved her madly! Then why could I not suffer beside her? Why was I hungry, while she was overcome by tears?)

She did not answer, and after I rose from the table to caress her hair, I returned, to drink water, to eat a banana, in short, to take something so that I could then kiss her. (I still had the superstition and modesty of the white man: not to speak with my mouth full, not to kiss with dirty lips, as if these
(it might have had something to do with love.)

“Allan, I want to show you something,” she said to me in her most humble and melodious voice. (She spoke in Bengali so she could address me intimately, for the placidity of English phrases, always in the second person plural, exasperated her.)
She showed me the little box given by Tagore, with the lock of white, perfumed, curling hair inside.

“Do what you want with it; if you wish, burn it. I can’t keep it upstairs with me anymore. I did not love him. My love for him was a mistake, for he was meant to be only my guru, and I thought I loved him otherwise. But now…”

She looked at me almost somnambulistically; her gaze passed through me, above me, to unite with some being from her vision—perhaps still me, Allan, but a fuller, warmer Allan, summoned and drunk in by all the thirst of her love.
“Now I love only you; never before have I loved. I thought I loved, but now I know, now it is different.”

I wanted to embrace her, but Mantu was coming down the stairs, so I contented myself with squeezing her arm. I handed the box back to her, for it would have seemed ridiculous to take revenge on the poor lock of white hair. And besides, what had I to do with her past, with her memories? In that hour, I felt so certain that I was the first and only one, I feared nothing. Her past did not torture me, as it would later, whenever it seemed that Maitreyi was drifting away from me, that perhaps she compared me to the other, that she lived in a time when I had not yet appeared in her life—a time that tormented me enough with its impenetrability.
But she probably understood my gesture differently: as a refusal, an indifference to her sacrifice, to her nakedness.
“Don’t you want to take this lock?” she asked me again, unable to believe it.
“What do you want me to do with it? Better you burn it,” I replied as warmly as I could.
“But for me it is worth nothing now,” she marveled.

I didn’t quite understand, but I took the lock, wrapped it carefully, and put it in my vest pocket. Then I went to take my bath, whistling with such good cheer as I splashed cold water over my body, that Lilu, passing through the courtyard, knocked on the tin wall of the cabin and asked:
“Did you have a bad dream?”

This joke, seemingly insipid, was tied to a very serious game of ours from the previous month, by which I tried to hide my melancholy and restlessness (“the Maitreyi problem,” as I called it in my journal) by saying I had nightmares. The memory of those times of uncertainty and agony made my present joy and certainty all the more vivid. I returned to my room, trembling with voluptuousness and victory.
I had barely managed to dress properly when Maitreyi knocked at
door. As she entered, she drew the curtain behind her (it would have been riskier to close the door) and threw herself into my arms.
"I can't be without you anymore," she said to me.
I kissed her. She struggled free and ran to the door.
"Isn't it a sin?" she asked.
"Why should it be a sin?" I reassured her. "We love each other."
"But we love each other without my mother and babà knowing," she trembled.
"One day we will tell them."
She looked at me as if I had uttered something insane.
"You can't say that!"

"One day we must," I repeated. "I will have to ask for your hand. I will tell them that we love each other, and Mr. Sen cannot refuse us. You know how much he cares for me; you saw how he himself brought me into the house, encouraged me to befriend you."
I did not continue, for Maitreyi showed signs of an unexpected suffering and agitation. I drew near again, tried to take her in my arms, but she resisted.

"You don't know something," she said. "You don't know that we love you differently (she hesitated and corrected herself), they love you differently, and I should have loved you the same way, not as I love you now... I should have always loved you as at the beginning, like a brother..."
"Don't talk nonsense," I interrupted, kissing her arm. "They weren't thinking of 'brother' either."
"Oh yes, they were," Maitreyi protested. "You know nothing..."
She began to cry.
"Oh Lord, oh Lord, why did it happen like this?"
"Do you regret it?" I asked her.
She pressed herself against me.

"You know I don't regret it, that whatever happens I will love only you, that I am yours. And one day you will take me with you to your country, won't you? I will forget India then, I want to forget it..."

She caressed me through her tears and pressed herself to my body with a freshness and yet a confidence I would never have suspected in a girl who had kissed her lover on the lips for the first time only the day before.
"But don't tell them anything. They will never accept me as your wife. They love you because they want you to be theirs, to be their child."
I was surprised and delighted by what I heard, but Maitreyi was trembling.

"They told me: 'Maitreyi, from now on you will have a brother, Allan. See that you love him, he will be your brother, and babà will adopt him, and when he retires we will all go to his country; there, with our money, we will live like a rajah; there it is not hot and there is no revolution, and the white people are not bad like the English here and will consider us their brothers...' And now, what have I done? The way I love you now, do you understand how I love you now?"
I had to catch her in my arms, for she was collapsing. I laid her down
on the armchair, dazed. We sat together for a long time, without saying a word.
chapters.summary: Allan faces emotional turmoil after a restless night, as Maitreyi confesses her devotion to Robi Thakkur and struggles to define her feelings.

chapters.title: Secret Confessions
paragraphs: From then on, the days began to change. Of each one I could write an entire notebook, so rich were they, and so fresh have they remained in my memory. It was the beginning of August, during the holidays. We spent almost all our time together; I withdrew to my room only to change, to write in my journal, and to sleep. The rest of the time we studied together, for Maitreyi was preparing privately for her Bachelor of Arts, and I helped her. Those hours of ours, listening to the commentaries on Shakuntala, side by side on the carpet, not understanding a single word of the Sanskrit text, but sitting next to Maitreyi, because I could secretly squeeze her hands, kiss her hair, gaze at her and tease her, while the teacher, a myopic pandit, corrected her translation or her answers to the grammatical questionnaire. How she interpreted Kalidasa for me, and how she found in every love verse a detail from our own hidden love. I had come to like only what she liked: music, poetry, Bengali literature. I strove to decipher the Vaishnava poems in the original, I read the translation of Shakuntala with emotion, and nothing that had once interested me could now hold my attention. I looked at the shelves of physics books without the slightest thrill. I had forgotten everything except my work (which I finished reluctantly, eager to return home sooner) and Maitreyi.

A few days after our confession, she came to tell me that she had hidden something from me then. I was so intoxicated by the certainty of Maitreyi’s love and by the voluptuousness that always seized me in her presence, that I immediately took her in my arms and began to kiss her.
“You must listen to me,” she repeated. “You must know everything. Have you ever loved like this, as you do now?”
“Never,” I answered quickly, not knowing whether I was lying or only exaggerating.
(Besides, what were those ephemeral, sensual loves of my youth, compared to this new passion, which made me forget everything and mold myself to the soul and desires of Maitreyi?)
“Nor have I,” Maitreyi confessed. “But I have had other loves. Shall I tell you about them?”
“As you wish.”
“I first loved a pcm, one of those we call ‘seven leaves,’” she began, preparing to tell her story.

I began to laugh and caressed her protectively, mockingly. — That is not love, my dear. — Oh, but it is love. Chabù loves her tree now too; but mine was great, for at that time I lived in Alipore, and there were many strong, tall trees, and I fell in love with one, tall and proud, yet so delicate, so caressing... I could no longer part from it. We would spend the whole day embraced, and I would talk to it, kiss it, weep. I composed verses for it, though I never wrote them down, I recited them only to it; who else would have understood me? And when it caressed me, with its leaves upon my cheek, I felt such a sweet happiness that I lost my breath. I would lean against its trunk so as not to fall. At night I would run from my room, naked, and climb into my tree; I could not sleep alone. I would weep up there, among the leaves, until dawn approached, and then I would begin to tremble. Once, my mother almost caught me, and I was so frightened that I stayed in bed for many days. That was when I fell ill with heart trouble. And I could not stay in bed unless every day they brought me fresh branches from my tree with the “seven leaves”...

I listened to her as one listens to a story, but at the same time I felt her drifting away from me. How complicated her soul was! I understood once again that we, the civilized, are the only ones who are simple, naive, and clear. That these people, whom I loved so much that I would have wished to become one of them, each hides a history and a mythology impossible to fathom, that they are tangled and deep, complicated and incomprehensible. What Maitreyi said pained me. It pained me all the more because I felt her capable of loving everything with the same passion, while I wanted her to love only me, forever. A being who loves ceaselessly, anyone; could there be a more unbearable torment for a lover?

I imagined her naked and adolescent, clinging to the tree with all the madness of her passion. It was an image that disturbed me, irritated me, for it seemed to me that the voluptuousness she had known then I could never give her, nor could I ever erase it. That union with the leaves and the branch was a different kind of love. Later, many questions tormented me: how did she give herself to it? How did those seven-fingered leaves thrill her bare flesh? What words did she speak when, for the first time, she felt herself possessed, enslaved to it alone?...

She had brought me, wrapped in silver paper, a twig with leaves, pressed, perfumed, dried. I felt an uncontrollable surge of fury at the sight of them and took them, tried to look at them with disdain, but I could not restrain myself and crushed them in my palms, biting my lips.
— And he wanted to do the same, Maitreyi confessed to me. But I did not let him...
I turned pale. So, he too had loved her so much and suffered just as fiercely, foreseeing himself in love, through a tree. Where was my certainty of being the first, my peace?

Maitreyi began to kiss my hands and tell me that now she had forgotten even her guru and the tree, that she loved only me, that her other loves had never been like this. I remained silent, with a searing pain in my soul; something had crumbled, I felt an exhaustion and a fury against myself, unknown to me until then. Is this jealousy? I wondered.
“If I did not love only you, I would not have the courage to tell you all this,” Maitreyi wept. “You must tell me, too, about all the girls you loved before me…”
“I have never been in love,” I answered, darkly.
“How could you live without love?” she marveled. “And you are so much older than I am, you could have given yourself freely to so many loves…”
I hesitated for a moment, lost in thought. Maitreyi guessed my mind.
“No, not your loves, the girls you have held in your arms. Don’t tell me about them. That was filth, not love…”

She began to sob uncontrollably. In the corridor, the chauffeur passed by, stopping for a moment, surprised by the crying, then walked on, his steps quiet. (He was one of those who spied on us, I noticed this later.)
Maitreyi tried to compose herself, gathering her shawl to her mouth.
“Why do you torment me?” she suddenly rebelled. “Why do you think I have not been pure in my love and in my body?”

I was frozen. I torment her? I wondered. She tells me things that burn me, and yet she is the one who revolts. I, who have said nothing, who love her like a madman, unable to resist either my passion or her desires. I, who desperately want the whole past to be erased, while Maitreyi brings it before me incessantly, lives it continuously. (I judged and suffered as a civilized man, as one who always prefers to forget and to cover with ashes, to ignore or to tolerate, so long as his peace and comfort are not disturbed. Maitreyi knew none of these pale superstitions and offered herself to me continuously, whole, with all that had passed and fertilized her soul until then. For her body, I knew this, she had kept untouched; at least, untouched by any man’s hand.)

She told me, that same afternoon, of another love of hers. She was then twelve or thirteen and had gone with Mrs. Sen to the great temple at Puri, to Jaganath. As they circled, together with the crowd, the dark corridors around the sanctuary, someone quietly approached Maitreyi and placed a garland of flowers over her head. At the first stop in the light, Mrs. Sen noticed the garland and, finding out it had been placed on her in the darkness, took it off and kept it on her arm. But as soon as they entered the darkness again, Maitreyi felt another garland around her neck. And this one Mrs. Sen removed in the light. This time she took her by the arm, but the same thing happened as soon as they stepped into the darkness. When they reached the sanctuary, Mrs. Sen had six garlands on her arm. She looked to the right and left, very troubled, for a garland hung around a maiden’s neck means betrothal. And then

A young man of rare beauty appeared, with long black locks falling over his shoulders, with piercing eyes and red lips (I suffered terribly listening to Maitreyi describe him to me), who fell at the lady’s feet, touched her soles with his hand, and said: “Mother.” That was all. Then he disappeared.

She loved this young man for years, even after she had begun to fall in love with Tagore. (I remembered this detail; what if it happens that she loves Tagore, even though she is now in love with me? Or if, after me, while I still love her, another will come?) Later, she confessed the episode in the temple to Tagore, and the “poet” told her that the young man was a messenger of love, that the six garlands were something symbolic, and other such things. Listening to her, I shuddered at how much jungle still lived in Maitreyi’s soul and mind. What darkness, what tropical flora of symbols and signs, what warm atmosphere of possibilities and sensuality. Where was I, in all this? And I was loved by a sixteen-year-old maiden, whom no one had yet kissed on the lips except me…

“Now I am yours, only yours,” burst out Maitreyi, entwining herself around me. “Only you have taught me what love is, only you have made me tremble; to you I have given myself. When you tore the leaves, I was happy. How much I love to see you angry like the wind, to have you trample me underfoot, to not care about me. I love you like that. Why are you afraid?...”

Indeed, I had no reason to be afraid. Maitreyi sought me out constantly in my room, at that hour of the afternoon when everyone slept upstairs, under the fans. She almost gave herself to me there, on the immense bamboo mat. Kisses now slipped along her body, descending down her neck, over her bare shoulders beneath the shawl, along her arms, over her breasts. When I caressed her breasts for the first time, with a hand both sincere and hungry, she gathered herself into a single frozen shiver. Then she relaxed and unfastened her bodice, with all that remained of fear and voluptuousness in her gaze. She gave herself to me, maddened, terrified, as if awaiting a thunderbolt to shatter us both. Never had I seen more beautiful breasts, not on any statue in the world, for that dark pallor of Maitreyi’s body was now blushing beneath its first unveiling, and the perfect, sculptural beauty of her bust was illuminated, awaiting me. Her whole body was an expectation, her face frozen, her eyes looked at me as at a miracle. That shudder which passed through her and killed her beside me was no longer sensuality. I awoke lucid and aroused, experiencing love in stages, while she had given herself wholly to the miracle of a man’s touch for the first time, still a virgin. I understood later that this voluptuousness, deepened in her flesh while she was still only in love, crucified her. Then she had the courage to ask me, with one arm clinging to the back of the mat and the other hand caressing my hair.
“Isn’t it a sin?”

I answered her, as usual, with a stupid consolation, a few phrases devoid of any real content, and continued to lose myself in the gradual discovery of her body. When I looked at her, from time to time, astonished myself by such complete abandonment, I saw her lying with her head on my chest, eyes closed, trembling, tears slipping down her cheeks, gluing strands of hair to the corners of her lips and on her chin.
“When we are united,” I consoled her, “we will love without limits. Then I will have you entirely.”
“But isn’t it a sin now?” she returned, clenching her thighs, biting her lips.
“Now I only kiss you and caress only a part of your body. Then it will be different, you will be mine, mine…”
“Am I not already?” she said, in a faint voice. “Isn’t it a sin?”

It took me several days to understand what she was trying to tell me. It was a sin, because she felt pleasure completely and feared that the dew of love thus wasted might disturb the order of the world. Once she had given me her lips and embraced me, her body pressed against mine, we were united. And love had to be fulfilled to the end, otherwise pleasure became vice, and the joy of our union, a sadness of the flesh. The sin was not in my attempts to know her body ever more deeply, but in the limitation of my embraces, which made her experience the most final spasms without the fruit of these joys being gathered, growing… The wasting of the fruit was the sin, in her Indian feeling and judgment. According to their custom, we had to be united in bed, and from our caresses living fruits should spring forth, children… For otherwise, love is lost, joy becomes barren, and our union a vice…

I shuddered, realizing that it was not sensuality and her love for me that compelled her to ask this of me, but a superstition, a fear of karma, of the gods, of the ancestors. That night I wondered where the true sincerity of the senses is found, the true innocence of the flesh, with them or with us, the civilized? Had not Maitreyi acted like one hypnotized, like an automaton, ever since she first kissed me? And the spontaneity, the vastness of her love for me—are they not simple consequences of that first fall, acts determined by her barbaric, superstitious consciousness?

I had come to avoid, as much as I could, prolonged embraces in solitude, because I almost adored Mrs. Sen and respected Mr. Sen, and I waited to find an opportunity to ask for Maitreyi for myself before having her. I was a moral man; from this all my tragedies spring. I have always loved on several planes, I never knew how to sacrifice everything for a single kernel of truth or life, and thus I have stumbled against every threshold and the waves have carried me wherever they wished.
Besides, I loved Maitreyi so much that I preferred a…

a warmer, more complete communion, such as we shared during our drives through the outskirts of Calcutta, tens of kilometers traveled until almost midnight, beyond Barackpur, Hoogly, Chandernagore. With her (I say with her — though we were always accompanied by Mrs. or Mr. Sen, by Lilu and Mantu, Chabù or Khokha — because we saw and felt only ourselves, only the two of us), with her I visited so many villages around Calcutta, longed for so many houses hidden among coconut trees, where, with a glance, we guessed we would have liked to hide away, left so many memories on those roads darkened by the shadows of the trees lining them. So many artificial lakes on whose banks we sat together, furtively squeezing each other’s hands, while the others brought baskets of sandwiches and fruit from the car. So many stops in the night, on the Chandernagore road, all of us frozen by silence, by the trees, by the fireflies that flew around us as if in an Urwald.

I especially remember one night, when our car broke down right on that magical road to Chandernagore, and the driver set off with Mantu to look for some tools in a nearby village. The engineer, tired, stayed behind to doze in the car, while the three of us, Maitreyi, Chabù, and I, went to explore the forest. A summer night without a moon, with as many stars as Bengal can hold and fireflies settling on our shoulders, our faces, our necks, as if in a fairy tale of jewels. We said nothing to each other and, imperceptibly, we linked arms, fearful of Chabù, encouraged by that enchanted silence and darkness. I do not know what unknown soul within me burst forth then, summoned by all this unsuspected India. The forest seemed to have neither beginning nor end here. Ageless eucalyptus trees, through which the sky could barely be glimpsed, so deceptive were the fireflies and so distant the stars. We stopped before an artificial pond, one of those basins where farmers raise fish. We all fell silent there. Who knows what wonders were being woven then among the lotuses with their tightly folded leaves, in that unmoving water, in which the flights of golden motes were reflected? I kept shivering, for our surroundings had turned into a fairy tale, and the young man within me, the man of that hour of enchantment, let himself be lulled by the sanctity and unreality of our presence before that motionless pond. We stayed there a long time and I did not dare to kiss Maitreyi. I no longer desired anything, felt no need for any gesture. There was an unnatural serenity in my soul, though the mystery and miracle around me had exalted, narcotized, and rebelled me. I do not know how this came to pass.

Another time, we found an abandoned house, on the edge of a rice field into which I had ventured and returned soaked almost to the knees. I sat on the ruined wall of the house, on those stones threatened by vegetation, drying myself. The stars had not yet risen, and the evening was warm, with wafts of eucalyptus. Beside me, trying to get just as comfortable, though she had come

in a sari woven with gold thread, Maitreyi searched with her gaze for the beginning of the forest, beyond the field. I do not know what secret sharing of our desire to flee, to be isolated together, passed then over everything. The forest beckoned us with its dense trees and shadows, with its happy birds. We looked at each other, and an emotion beyond nature invaded us, just as it had in the library. I helped her jump down from the wall and kissed her hair in passing, but the kiss was my whole soul, for Maitreyi abandoned herself with closed eyes, no longer thinking of Lilu or Mrs. Sen, who could have seen us from the car. We always returned to them with frightened hearts: had they seen us?

Those walks remain with me now, fresher and deadly sweet in memory. For if the memory of the flesh passes easily, if the union, however perfect, of bodies is like thirst and hunger and is forgotten, nothing of that opacity was present in our communion outside the city, when our eyes told everything by themselves, and a simple embrace replaced a night of love. Only there could I find again the thrill of those fixed, hypnotic, insatiable gazes, discovered on our very first day, in the library. When we stopped at the barriers, in full light, our eyes sought each other, found each other, and chained themselves together in exasperation, giving so madly of their glances that I still wonder how the others did not guess our passion. Did they believe, perhaps, that it was the love they had wished for us?

Once I saw Chandemagor by night. The boulevard lit on both sides could not erase the impression of weary melancholy left by the palace ruins, once so glorious in this old and God-forgotten French colony. On the way back I thought seriously how powerful and imperishable this India is, which endures and swallows everything without caring for invaders or masters. I was speeding in a twentieth-century car and beside me was a soul unfathomable and misunderstood, as chimeric and holy as that other Maitreyi, the hermit from the Upanishads. I touched her arm to wake myself. Does this girl love me?

At Belur-Math, in the ashram of Swami Vivekananda, we came most often, especially on holidays, because the Ganges flows there right by the steps of the math, and the view is wonderful, the air perfumed. There we walked untroubled, without many words and without gestures of love. There it seemed to me I found a peace my soul had never known before. Was it love for Maitreyi or my well-justified convictions, those that for the first time made me think of conversion? I wanted to embrace Hinduism, and then there would be no more obstacle to our union. And I asked myself thus: if it is true that all religions are good, that the same God manifests in each of them, then why should I not embrace Maitreyi’s faith? I do not cast off my law out of fear or for the sake of gain, but for

that love is putting me to this test. If a dead dogma can stand in the way of a living love, what kind of love is that? If I am convinced that truth is everywhere, in all faiths, why not turn this conviction into action? It is very easy to say, like any modern missionary, that all religions are good. I am tired of words. I want to prove to myself that Hinduism is just as good as Christianity, if I truly believe in a single God; just as both laws would be useless, if I did not believe.

When I told Maitreyi this, there at Belur-Math, she was stunned for a moment by my resolve and confessed to me that, if I converted to Hinduism, no one could ever separate us. She cited several cases of such conversions. (A Frenchman, a professor at Shantiniketan, married to a Bengali woman, I had met myself, and I had been impressed by his serenity and happiness, rooted in foreign soil, raising sons and daughters as true Indian children.) And that same evening, upon our return to Bhowanipore, Maitreyi confessed my decision to Mrs. Sen. She was so happy that she came down to tell me that “mother” was overwhelmed with joy, that all the women upstairs spoke of nothing else, and that now, waiting only for the right moment, I could ask for her hand without fear. We embraced then with a certainty and self-assurance that later gave me pause. Was this tolerance, this general patronage, to be the boundary of our love? I wondered.

When Mr. Sen heard of the conversion, he became upset and told me that I should not become so quickly enthusiastic for a religion that, for now, attracts me only by its novelty and ceremonial; that my own religion is much better than his, and if he cannot abandon his, because he would lose his place in society, I have no reason to attempt such an experience. Besides, he would only accept it after receiving the consent of those back home. I must never forget that a religion is preserved not out of conviction, but out of love and respect for those close to us who still believe in it. (But what about my new and living love? I asked myself as I listened to him, for he was right, but so was I.) This clear and vigorous opposition from Mr. Sen depressed both me and Maitreyi. We decided that I should go away for a month to Puri, in October, and return already converted. Then, no further discussion would be possible.

Moreover, it so happened that Mr. Sen, who had been suffering for several months from increasingly severe high blood pressure, had two or three repeated attacks of “mouches volantes,” which alarmed the whole household. Our car rides became rare, and I spent most of my time in Mr. Sen’s room, reading to him either novels or books on psychology and medicine. (For the engineer, since he had been forced into immobility, had begun to think about the soul and about illness, and wished to inform himself.) We took turns, Mantu, Maitreyi, and I. Mr. Sen was not in pain, but he was forced to

he would spend a good part of the day lying on his bed, dark glasses over his eyes. This illness, which had lasted for several months, I had scarcely noticed, so absorbed and fascinated was I by the play of our love.

Only then did I realize how many things had happened around me without my paying them any heed. The civil revolution was threatening once again, with fifty thousand nationalists in prison. I had to witness a few brutal scenes, some charges by mounted police, the devastation of the Sikh quarter in Bhowanipore, children beaten and women wounded, before I too became truly outraged. But then I stopped reasoning and condemned the British without reserve; every new act of brutality I read about in the newspapers infuriated me, I looked with disgust at any white man I met in the trams, and I gave up English tobacco, English toothpaste, anything brought from England. I bought only swadeshi goods, or, if I could not find those, Japanese merchandise. In any case, my life in Bhowanipore had long since forced me to give up most European purchases.

A few days after the devastation of the Sikh quarter, Harold came to visit me. I had guessed it; he had come for a loan, this time a large one—a hundred rupees. I had the money at the Chattered Bank and gave him the check, delighted to be able to help him (the poor fellow had not paid his rent for three months and had nothing to eat until his salary came), but at the same time furious that I was helping an enemy of India. I had become almost a chauvinist, and after Maitreyi served us tea and lingered a little in my room, I tried to bring up the subject of Gandhi and the civil revolution. Harold, like any Eurasian, could not bear to hear of such things and was happy about the terror unleashed by the police and army; but that day he had come to ask me for a hundred rupees and could not contradict me. I sensed then his cowardice, and I recognized myself so well in his embarrassment at discussing a belief that I grew sad. But there was something else: Harold had also come to spy on me, to see how I lived here, whether I truly led the life of a “black brute,” as he imagined, or whether I had some comfort. Above all, he had come for Maitreyi; and when he saw her serving tea, blushing as she glanced at me furtively, smiling, at ease in my room and in my presence, he understood and told me so.
“My dear Allan, you are lost now, with no hope of escape…”

“It would be the greatest happiness of my life if I managed to be accepted into this world,” I replied, provoked, looking him straight in the eyes. “A living world, with living people, who suffer and do not complain, who still have an ethic, and whose daughters are saints, not whores like ours. Marry a white girl?” I asked, trying to be sarcastic, “a girl who has never known virginity and will never know perfect surrender? Ours is a dead world, our white continents. I find nothing there anymore. If I were accepted, as I pray to

God, if I were in an Indian family, I would find the strength to rebuild this life of mine, constructed on trifles, on stupid interests and abstractions. I would like to start over, to believe in something, to be happy. I can only be happy in a perfect love, and I find such love only here, here, in this house, in this neighborhood...

I had spoken passionately, sincerely, revealing even to myself certain thoughts I had not fully formed until then. Harold looked at me surprised, amused, embarrassed. He had nothing to answer, for he had understood almost nothing of that “death of the white continent” which had obsessed me for so many years, and besides, he was not in the mood for conversation, eager as he was to leave and savor a glass of whisky, which he had not tasted in quite some time. He asked me absently:
“But your religion?”

“For me, Christianity has not yet been born. There have only been Christian churches, dogmas, and rituals. Christianity is born here, in India, on the land most reconciled with God, where people thirst for love, for freedom, and for understanding. I cannot conceive of a Christianity without freedom and without the primacy of spirituality...”

Harold, who had only ever heard me speak of constructions and physics or comment on the latest frivolous events, was even more surprised to hear my apology for the new Indian Christianity. In fact, at that moment, I myself hesitated, for I was perfectly aware that all my zeal was owed to my love for Maitreyi and its religious and political consequences. Isn’t everything we do determined by such sentimental captivities? I asked myself later, in those months when I tried once more to find the truth. The truth.
“I don’t really understand you,” Harold told me. “May God grant it all turns out well and protect you from enchantments,” he added, rising to leave.
I was somewhat heated from the discussion and paced the room, wondering if I had said all I thought, when Maitreyi entered and embraced me.
“I’m glad he’s gone,” she said. “I missed you...”

Holding her in my arms, I felt for the first time the fear that Maitreyi’s love might one day tire me. I would have liked to be alone, even for an hour after Harold’s departure, for his presence had agitated me and I wanted to meditate, to make an effort to understand, to clarify certain decisions. And Maitreyi had barely waited for the guest to leave, just to fall into my arms. I felt that something of mine was being stolen, that a patch of ground reserved only for me was being trampled. I had given myself completely to Maitreyi and was not alone for a single moment; even on the verge of sleep, her image pursued me. When I needed solitude, why could she not sense it? Why can even the greatest love not divine the other’s desire?...
I still held her in my arms, resting my lips on the crown of her head...

chapters.title: Discovered
paragraphs: Returning from the city, I found a note on my desk: "Come to the library!" I met Maitreyi there, who told me, frightened:
— Khokha knows!
I tried to appear untroubled and to convince her that this meant nothing. Maitreyi looked at me intently, squeezing my hands, as if seeking in my certainty some support.
— We must become engaged before telling baba. He is ill now, it would be hard to tell him, it would disturb him even more.
— But haven’t we been engaged for so long? I wondered. Didn’t you give me the garland, and didn’t I hold you in my arms?
— Now Khokha has seen us, Maitreyi explained, glancing fearfully in all directions. We must strengthen our union, so we are not cursed, so we do not upset the rhythm.

I felt the same mixture of disappointment and delight that I always experienced when deciphering, in Maitreyi’s love and soul, the jungle of superstitions. The rhythm, karma, the ancestors... How many powers had to be consulted and invited to ensure our happiness?...
— I have chosen the stone for your ring, Maitreyi told me, untying from the corner of her sari a green-black gem shaped like a lizard’s head, crossed at the crown by a blood-red streak.

She began to explain the ring to me. It would be crafted according to the Indian marriage ceremony—from iron and gold—like two entwined serpents, one dark and the other yellow, the first representing virility, the other femininity. She had chosen the stone herself from an entire pile, gathered from ancestors and kept in Mrs. Sen’s chest. It had no price, and no one could say she had stolen it by taking it without her mother’s knowledge. Besides, there were many others like it there, in the jewelry chest. (Why did she try so hard to excuse and defend herself? I learned later; she feared I would judge her “in the Christian way,” by some moral or civil criterion.) Not all engagements are sanctified in this way. Usually, Maitreyi explained, only the wife receives a bracelet in which, on the inside, the two threads of gold and iron are intertwined; the husband wears only a ring. But since she could not wear the betrothal bracelet, we had to combine both symbols into a single ring... She spoke to me at length that evening, and I listened, enchanted; although the remnant of lucidity I still possessed rebelled against this uncertain and mystified ceremonial. It seemed to me that any tendency to legislate and

symbolic exteriorization. What I thirsted for most in our love was precisely its spontaneity and autonomy. Yet, when the jeweler brought me the ring, I took it in my hands and turned it every which way with a childish delight. It was crafted with such mastery that it could easily pass for an ordinary ring—more original than others, it’s true, but perfectly camouflaging its symbol. Everyone in the house saw it as such, and if Lilu and Mantu made remarks about a possible or anticipated marriage with an Indian woman, all of it unfolded in an atmosphere of jest. Besides, the engineer was still ill, his leave had been extended, and everyone in the house was concerned only with his care.

The next day, Maitreyi pretended to be more tired than she was and asked to go for a drive to the Lakes in the evening, when she knew almost everyone would be busy. Only Chabii wanted to accompany us, but as she hadn’t been feeling well for several days (she was silent all the time, without saying what was wrong, staring blankly into space, singing without any sense), Mrs. Sen didn’t let her and instead gave us as companion Khokha’s sister, a young and timid widow who worked like a slave and never otherwise had the chance to go for a drive. As we left, I sat beside the driver, while the two of them sat in the back, but as soon as we reached the Lakes, the widow remained in the car (which I had pulled up alongside the path, near a giant eucalyptus), the driver went off to buy himself lemonade, and the two of us set out along the water’s edge.

The Lakes were what I loved most in Calcutta; precisely because they were the only artificial thing in this city risen from the jungle. They had the stillness of an aquarium and, at night, seemed frozen beneath the breath of the bracelet of electric globes. The park seemed endless to me, though I knew well it was fenced in, on one side by the railway, on the other by the road and the slums. I liked to wander along the paths and descend to the water’s edge, where younger trees, planted after the works were finished, grew freely, with a perfect individuality, as if sensing the jungle that had once been there and striving to regain that lost freedom. Beside such a cluster of trees we stopped then. They hid us securely, on all sides. Maitreyi slipped the ring from my finger and closed it in her small fists.
“Now we are engaged, Allan,” she said, gazing ahead at the water.

This solemn beginning irritated me a little. I could not escape my lucidity. (And I loved her, God, how I loved her!) It seemed to me it would be a scene from novels, from the ballads of that Indian Middle Ages, with legendary and mad loves. I carried with me the fears and superstitions of an entire literature, which, if I had not read, I had seen evolving beside me in adolescence and in the first years of youth. I was embarrassed, like any civilized man (I, who believed I could dispense with civilization, could uproot it from myself), by every solemn gesture, every responsible word,
every promise.

Yet Maitreyi continued with a simplicity that began to win me over. She spoke to the water, to the starry sky, to the forest, to the earth. She pressed her fists—bearing the ring—deep into the grass and vowed:

“I bind myself to you, earth, that I shall belong to Allan, and to no one else. I shall grow from him as the grass grows from you. And as you await the rain, so shall I await his coming, and as the rays are to you, so shall his body be to me. I vow before you that our union will bear fruit, for I love him of my own will, and if there is any evil, let it not fall upon him, but upon me, for I have chosen him. You hear me, mother earth, you do not deceive me, my mother. If you feel me near, as I feel you now, with my hand and with the ring, strengthen me to love him always, to bring him unknown joy, to give him a life of fruitfulness and play. Let our life be like the joy of the grasses that grow from you. Let our embrace be like the first day of the monsoon. Let our kiss be rain. And as you never tire, my mother, so may my heart never tire in its love for Allan, whom the sky has birthed far away, and whom you, mother, have brought near to me.”

I listened to her, more and more fascinated, until I could no longer understand her words. She spoke a child’s Bengali, simplified, almost cryptic. I heard the sounds, guessed here and there a word, but the meaning of this incantation escaped me. When she fell silent, I almost feared to touch her, she seemed so enchanted, so inaccessible. She was the first to speak again. (I had remained with one hand on my knee and the other pressed palm-down on the earth, as if I too had bound myself, through some magic of the gesture.)
“Now no one can separate us, Allan. Now I am yours, wholly yours…”

I caressed her, searching for words I had never spoken to her before, but I found nothing new, nothing that could match the fever within me and her transfiguration. (Long ago she had ceased to be the Maitreyi from the car; there was a strange fixity in her face, which haunted me for a long time afterward.)
“One day you will make me your wife and show me the world, won’t you?”
She said this in English and seemed to think she had expressed herself crudely.

“I speak very poor English now, don’t I, Allan? Who knows what you thought of me, hearing me… But I would like to see the world with you, to see it as you see it. It is beautiful and vast, isn’t it? Why do people fight around us? I wish everyone could be happy. No, I’m talking nonsense. How glad I am that it is so, how glad I am…”

She began to laugh. I found myself with the Maitreyi of winter, that innocent and timid girl, speaking discontinuously and paradoxically. It was as if her entire experience, which had matured her, gathered her, brought her closer to womanhood, had been wiped away.

In the days that followed, I understood that this engagement had restored to her both her peace and her passionate playfulness, her sense of free joy. From the moment she confessed our union, her fear vanished, and the obsession with sin no longer tormented her. I rediscovered in her the same enigmatic Maitreyi whom I had first regarded with astonishment and admiration, and who had imperceptibly entered my soul during our games, through those perfectly banal intellectual traps which I believed I had set for her.

We had to hurry to the car, for night had fallen completely. That was the only hour when I did not embrace Maitreyi. We found our companion dozing in the back of the car, her shawl pulled tightly over her head, and she looked at us with a conspiratorial joy when she saw us coming, side by side—myself taller than Maitreyi, but she younger and unimaginably beautiful, her face alive with attentive curiosity, radiant with the joy of newfound freedom in play. (I learned later, also from Maitreyi, that Khokha’s sister had been the first to know of our love and had protected her as best she could; that she—who had suffered so much from an ill-suited marriage, having been wed at twelve to a man she had never seen and whom she feared because he had brutally violated her and beat her every night, before and after love—she had always advised Maitreyi not to be intimidated by the laws of caste and the strictures of family, but to act, and, in case of stubborn opposition, to run away with me into the world. This friend of mine and companion to Maitreyi, the only one who consoled her in her days of cursed misery, I saw very rarely, spoke to only by chance, and never knew her name. I reread my journal several times to find it; I could not, for I had never written it down. And yet, this woman was the only one in the Sen household who loved us both with understanding and selflessness.)

That very night, Chabù grew worse and had to sleep in Mrs. Sen’s room. No one could guess what was wrong, but the symptoms were worrying, for Chabù constantly wanted to lean out the window or over the balcony, always thinking she saw something down in the street, something that was calling to her.

I went to bed, a little tired from the day’s events, and must have begun to dream something strange—of drifting on water, of swans, of fireflies—for I awoke somewhat bewildered, hearing a few knocks at the door. I asked who it was, but no one answered. I must confess I was a little afraid, and I lit the lamp. The fan whirred with that noise you only notice when it stops. I opened the door and stood petrified. Maitreyi had come, trembling all over, barefoot so as not to make a sound, wearing a thin, greenish sari. I didn’t know what to do.
“Turn off the light,” she whispered, entering the room and quickly crouching behind the wicker armchair so as not to be seen by chance from the street.
I turned off the lamp and approached her, stupidly asking:
— What is it with you? Why have you come, Maitreyi? What is it, Maitreyi?

She did not answer me, but simply untied the edge of her sari and remained bare to the waist, in a few gestures she performed with her eyes closed, pressing her lips together and stifling her sigh with difficulty. The vision of her naked body, in that very pale luminous haze in the room, struck me like a miracle I could never have foreseen in all its precise and carnal details. For although I often thought of the first night we would spend together, and although I thirstily imagined our bed where I would come to know her, never could I have pictured Maitreyi’s adolescent body unveiling itself willingly and of her own accord, at night, before me. This I could not imagine, though I sometimes dreamed of a vertiginous union in strange circumstances. What struck me in this act was precisely its simplicity and naturalness; the maiden who comes alone to her fiancé’s room, because nothing separates them anymore.

Slowly, I drew her into my arms, hesitating at first to bring her too close to me, so naked as she was, but encountering her hips still covered by the sari, I slid my hands in a single caress down the arch of her back and uncovered her to her thighs, trembling all over at this sacrilege and kneeling before this naked body, which for me surpassed all beauty and now took part in the miracle. She entwined her arms around my shoulders herself, imploring me to rise, without a word (for she was trembling all over, and the immense joy that had brought her to my room could not entirely banish the fear of that hour). She approached the bed with small, soft steps, and her whole body had acquired a different rhythm in that advance. I wanted to carry her in my arms, but she resisted and lay down herself, kissing my pillow. Only for a moment did I see her stretched out like living bronze on the white sheet, shivering, breathing, and calling me. The next moment I was closing the windows with the wooden shutter, and our room melted into darkness. I felt her beside me, drawing herself in, as if she were trying to hide, to forget herself. It was no longer a bodily thirst, but a thirst for all of me; she would have wished to pass entirely into me, as her soul had passed. I remember nothing after that; for I came to know her without knowing, without memory. Some hours later, as dawn approached, she rose from beside me and put on her sari without looking at me. She said only this, when I opened the door for her (with what precautions, with what heartbeats):
— Our union was ordained by Heaven. Don’t you see that today, on the day of the ring, Chabù did not sleep with me?
I listened to her climbing the stairs to her room, but I heard nothing more, so lightly did she slip along the wall.

In the morning, it was she who called me to tea. She had also brought flowers from the garden and arranged them in vases for me, with a smile as precious as an embrace. She was strikingly pale, her hair loose over her shoulders (I had tangled it, she told me later, and it was impossible for her to comb it) and her lips were bitten. I gazed with immense bliss at the traces of our first night of love. Maitreyi was now possessed of a heightened beauty, as if her whole body had awakened within her, and that lower lip, full and tender, bore its bites like a victory, tempting the gaze and troubling it.

I wondered how this change had gone unnoticed, how her explanations had been so easily accepted. (That Chabù’s illness had kept her from sleeping, that, on the verge of tears all night, she had bitten her lips until they bled, that her father’s illness had exhausted her too much, and so on.)

The day passed quickly, almost without seeing her. For I had to remain at the office all day, working with Mr. Sen’s substitute. When I returned home, I found Maitreyi waiting for me on the veranda, beside the letter box. She showed me a ring made from a hairpin twisted around her finger, bearing instead of a stone a wisteria bead.
"Tonight, don’t lock the door with the bar," she told me, running away.

She came around midnight; this time without trembling. She almost laughed as she embraced me. I was happy that sin did not depress her, that she did not come to our hours of love with the fear of doing wrong. I did not recognize her, so sincere were her embraces, so thirsty her calls, so skillful her caresses. When I caught her caressing me, I could hardly believe she had been a virgin the night before. I had the impression that nothing embarrassed her anymore, though she had not made a single immodest gesture or shown any unconscious exhibitionism. She had found herself in our embrace, rediscovered the game and fulfilled it by giving herself to me entirely, without restriction, without fear.

This girl, who had known nothing of love, was not afraid of it. No caress wearied her, no masculine gesture surprised her. She accepted the courage of every embrace almost without modesty, finding the utmost delight everywhere, nothing disgusting her, nothing tiring her. If she had not feared being heard, she would have sung after every embrace, would have cried out in pain and joy at the moment of union, would have danced about the room with her soft, inhuman steps. She discovered gestures of a lover that humbled me. I, who believed my previous experience would give me some superiority, at least technically, in our nights of love, had long since been surpassed in the imagination of caresses. The certainty with which she kissed, the perfection of her embrace, the astonishing rhythm of her body, different every hour, each time bolder, newer, more spontaneous—all these things almost humbled me. She guessed every suggestion and completed every beginning with an instinct I envied.

She deciphered the longing of my body with a precision that at first embarrassed me. She knew perfectly the moment when I wanted to remain alone, beside her, in bed, far from touch, holding only her hand, and she would withdraw simply, as if for a moment of rest. When I fell into thought, she curled up next to the pillow, embracing it, and closed her eyes, as if asking me not to disturb her. I had discovered a small bedside lamp, which I would place behind the curtain, covering it with her shawl, and which cast a humble light in the room, in which her forms rounded and bronzed. Maitreyi could not bear darkness for long... She wanted to have me with all her eyes, with all her thirst for me, and the embrace in the darkness of those first nights had frightened her.

Often I wondered when she slept, for she always left at dawn, and after two or three hours (during which she meditated and wrote, to delight me the next day at the office with poems and letters composed for our love) she would come downstairs to prepare the tea. She was also the one who knocked at my door in the morning, very discreet and very prudent. And whenever I lingered with my washing, she would scold me childishly. Then her voice was that of an aunt, something familiar and protective, almost maternal, which at first embarrassed me, for I had wanted her only as a lover, but which in the end managed to charm me, revealing to me depths and kinds of love I had not known and which I had condemned a priori, without suspecting their sweetness.

I was tired every afternoon and at the office I worked poorly, disgusted, humiliated by my new boss, an engineer freshly arrived from America and a great enemy of Indian tradition. (Though Bengali, he wore only European suits, even at home, and was utterly ridiculous.) Khokha had undoubtedly noticed my change, for he said to me:
— You look very pale. Why do you sleep with the windows closed?

This made me understand many things. Khokha was spying on us, with cunning and jealousy. From then on I was sure that he knew of Maitreyi’s nocturnal visits and I was afraid he might betray us. That is why I behaved as well as possible with him, bought him cigarettes, gave him books. He was a clever and ambitious boy and wrote film scripts for Indian companies, which were, however, always rejected. He hated us all, though he laughed a lot and appeared friendly.

Chabù was getting worse and worse. The doctors called (first the Indians, then the most renowned English ones) did not know what to say. Probably early madness, some thought; others, a sexual neurosis, caused by a displacement of the uterus. (The poor girl had recently made several dangerous jumps from trees and always skipped the steps, on any staircase.) Chabù now had to stay in bed, in a little room next to Mrs. Sen’s bedroom. She spoke very little and, when she did, she mentioned Robi Thakkur, the “path,” that is, the road she saw from Maitreyi’s room, and whenever she was left alone, she would run to the balcony to look at it, and

she would sing from there, wave her arms, and weep. That is why she was always guarded by Lilu and Khokha’s sisters. Strangely, she recognized only Maitreyi and me; very rarely did she recognize Mrs. Sen. (I wondered, then, how poor Mrs. Sen could maintain her calm and her smile, with her husband suffering from an eye illness and her child nearly mad, how she could manage everything in this large house, be attentive to each of us, never be late with meals, with tea... I sincerely reproached myself that, during all this, I was sleeping with Maitreyi. I awaited the day when she would know and forgive us. My departure to Puri, for a possible conversion, had been postponed again because of the engineer’s illness. Besides, Maitreyi opposed it, and Mrs. Sen was afraid, as the political movements in southern Bengal were becoming ever more bloody.)

Chabù saw my ring and begged me to give it to her to play with. I hesitated then, for I had promised Maitreyi that I would never part with this ring, not even for an hour. I looked at her for permission, and she too had to consent to this separation, for Chabù was crying and incessantly asking me for the ring. When I gave it to her, she knotted it into a handkerchief and tied the handkerchief around her neck. I do not know what drew her to that black stone; she gazed at it constantly, turned it between her fingers, tried to see through it.

Despite all the doctors’ interventions, Chabù’s madness remained unchanged. Then, once more, healers and enchantresses were summoned. An uncle of the girls came, a very gentle and soothing old man, who sang Vaishnava hymns all day long—heartrending and cruel melodies that melted your will and softened your soul—and then the whole household attended, with the engineer sprawled on a chaise longue, a pillow under his head and dark glasses on, while the women, with Mantu, Khokha, and myself, sat on the floor, listening to the song with our heads resting in our palms. Then I witnessed that miracle, the emotion that overwhelmed everyone so deeply that even the engineer himself wept rare tears, and Maitreyi had hidden her head in her shawl and was sobbing. I rebelled against this suffering, which violated the soul, and I left the room. But I could do nothing once I reached my chamber, for the kirtan echoed through the whole house and I heard it even more hauntingly from my isolation.

The same uncle, who tried to calm poor Chabù’s mind with song, had brought a folk remedy, a sort of paste of herbs kneaded with honey, which had to be placed on the crown of her head, directly on the skin. And I witnessed a bitter scene, when no one had the courage to cut the girl’s hair at the root, and they decided that I should do it. Chabù was unaware of anything. I caressed her forehead, looked into her eyes, and let the scissors cut freely while I spoke to her so she would not hear the grinding of the metal, and Maitreyi, from behind the bed, gathered the locks in her hands and hid them in a kerchief, so that Chabù would not notice. It took me about a quarter of an hour to manage to leave her crown bare, and then Mrs. Sen applied the paste

that warm one. Chabù looked at all of us once, tried to feel her head, then tore off the scarf with a ring from her neck and began to cry, softly, only the tears streaming down her beautiful, dark face, without sobbing, without trembling. I did not know if she was crying because she realized she was half bald, for she had been crying constantly, and out of the blue, ever since she had fallen ill, and even more fiercely when she wanted to get up and look out the window, and we would not let her.

There were days of which I remember nothing now, so restless did they pass. I know that I would come home from the office and go straight upstairs to find out how the engineer and Chabù were doing, then I would go down to bathe and eat, then go up again to keep watch at the girl’s bedside (she often called for me in her delirium, calling me “Allan-dadà,” and whenever I came, she would calm down a little), and at night I spent the hours with Maitreyi, who gave herself to me in madness, frightened by all that was happening around us, desiring me ever more sincerely and thirstily. I would wake in the mornings with a dreadful exhaustion and an unexplainable fear. Mr. Sen kept postponing his eye operation, and the doctors had recommended him complete rest, yet everything that happened in the house and everything that might break out at any moment endangered his sight. That is why I feared we might betray ourselves too soon, for Maitreyi would come to me at night, when the others had not yet fallen into a deep sleep, and in Chabù’s room she would squeeze my arm, lean her body on my shoulder, kiss my hand, and all these things could be noticed at any moment. Besides, Khokha had caught us in each other’s arms several times, and Lilu and Mantu suspected our love very much, though not at all the fact that we were lovers.

Yet sometimes Maitreyi behaved in a way I could not understand, which made me doubt wildly and tormented me. Because she had once suffered from beri-beri, her calves would swell slightly in the evenings, imperceptibly, and the doctors had recommended massages on days of great humidity. There were mornings when Lilu or Khokha’s sisters would massage her whole body, naked, with a kind of greasy oil, which they could then barely wash off. But sometimes, Maitreyi would feel pain, and massages had to be done immediately, only on her calves, and for this she would call Khokha into her room. This irritated me, and I once told Maitreyi so, but she looked at me in astonishment and replied that surely I did not expect her to call me for such an unpleasant thing, which masseurs do for money. But Khokha was not a professional, he was young and made her laugh, and this touching of her body with his black, greedy hands made me shudder. Once, in the evening, Maitreyi called out to Khokha from the inner balcony, seized by stabbing pains (for it had rained two days in a row), and because he was absent, she called for the chauffeur. This made me lose my mind, and I was tempted to go up to her room and say something wild to her, but I was ashamed of

my thoughts, although I did not feel ashamed, a few minutes later, to spy on her from the garden. Indeed, the light was not yet lit in her room, though she could have done so, out of decency and out of love for me. I imagined all sorts of disgusting scenes, I recalled so many episodes from the novels I had read, in which chauffeurs become the lovers of worldly women, so many reflections on the faithlessness of women, on the total lie that ferments in their souls. A host of small, unnoticed details then flooded my mind. Once, Mantu had locked the door with the bar, in Maitreyi’s room, and I could hear them from below, struggling and shouting, for, supposedly, it was a hand-to-hand fight, but when they came out, Mantu was red and flustered, while Maitreyi was pale, her hair disheveled over her shoulder. (It is true that she had told me long ago that Mantu was disgusting, that he had tried to touch her, and she had slapped him, that she had complained to her father, but since he had fallen ill, Mantu had become indispensable to the household and could not be dismissed. Likewise, I remember that Maitreyi had also told me that another uncle of hers, also a cousin of the engineer, had once tried to kiss her breasts and embrace her, but then Mr. Sen had intervened at once, and that poor man still regrets his gesture, for he was dismissed from his post and retired to his village, where he lives a dog’s life. Maitreyi did not often complain about this carnal passion she aroused in men, even those bound to her by blood, and which caused her so much suffering, for she would have wished to awaken something else in people besides a mere desire for possession.)

Other scenes flashed before my eyes then: Khokha, for instance, with whom Maitreyi lingered long on the veranda, in the dark, and she came to dinner troubled, while the boy did not even have the courage to appear, so much, I believed, was he excited. And all these details tormented me, and it seemed to me that everyone desired Maitreyi, that she abandoned herself to all.
