Why does the chauffeur spy on us, if he does not desire her, if he does not hope that, one day, he might risk everything and enter her room, even if he would have to flee that very night, without his wages? I imagined things utterly absurd and suffered terribly, for my imagination did not spare me for a moment, but filmed for me the most tormenting details. I was incapable of tearing myself away from this sickly pain of seeing Maitreyi in the arms of others.

I returned to my room, crushed to death, and during dinner, I kept my feet hidden, tucking them under my chair. I set the wooden bar across the door when I went to bed, resolved not to open for Maitreyi, whatever might happen. I was awake when she came and tried the door, but I pretended to be asleep and not to hear. She began to knock harder, then to call me, ever more insistently, at last shaking the door. I was afraid someone might hear, so I opened for her.
“Why won’t you let me in?” burst out Maitreyi, her face in tears, pale, trembling. “Don’t you want me anymore?”
I closed the door again and, both of us sitting on the bed, I

Avoiding her embrace, I told her, as best I could, of my suffering. She wound her arms around my shoulders and began to kiss me greedily, digging her nails into my flesh at the same time. I went on speaking, insensible to the warmth of her body, telling her everything I had endured when I knew she was alone with a strange man, who was caressing her thighs. I showed her how hideous was this abandonment to the caresses of another.
“I would have preferred if he had forced me,” Maitreyi said suddenly, bursting into tears.

“With you, as you are—sensual and unconscious—it would have been very easy for him to do so,” I replied, looking at her savagely. “You still like these improbable possessions, these barbaric and grotesque acts, fundamentally cheap, with which that old beast, who was supposedly your spiritual master, has filled your head…”

I rose from beside her and began to pace the room agitatedly, saying cruel things and wounding her with every word. I hated her terribly in those moments, not because she had betrayed me, but because she had made me believe blindly in her love and purity, had made me ridiculous by forcing me to give all I had, to reveal myself before her, to assimilate her desires and will; I was maddened by the thought that I had renounced myself for a virgin who deceived me with the first man who came along. For, although I had not believed for a moment in the reality of this “betrayal,” I had worked myself up by speaking and ended by seeing in all of Maitreyi’s behavior a farce.

If she had been a white woman, I would not have believed all this, because, although I knew their insubstantial nature and their mad caprices, I also knew them to be animated by a certain pride, a certain restraint, which would have prevented them from giving themselves to the first comer. But I could not understand Maitreyi, I could not fix her within a well-defined framework of possible reactions, and it seemed to me that, primitive and unconscious as she was, she could have given herself to anyone, without thinking for a moment of the horror of such an act, without being responsible. In those moments of jealousy turned to hatred, I forgot all my experience of the last seven or eight months, I forgot Maitreyi’s almost superstitious innocence and considered it all deception. Then I understood that nothing endures in the soul, that the most tried and tested trust can be annulled by a single gesture, that the sincerest possessions never prove anything, for sincerity too can be repeated, with another, with others; that, in the end, everything is forgotten or can be forgotten, for the happiness and trust accumulated in so many months of love, in so many nights spent together, had now vanished as if by magic, and only a wounded masculine pride and a terrible fury against myself survived in me.

Maitreyi had listened to all this with a suffering that exasperated me even more. She bit her lips until they bled, looked at me with wide open eyes, as if she could not tell whether she was dreaming or living this scene in reality.
“But what did I say, my God, what did I say?” she burst out at last.
“You spoke of a rape,” I clarified, trying to control myself.

“But why don’t you understand?” she lamented, weeping. “You are so disgusted with me that you don’t even want to understand me. You don’t think of me at all. You once told me that if I had been violated and thrown out of my home, you would still love me. I thought how good it would have been if that had happened. Then there would be no obstacle left in the way of our union. Allan, understand that we will never be united and we will die like this, with our sin upon us. Even if you convert, they will not accept you as my husband. They want something else, why don’t you remember? But if someone were to dishonor me, they would have to throw me out into the streets, because otherwise the sin would fall upon the whole house. And then I could be your wife, I would become a Christian too, because for a Christian it is not a sin to be dishonored by force, and you would love me even then. Wouldn’t you always love me? Tell me, Allan, tell me you will never forget me. You know what awaits me if you forget…”

I was moved, I confess, as if I had awakened from a nightmare; my anger had passed, and her words pained me. I wanted to ask her forgiveness, but I didn’t know how, every gesture I imagined embarrassed me, every gesture of reconciliation (I saw myself falling at her feet, and that act seemed false, ridiculous, hideous; or to take her hand, at first as a friend, then to squeeze it more warmly and kiss it? That attempt at closeness meant nothing to me either, it was more an automatism, and it seemed to me that Maitreyi would immediately sense the awkwardness with which I would do it). I did not know what to do and only looked at her, trying to put all my remorse and all my love into my gaze. But Maitreyi’s eyes were full of tears and she was too lost to see my regret, and then she collapsed at my feet, clasping my knees and asking me if her love tired me, if I was afraid of our sin, and other such questions, which now, as I write, seem foolish, but then they seemed to be carried by fire, so suffocating and tormenting did I feel them.

I took her in my arms, and Maitreyi felt from my embrace and the incoherent words I uttered that love burned in me just as insatiably, and she guessed how much I suffered from my blindness, from my lack of understanding. We both avoided speaking further of marriage, for I was beginning to understand that things were not as simple as I had thought at first, and so I preferred to avoid that thought rather than endure the image of a possible and eventual separation from Maitreyi.
We both thought we heard footsteps outside the window and fell silent, extinguishing the lamp. But then the footsteps turned toward the veranda and we heard knocking at the corridor door.
We were both petrified with fear. The knocking ceased for a few minutes, only to return at my shuttered window. I

I understood then that it was Khokha, probably returning late from a neighborhood cinema, and I pretended to delay opening the door, to give Maitreyi time to reach her room upstairs. Khokha asked me in passing:
"Did you speak with someone?"
"No," I replied curtly, closing the door.
But then I heard Mrs. Sen's voice as well, upstairs, on the gallery parallel to the room where Maitreyi slept.
chapters.summary: Allan and Maitreyi's secret relationship is threatened when Khokha discovers them, leading to a symbolic engagement by the lakes.

chapters.title: Love Under Suspicion
paragraphs: I thought everything had been discovered and I tossed and turned all night, unable to close my eyes. Toward morning, Maitreyi came to me again, without my noticing, and slipped a note under my door: "Mother knows nothing. Don't worry. Don't betray yourself. Maitreyi."

When I read it, I felt as if I had been pardoned or that my sentence had been postponed. I wrote Maitreyi a long letter, in which I told her that we must restrain our imprudent nightly meetings now, when everyone is watchful—both the engineer and Chabù. The truth was that I myself did not know how this relationship of ours would end. Maitreyi had made a number of allusions to Mrs. Sen, pretending that I had fallen in love with a friend of hers (whom we had nicknamed Anasuya back when we were reading and discussing Shakuntala together), and that I did not know how to ask for her hand in marriage; and Mrs. Sen had replied that such marriages, resulting from a simple sentimental infatuation, lead only to misfortune for both spouses, because nothing lasting and nothing happy can come from a passion when that passion has not been corrected by tradition—that is, by family, by people who know what marriage and love mean, matters far more serious than we young people imagine, for to be married does not mean "to gather flowers together," nor to let oneself be consumed by an ephemeral and deceptive passion.

I confess that I recognized myself entirely in Mrs. Sen's judgment, for I had no other source than passion and we had thought only of ourselves, loving each other. And Mrs. Sen, discussing my camouflaged love for Anasuya, told Maitreyi that a marriage is never founded on love, but on sacrifice, on renunciation, on complete abandonment to the will of destiny. This was a conception that not even my sincerest Indianization could accept. But it made me understand how many obstacles I would encounter the day I decided to ask for Maitreyi's hand in marriage. I even wondered whether her solution—rape—might not be more effective. Then they would be faced with a fait accompli and would have to give her to me, for no one else would be
taken her. Only now do I truly understand how much I loved Maitreyi, if I could contemplate such fantastic solutions.

The days passed, all the same, filled with repeated fears and ever more dangerous risks, until the event which I shall recount below. Only one occurrence interrupted this succession of desperate, memoryless days (for, if I did not have my journal, I would remember nothing from that time, so vivid and attentive was I to everything happening around me, and I never had a moment to recall or to meditate, to connect events one to another, to relive certain scenes; so now I must rely on those very brief notes, as if deciphering someone else’s life, for the memory of those days and nights of burning agony is lost to me). That event was Maitreyi’s birthday, on the 10th of September. The engineer insisted on celebrating it with all possible pomp, though he was still ill, and Chabu almost unconscious. Maitreyi was turning seventeen, and this age holds some hidden meaning in India; moreover, her volume of poetry, Uddhitta, printed just a few days before, had been received by the Bengali press as a true revelation, and Mr. Sen wished to invite all the elite of Calcutta’s letters and arts to this ceremony, which he wanted transformed into an artistic tournament. All that was most distinguished in Bengal was to come, except for Tagore, who was still in Europe. Chatterji, author of Srikantha, was expected, as well as the dancer Uday Shankar, whose godlike beauty and fascinating rhythm had long made me jealous, for at one of his festivals, in August, Maitreyi had utterly forgotten me and watched him, her arms resting on the balcony, enthralled, hallucinated. For several days after, she spoke only of him and insisted on meeting him, to “learn,” she said, “the secret of dance.” The editorial staff of the magazine Prabuddha Bharatta was also to come, among whom Maitreyi counted many admirers, such as the very original poet Acintyia, much discussed at the time, for he had begun publishing a novel similar to James Joyce’s Ulysses and had aroused against himself the entire cohort of elderly Bengali writers.

I was a little intimidated by the preparations being made for the 10th of September. I knew that on that day Maitreyi would belong to me less than ever, for she was proud and gracious, and would try to charm all the guests. I had bought her a few books as a gift, and wanted to give them to her at the very break of day. That night she had stayed with me only half an hour, for she had worked like a slave to tidy the house (the staircase was all draped in old carpets, vases of flowers placed everywhere, two rooms upstairs emptied for receiving guests, mattresses and shawls brought in to transform them into two immense divans, on which one had to climb barefoot to take one’s place; all the women had worked terribly hard for this ceremony, and Maitreyi, who wished to decorate the carpets on the stairs with paintings, had dropped a frame with a portrait

the magnificent one by Tagore, given by the poet himself with a dedication, and this fact shook her, for she saw in it a very bad omen, especially since the frame had splintered and the canvas was torn).

I met her at dawn in the library, where I brought her the books, each with an innocent dedication, and I embraced her, wishing her a serene life and all the happiness she deserved. I had tears in my eyes as I spoke those few banal words. Yet it seemed to me that she was somehow absent. She slipped from my arms much more easily than on other occasions.

The afternoon was for me an endless masquerade. I had put on the Bengali silk costume and had to entertain all those illustrious people like a true host, for the engineer was immobilized on a divan in the middle of the room (the only chair there; all the others sat on mattresses), Mrs. Sen and the other women were taking care of the ladies, who stayed in another room, unseen, while Mantu remained downstairs, in the corridor, to serve as a guide for the guests. Only Maitreyi came among us, to distribute volumes of Uddhitta and to bring the sweets. I saw how everyone devoured her with their eyes (for she was admirable then, pale and gentle, with bare arms emerging from a blue silk sari), how they desired her, and this spectacle was unbearable to me, because no one there knew that Maitreyi was mine and mine alone, and perhaps each of them was imagining a host of possibilities concerning her. When the handsome Uday Shankar arrived (it is true, less handsome seen up close than he was on stage, but, in any case, the most fascinating man I have ever met, precisely because, alongside a virile and supple body, he had an extraordinary grace in his gestures and glances, a femininity that did not embarrass, a warmth and an extraordinary communicativeness), Maitreyi blushed all over and invited him to eat on the balcony, for so many visitors crowded around him that poor Uday could not swallow a bite. I tried to hide my agitation, for I sensed in this magnificent dancer something more than a seductive man, I sensed outright a kind of magic, which could have driven an entire city mad, not only a lovesick, bewildered girl like Maitreyi. I knew that no one could have resisted him, and if I envied him for this, I did not hate him, for I would have liked to discover in Maitreyi’s eyes a preference for him, so that I too could free myself from love. I knew that the moment I saw with certainty a preference, my love would collapse without hesitation. I told myself that if Maitreyi could not oppose to Uday Shankar’s magic the mysticism of our love, she deserved nothing more than to be abandoned like the most ordinary woman.

I happened to step out into the corridor and saw Maitreyi sitting next to Uday, asking him very shyly questions I could not hear. I was surprised at how calmly I regarded this scene. A few minutes later I met Maitreyi on the stairs, and she said to me, squeezing my arm furtively:

"I tried to learn from Shankar the secret of the dance, but he cannot tell me anything. He is a great fool. He does not understand rhythm and speaks as if from books. I should not have invited him. On stage, he was like a god, but when I asked him to speak to me, he stammered nonsense, like a mere craftsman... How is it that the dance did not make him wise?
I did not know how to thank her for these few words. She led me to the library and, her face aglow, caressing my hand, she said:
'You are dear to me, Allan, more and more dear to me...'

I was preparing to embrace her when we heard a commotion upstairs, Mrs. Sen calling for Maitreyi and other alarmed women’s voices. We both rushed up with an inexplicable fear in our hearts, as if we sensed some misfortune. We found Chabù struggling to leap over the balcony into the street, and several women trying to hold her back. The poor girl had been left almost alone on this day when no one knew where their head was, and so she had dressed herself in the most beautiful sari she owned (usually she wore short, European dresses, and when she put on a sari, she seemed much older) and wanted to attend the celebration as well. When she went out into the corridor, she saw too many people and became frightened. Then she went to the balcony, where Shankar had stood only a few minutes before, and from there began to contemplate the 'road' and to sing, as was her habit. Two guests noticed her just as she was about to climb over the balustrade and rushed to catch her. She struggled a lot, and everyone crowded into the corridor (the engineer had lost his temper again and was scolding his wife harshly). I had to take her in my arms and carry her like a child to her room, for she recognized me at once and clung to my chest, weeping, calling out to me:
'Allan-dadà, Allan-dadà.'
When I laid her on her bed, she asked me, suddenly sullen:
'Do they want to sell Maitreyi?'

The next day, everyone was exhausted from the great ceremony, which had cost almost five hundred rupees and so much effort. There had been speeches, a lavish meal on the terrace, and Maitreyi had received numerous gifts, mostly books. Only on the morning of her birthday, someone had sent an enormous bouquet of flowers, with an envelope, and when Maitreyi saw the handwriting, she became completely unsettled and read the letter quickly, constantly afraid someone might catch her. Hearing footsteps on the stairs, she hurried into my room and handed me the letter:
'Hide it in your desk and make sure no one takes it. I’ll ask for it later,' she said, blushing.
I confess that I understood nothing, but I did not suspect

something bad, for otherwise she would not have given me to keep a letter which, although written in Bengali, I could decipher or could ask an Indian friend to translate for me precisely. I still keep that letter, although I have not yet dared to read it. I often wonder what admirer sent her those flowers then, and why Maitreyi lied, saying she had received the bouquet from a school friend who could not come...

Then followed the same days and the same nights, of very short duration, it is true, for only a week after Maitreyi’s birthday the event occurred for which I began to write this notebook. I should recount these last days in greater detail, but I remember almost nothing, and the journal—which did not foresee so sudden a change—preserves only the skeleton of a life I can no longer sense or evoke. Later, and even while writing this story, I have reflected on my fate never to guess the future, never to foresee anything beyond the facts of each day. Who would have believed that, imperceptibly, such great changes could come to pass...

Every evening I went to the Lakes, and sometimes I took Chabù along. The Engineer was the one who convinced us that both Maitreyi and I needed to rest in the evenings, after the agitated life we had led in the past weeks, caring for the sick. It is true that Maitreyi had begun to lose weight, and Chabù, who had suddenly calmed down after the crisis of September 10th, also needed walks in the open air, after so much time spent shut up in a single room. And so we would leave every dusk, to return at nine or ten at night. Chabù spoke almost nothing and usually sat on a bench or at the edge of the water, watching, singing softly, weeping. The two of us remained close to her and talked at length, embraced in secret, sought each other’s hands, made plans. Maitreyi would always say to me, like a refrain that obsessed her:
“One day you will take me away from here, and I will go into the world, you will show me the world too...”

She had begun to think seriously of running away, especially since I had confessed to her that I had considerable savings in the bank, for from my salary of 400 rupees I had spent almost nothing since coming to Bhowanipore.

One evening (it was September 16th), Chabù felt ill while looking at the lake, and I took her in my arms to lay her down on a bench. There we sat, Maitreyi and I, close to her, stroking her head, speaking gently, trying to make her laugh, for in those last days Chabù laughed at every little thing, and the doctors said it did her good.
“Why don’t you love dadà?” she suddenly asked Maitreyi.
We almost burst out laughing, for Chabù often spoke nonsense and we were not afraid of her.
"— But I love him very much," answered Maitreyi, smiling.
"If you love him, kiss him," demanded Chabù. Maitreyi began to laugh even harder and told her she was talking nonsense, that a well-behaved girl like her shouldn't say such things.

"Love is not nonsense," said Chabù, very seriously. "Come on, kiss him. Look, I'll kiss him." Indeed, she got up from the bench and kissed me on the cheek, and then, still laughing, Maitreyi kissed me on the other cheek.
"Are you satisfied now?" she asked her.
"You should have kissed him on the mouth," replied Chabù.
"Come on, control yourself," said Maitreyi, blushing.

But I was happy that this little sister of mine (for truly, I loved Chabù very much) had understood our love, and I urged Maitreyi to kiss me. Since she refused, I slipped my hand toward her breast, under her shawl, and let my palm rest, gently cupping her left breast, pressing to feel her heart and at the same time to compel her to kiss me. (Maitreyi could not endure this caress without immediately falling into my arms.) By chance, Chabù also wanted to put her hand on Maitreyi’s chest, to urge her to kiss me. And there she encountered my hand, which I withdrew as quickly as I could, but not before attracting Chabù’s attention. She began to laugh.
"Did you see that dadà had his hand on your chest?" burst out Chabù, triumphant.
"Don’t talk nonsense," snapped Maitreyi. "It was my hand."

"As if I don’t know, as if I didn’t feel dadà’s ring..." Her clarification sent a shiver through me, but since I knew that Chabù often spoke without rhyme or reason, I was not afraid of the consequences. Maitreyi did not kiss me on the mouth, and soon we had to return to the car, for night had fallen. By the time we reached home, I had forgotten the incident. That night, Maitreyi did not come to me. Out of caution, she confessed to me the next day.

I do not remember how I spent the time until nearly six o’clock, when I dressed in my Bengali costume, waiting for us to leave by car. But no one came to announce me. A little irritated, I asked the driver if we were not going to the Lakes that evening, and he replied (did it only seem so to me, or was he truly insolent?) that he had received orders to take the car to the garage. A few minutes later I met Lilu in the corridor. He told me that Mrs. Sen would no longer allow either Maitreyi or Chabù to go out to the Lakes.

All this seemed very obscure to me; the mystery vexed me, it seemed as if a truth was being hidden from me, a truth I absolutely and urgently needed. I tried to meet Maitreyi, without success, and so I remained in my room, tormented by thoughts. (Strangely, I was not afraid; I only wanted to know precisely what had happened, why Mrs. Sen had ordered the driver to take the car to the garage and why...
(that I could not see Maitreyi.)

At the table, when the servant called me (usually someone from the household would announce me), I found Mrs. Sen and Maitreyi. They were silent. I wanted to appear untroubled, and I think I succeeded marvelously. Mrs. Sen sought my eyes, and I did not avoid her gaze. I was astonished by her direct, scrutinizing looks, as if she were trying to penetrate the depths of my true soul; her face had taken on a strange concentration, with a mocking smile twisting her lips, always reddened by pan. She served me in silence, politely, and then sat again with her elbows on the table, watching me. Perhaps she wondered how I had managed to deceive her for so long, how I had fooled her with my purity and respect. In her hostile and ironic presence, I sensed an unceasing question: could I really have been like that? I did not know what kind of “like that” Mrs. Sen imagined, but I felt the question, and so I tried to appear as relaxed as possible, I spoke, looked her in the eyes, asked how Mr. Sen was doing, why the others were not coming to the table, as if nothing had happened.

Maitreyi pressed her legs against mine, as if to break them. She put all her final passion and all her fear into this clenching of her thighs. She wanted to caress me more sweetly than ever, and I felt her warm foot slowly, gently, soothingly touch my calf; it was as if she wanted to console me, to strengthen me in this danger, which I sensed but did not know. Then she caught my foot between her thighs and squeezed it as in a last embrace, as if she were striving to communicate to me a warmth and a passion I would not forget when I would be left separated from her, far away.
Someone called Mrs. Sen upstairs, and as soon as we were alone, Maitreyi whispered to me, biting her lips to master her emotion:
“Chabù told everything to Mother, but I denied it. Do not be afraid, I remain yours. If they question you, confess nothing, otherwise, who knows…”
Tears welled up in her eyes and she wanted to seize my arm, as was her habit, but Mrs. Sen was coming down the stairs, and then she whispered through clenched teeth:
“Come tomorrow before dawn to the library…”

These were the last words Maitreyi spoke to me, for Mrs. Sen took her upstairs, and I went to my room extremely downcast, bewildered, and almost incapable of understanding what might happen the next day.

I could not sleep at all, but smoked pipe after pipe, in the broad and restful jet, waiting for dawn. The hours struck one after another in the night, and with each of them I evoked the coming of Maitreyi into that room, and I could scarcely believe it possible that I might never see her here again, beside me, ready to undress as soon as I closed the windows, ready to embrace me and weep. I thought it could not be that after only two or three weeks of love, Maitreyi should be taken from me. As I sat alone, in the darkness, I saw her again in every corner, in every

her attitudes as a lover, I forgot all the torments I had endured because of her, all the doubts, and I felt within me, boundless, a love that Maitreyi had never even suspected. I awaited the dawn so I could tell her that a simple separation for one night and the threat to our love had revealed to me my true feelings, and only now did I understand how dear she was to me—now, when I feared I might lose her. I almost wept there, alone, thinking that I could lose her; the mere thought that I might never have her by my side again sent a shiver through me and clouded my mind. I did not believe I could survive, sane, a separation from Maitreyi. If, when I knew she was mine, with no one to hinder me from speaking to her and drawing her close whenever I wished, I loved her, then now, when we were separated by some unknown danger, my love had grown until it suffocated me, and I felt I was going mad waiting for the hour when I could see her and hold her in my arms again.

During the night I went out several times into the courtyard to spy, and I always saw light in the engineer’s room, I heard voices there, sometimes a whimper, which I could not guess whose it might be (Maitreyi, Chabù, Khokha’s sister?). All this alarmed me greatly. I returned again to my seat and tried to understand what Maitreyi’s words could mean: “Chabù has told everything…” What could Chabù have said in her madness? Everything she had seen and understood? I thought perhaps she had once caught Maitreyi coming or going from her room, but I learned later that what she had said was less grave. That day, Mrs. Sen was washing her hair, and Chabù kept crying. She asked her why she was crying and Chabù replied that no one loved her, while everyone loved Maitreyi. Everyone came for her birthday, bringing her gifts. And especially I loved Maitreyi very much. “How do you know?” Mrs. Sen asked, jokingly. “Allan dadà kisses her and puts his hand on her chest, but no one kisses me…” She suffered and wept so sincerely that Mrs. Sen questioned her several times, and Chabù confessed everything she had seen: how the two of us sat together and laughed, and kissed, and embraced at the Lakes (and I, who thought Chabù noticed nothing). Mrs. Sen immediately called Maitreyi and asked her if what Chabù had said was true. Then she ordered the driver to put the car in the garage and took Maitreyi upstairs, onto the terrace, made her swear on her ancestors and the gods, and began to interrogate her, threatening her. Maitreyi denied everything, admitting only that she had kissed me a few times in jest, and I had kissed her on the forehead, but nothing else had happened. And she begged her on her knees not to tell the engineer anything, for I would suffer, and I was not guilty. If she was asked, Maitreyi would never see me again, for only she had sinned. (She thought, as I learned later, that in the meantime she could run away with me. She feared only Mr. Sen, who might lock her in her room or marry her off in a few days,

before she had time to see me and arrange her escape. That night, they locked her in Mrs. Sen’s room, and Mrs. Sen told the engineer everything, staying up late to discuss what must be done, so that nothing would be discovered by the neighbors, for then the curse would fall upon the entire family...

All this I only learned on the second or third day, from Khokha, but that night I suspected far graver things; I suspected that Chabà had caught her one night and told Mrs. Sen. Before four in the morning, I went to the library to wait for Maitreyi with news. I stayed there until daylight, hidden behind the shelves, but Maitreyi did not come, nor did Khokha’s sister or Lilu, through whom she might have sent me a written note. At seven, Mrs. Sen came downstairs to prepare tea, and I had to slip very carefully into my room so as not to be seen.
I was just waiting to be called for tea when the engineer entered my room, his black glasses well hiding his gaze, trembling a little from weakness, and began, somewhat moved but friendly:

“My dear Allan, I have decided to undergo that eye operation the doctors have been urging me to have for so long. I will probably have to stay in the sanatorium for two or three months, and so I thought to send the family to Midnapur, to some relatives of mine. And since you too are a bit tired, it would be good for you to take a rest somewhere in the mountains.”
“When must I leave?” I articulated with a calm that surprised me. (In fact, I still did not quite realize what was happening to me, and that day I did a number of things without being aware of them.)
“Today, in fact, for this afternoon I am going to the sanatorium,” said the engineer, watching me from beneath his black brows.
“But I have nowhere to go, I must find a place to stay, I have to take my things...”

I found the strength to resist, though it felt as if all the blood had drained from my veins, and I feebly pointed to the few things I owned: a bed, a wardrobe, the bookcase, two trunks, the writing desk. The engineer smiled very politely.

“A resourceful young man like you always finds a way out. If you leave right now, you’ll find a place by one o’clock. Khokha will bring your things in the afternoon with a truck. Perhaps you’ll stay with one of your friends until you leave for the mountains, and then you’ll settle in better...”

I was trembling all over when he stood up to leave. I instinctively moved toward the wardrobe to take my helmet and leave at once, but Mrs. Sen, who had been standing in the corridor and had listened to everything, entered the room and said to me with a smile:
“You can’t leave here until you’ve eaten...”
“I can’t eat anything anymore,” I replied faintly.
"I will ask you myself, and you will eat," continued Mrs. Sen in the same tone. "The tea is ready."

"What good is it now?" I asked, my voice growing fainter. (I felt I might collapse at any moment, for I knew I was leaving and I had not yet seen Maitreyi, and I did not know what she was doing up there.)

The engineer left, and I burst into wild sobs, tearing at my hair, biting my fists. I stretched out in the armchair, exhausted, almost suffocated by a pain for which I no longer knew a name, for it was neither love nor suffering, but a feeling of utter collapse, as if I had suddenly awakened alone in a cemetery, with no one beside me to whom I could complain, from whom I could expect comfort. It was as if I had been torn into ten pieces, for I felt my body was nothing but a wound, my soul scattered, I had neither will nor strength to collect myself even for a moment.

Lilu entered, in tears as well, and quickly handed me a scrap of paper. "They won't let me see you. Do not waste your life, do not let yourself be defeated. Go out into the world and show everyone your purity. Be a man and you will hear of me soon. Maitreyi." The handwriting was shaky, in makeshift English, stained with ink. I quickly hid the paper in my palm, for Mrs. Sen was coming, with the servant, bringing me tea.
"I cannot eat, I cannot eat anything," I said, weeping.

"Please, take a cup of tea," Mrs. Sen spoke gently. I thought I detected in her voice a hint of pity and a little understanding, and, remembering how kind she had been to me, how much she had loved me and called me her son, for she had so wished for a son alongside her two daughters, I could no longer restrain myself and fell at her feet, embracing them, weeping.
"Forgive me, mother, do not let me leave this place!" I burst out, "forgive me, forgive me..."

Lilu was crying, leaning against the door. Mrs. Sen did not make a single gesture of comfort, but remained upright and smiling while I writhed at her feet. I felt this coldness and stood up, wiping my eyes, sighing.
"Take your tea," she said.

I reached for the cup, but a sob choked me and I hid my face in my arm. Lilu could bear it no longer and fled down the corridor, crying. Mrs. Sen remained there, by the door, looking at me with the same frozen, slightly mocking smile, urging me:
"Take your tea..."

I peeled a banana as if in a dream and sipped from the cup in which the tea had grown cold. My tears had suddenly ceased, and I only sighed. When she saw I had finished my cup, Mrs. Sen went out into the corridor and called the servant to take away the tray.
"May I see the children before I leave?" I begged, pleading.
Mr. Sen entered just then and said to me:
"Maitreyi is a little unwell, she cannot come down from her room." Then, turning to Mrs. Sen:
“Call Chabù.”
As soon as Mrs. Sen left the room, the engineer handed me a sealed envelope and said:
“Read this only after you have left my house. And if you wish to thank me for the good I have done you here, in India, respect what I ask of you…”

He left before I had time to utter another word. I took the envelope with a trembling weakness and slipped it automatically into my pocket. When I saw Chabù, I immediately gathered her in my arms and began to rock her, weeping.
“What have you done, Chabù, what have you done?”
The poor girl understood nothing, but seeing me cry, she too began to weep and kiss me on the cheek, for I had bowed my head to her frail body and rocked her thus, without knowing.
“What have you done, Chabù?” was all I could say.
“But what did I know?” she asked, as if trying to awaken. “Why are you crying, dadà? Why are you crying?”
I let her go to wipe my face. Besides, Mr. and Mrs. Sen had returned and were standing in the doorway, both cold as ice, as if to say: “Come, it’s time for you to leave…”

I kissed Chabù once more on both cheeks, then, regaining my composure, I took my helmet, knelt before Mrs. and Mr. Sen, placing my palms on their right foot—the most vulnerable greeting I knew—and left.
“Good-bye, Allan,” said the engineer, extending his hand.
But I pretended not to see and went on ahead, down the corridor. Chabù ran after me, sobbing.
“Where are you going, dadà? Where is Allan-dadà going?” she asked her mother.
“Dadà is ill and is going to get well,” Mrs. Sen told her in whispered Bengali, holding her in her arms so she would not run out into the street after me.
As I descended the steps of the veranda, I lifted my eyes to the balcony wreathed in wisteria and saw Maitreyi for a moment.
Then I heard myself called, a short, frightened cry, and saw her collapse onto the balcony. I wanted to turn back, but met the engineer in the corridor.
“Have you forgotten something, Allan?” he asked, suspiciously.
“Nothing, sir, I have forgotten nothing…”

I left quickly. I got into the first car and gave Harold’s address. As we started off, I tried to look once more at the house in Bhowanipore, but my eyes filled with tears, the car turned, and I saw nothing more.

I came to myself as the car was just turning toward Park Street. I opened Sen’s envelope and read, with a tightened heart, what he had written to me in English, without any opening salutation, on a sheet bearing in the upper corner the words “strictly confidential.”
underlined.

"You are a stranger, and I do not know you. But if you are capable of considering anything sacred in your life, I beg you never to enter my house again, nor to try to see or write to any member of my family. If you wish to see me personally, seek me at the office, and if you ever wish to write to me, write only those things which a stranger may write to a stranger, or a subordinate to his superior. Please do not mention this note to anyone and tear it up after you have read it. The reason for this conduct must be evident to you, if you have any sense left in your madness. You know your ingratitude and the offense you have brought upon me!
Narendra Sen
P.S. Please do not be importunate by trying to explain yourself and thus adding further lies to your depraved character."
chapters.summary: Allan, tormented by suspicion and fear, navigates the tense atmosphere surrounding Maitreyi's birthday celebration, grappling with jealousy, family scrutiny.

chapters.title: Exile in Calcutta
paragraphs: I did not find Harold at home, but the landlady unlocked my room and let me in, and I threw myself onto the bed, face up, beneath the fan. Poor Mrs. Ribeiro did not know how to behave with me or how to ask me anything.
"Nothing unfortunate has happened to me, Mrs. Ribeiro," I assured her. "My employer, engineer Sen, must undergo an operation today, and that is making me uneasy."

I did not want to betray myself, I did not want to tell even Harold the reason for which I had left Bhowanipore. Their gossip would have disgusted me terribly, for I had no doubt that Harold would have repeated my story to all the Eurasian "friends," and the girls would have tried to console me with their eternal sentimental stupidities, urging me to drink and make love, while I was incapable of accepting any consolation, however brutal. It seemed to me that I had no right even to mention Maitreyi’s name in their midst. Yet I was so stunned, so completely surrendered to my pain, that I could not think of anything precise; I only tried to intuit, to feel concretely my separation from Maitreyi. I could not succeed; I started in fright every time I saw again her last image, her body collapsed on the balcony, and I drove it away. I did not know what to fix my thoughts upon, and I chose a few scenes that were comforting to me (the jasmine wreath, the library, Chandernagore), which I contemplated, calming myself, but

As soon as the film drew toward its end, I would see again Mrs. Sen at the table, looking at me with hostility, or Mr. Sen saying to me: “If you wish to thank me for the good…,” and this would remind me once more, just as acutely and wrenchingly, of my separation from Maitreyi, and I had to close my eyes, shift in bed, sigh deeply, to chase away these thoughts.

Mrs. Ribeiro, after having been absent for about an hour, busy with household matters, entered the room again, asking what I would like to drink; tea, whisky, or beer? I refused with a gesture so weary that the old lady came closer to my bed, seriously concerned.
“But you are ill, Allan,” she said to me.

“I don’t know what’s wrong with me,” I feigned. “I’ve been exhausted these last months, because I didn’t go anywhere this summer, and the engineer’s misfortune has affected me deeply. I want to leave Calcutta for a while… Do you have any vacant rooms, Mrs. Ribeiro?”

When she heard about a vacant room, my hostess was all aflutter with happiness, urged me to see the room next to Harold’s, asked why I no longer wanted to stay in Bhowanipore, then, seeing that these inquiries tired me, changed the subject, asked about my temperature, advised me to leave Calcutta at once for two or three weeks, somewhere in the mountains (Darjeeling, for instance, or Shillong, or even by the sea, at Gopalpur-at-Sea, where father Justus recovered from exhaustion, because the air is wonderful and hardly anyone stays at the hotel anymore). I listened to her talking and agreed with everything she said, just so she wouldn’t force me to answer, to discuss, to think. She immediately brought me The Statesman from the hall, to look up boarding house addresses, and commented on each place, told me who had been there and on what occasion, and as I listened to her, it seemed as if I were living in a dream, so improbable was my presence: here, and even my life itself, my whole body stretched out on the bed, the cigarettes I was smoking, while I ought to be dead, for I had been separated from Maitreyi. How could such things exist in the world? I asked myself, not thinking the question, but only feeling it—how could it be that an hour after leaving Bhowanipore I could listen to the chatter of this old woman, who had no idea what a wreck she had before her? Everything seemed irrational, impossible, and I sensed that I would go mad if I stayed long among such people, if I did not bury myself somewhere in solitude, to forget, to lose myself. Leaving appeared to me as the only salvation, at least for a while. I resolved to leave the very next day, anywhere.
“Please telephone Mr. Sen, South 1144,” I said to Mrs. Ribeiro, “and ask him to send my things here…”

Mrs. Ribeiro would have felt insulted at any other time to telephone a “native,” but at that moment she was so happy that I listened to her speaking politely, probably to Mantu, and thanking him for his kindness.
“I’ll go arrange the room,” she told me.

I was glad that she was leaving and that now I could sigh and weep freely. Suddenly, the thought struck me that I had grown old and that my hair was white from sorrow, and I jumped up to look at myself in the mirror. I barely recognized myself. My face was pale, drawn, dry, and my eyebrows disheveled, as if I had torn at them; some line had deepened at the corner of my lips, which changed me completely, giving me an air of fierce will. I marveled to discover on my face a virile determination and power to act, qualities I had long since lost. (Since then, I no longer believe in people’s expressions. It seems to me that the rules of changing one’s face have nothing to do with true inner experiences. Perhaps only the eyes, and only they, can betray a man.) I returned, dejected, to bed and lit another cigarette.

When Harold arrived, he greeted me with cheers. Mrs. Ribeiro had explained my visit to him in a few words. He tried to make me talk, but I pretended to have a headache and told him only in passing why I had come. He immediately called for drinks. He told me that any fever and any pain goes away with whisky. I drank a glass too, but the dizziness only made me feel more keenly the distance from Maitreyi. I almost felt like hating. When Khokha arrived, I thought I would embrace him from emotion. It was as if he brought with him all the love, all of India. He had come in a rather dirty dhoti, his cracked feet bare without sandals, and everyone in the house looked at him with disdain, with disgust, but he, knowing he was “with me,” walked in and out proudly, bringing things from the truck, directing the porters through the hall. I was burning with impatience for him to tell me what had happened there, in Bhowanipore. When I had paid the truck driver and the porters, I took him with me into my room, asked Mrs. Ribeiro for tea, and opened a new box of cigarettes. Harold fumed that I wouldn’t stay and talk with him, but he probably guessed in my sudden departure from Sen’s something more than I had confessed and did not dare come and interrupt us.

Khokha brought me a copy of Uddkita, on which Maitreyi had written her last words: “To my dear one, to my dear one, Maitreyi, Maitreyi.” Is that all? I grieved. Khokha told me to look at the end of the notebook as well. “Farewell, my dear, I have said nothing that would make you guilty. I only said that you kissed me on the forehead. I had to say it; it was our mother and she knew. Allan, my friend, my dear, farewell! Maitreyi.”
I remained mute, gazing at her handwriting. Khokha smoked, silent as well, for a while, then spoke suddenly, as if continuing a thought.
“…And then it had to come out. You were too imprudent. Everyone saw you when you kissed on the jetty. The driver told both Mantu and Lilu. No one had the courage to warn you…”
I wonder whether Khokha knows only as much as the others or has understood more. But I realized how little it matters
now this, and I let myself be carried away by other thoughts.

— Chabù has come to her senses, Khokha spoke again. When she saw Maitreyi fainted, it was as if she woke up from a dream. She asked about you: “Where is dadà?”—that’s how she asked everyone, clinging to Mrs. Sen, tugging at her sari and questioning. I told her I was coming to see you, and then she gave me this note...

On a page torn from a school notebook, Chabù had written in Bengali, in her most beautiful handwriting: “Beloved dadà, can you ever forgive me? I don’t know what made me speak; I thought I was doing no harm by telling, for you do no harm by loving each other. Maitreyi is suffering terribly. Can you make her stop suffering? Then where is your love? I wish I could die.”
— She was crying when she wrote it and told me I must give it to you and that you should call her one morning. She’s not mad anymore, she doesn’t seem mad anymore. Poor thing...
He fell silent again for a while, then suddenly sighed.
— What is it, Khokha? I asked him.
— Ah, what can I tell you I feel, when I see how much you suffer!...

He spoke emphatically, theatrically, forcing himself to wear a mask of pain, hoping to draw my attention. But the tone with which he uttered those few words made me feel at once estranged from him. Perhaps Khokha sensed this discomfort, for he changed the subject.

— When I began to take your things out of your room, Maitreyi ran downstairs and started to embrace them, to scream. They had to drag her back by force. Mr. Sen, who is a brute, struck her across the face with his fists until blood gushed out. She fainted in her room...

I listened, weeping, but without my pain increasing. What more could they do to us than separate us? If he beat me as much as he wanted, if he slapped me, would I suffer more? I saw her with her face bloodied, but it was not her wounds that tore my heart, but her very being, her presence, which I knew was far away.

— They locked her in her room, almost naked, so she couldn’t come down to your room anymore. While she was unconscious, they sprinkled her with water to revive her, then, when she woke, they beat her to make her confess. “I love him, I love him,” that’s all I heard from downstairs, how she screamed. “He is not guilty, what do you want from him?” my sister told me she shouted at them. “What do you want from him?”...
And yet, they had done nothing to me. Better if they had slapped me, I thought. Why didn’t Mr. Sen have the courage to slap me? Why did he shake my hand, cowardly, saying: “Good-bye, Allan!”

— Before they came to take her upstairs, Maitreyi whispered to me: “I’ll call him tomorrow.” But perhaps she won’t succeed. Mr. Sen keeps her locked up. I heard him talking to mother about marrying her off as soon as possible.
I froze. Khokha noticed my terror and continued, more fervently:
— They want to marry her to a professor from Hoogli, and that as soon as they return from Midnapur. Do you know they’re planning to leave for Midnapur?
"I know," I replied, almost indifferent.
"They're brutes, all of them are brutes," Khokha burst out. "Don't you hate them?"
"Why should I hate them? I did them all the wrong. What fault can they have? Except, perhaps, for bringing me into their house..."
"They wanted to adopt you," Khokha explained.

I smiled. How empty, how useless all these things seemed to me, all the deeds that could have come to pass if I had been different, all the happiness I might have had, if... It seemed pointless to think about what could have happened. I was alone, alone—that was the pain, the present. I could understand nothing else.
Khokha looked at me, saw my tears, and sighed.
"My mother is very ill, and I have no money, not a single rupee to give her. I was thinking of asking you for a loan until I get my fee from the Bengal Film Company..."
"How much do you want?"
He was silent. I did not dare to look him in the eye. His lie pained me, for I knew his mother was not ill and that she was cared for by his brother-in-law, a merchant in Kalighat.
"Will thirty rupees be enough for you?" I asked, and without waiting for an answer, I wrote the check and handed it to him.
He thanked me awkwardly and began to talk again about Maitreyi. I asked him, quietly, to leave.
"Khokha, I'm sleepy, I have a headache..."

In the evening, as Harold had announced, the girls came to see me. They set the gramophone in the hall, ordered whisky and orangeade, and exaggerated their cheerfulness to console me (Harold had told them I was suffering from a nervous depression, exhaustion or something of the sort, and that before leaving the city I needed to 'have some fun' to forget).
"Hey, Allan," Geurtie said to me, "why are you sitting there so glum, boy? Don't you have your girl by your side?"
She sat on my knee, and her touch was so odious to me that I trembled all over, and I begged her to let me be, for I was tired and ill.
"Are you in love, perhaps?" she winked slyly. "Some Indian girl must have bewitched you. Some unwashed black one, just as you like..."
They all burst out laughing. Mrs. Ribeiro, who was tidying the room next door, came in as well.
"Leave the boy alone. Come, Allan, have a glass of whisky. You'll see, everything will pass. An eye operation isn't such a terrible thing..."
"But what do you think, Mrs. Ribeiro," Geurtie asked sarcastically, "that Allan is crying over that operation? He has something much graver, maybe he's..."
some fiddler ran off with the girl...
"Shut up," I snapped, suddenly furious, rising from my chair.
"Please be more polite with me," Geurtie replied, blushing. "You’re not among your blacks from Bhowanipore here."
"Geurtie!" Clara cried, grabbing her arm. "Leave him be, poor boy..."
"You’ve all spoiled him too much, 'poor boy' this, 'poor boy' that. He cries like a woman and consoles himself with his dirty Bengalis. He has no right to insult me, a Christian."
"But he’s a Christian too!" Clara intervened.

"Ha! You think he’s still a Christian?" Geurtie laughed. "What do you say, Harold? But when he was talking to you about Hinduism and his cows, and cursing our Lord Jesus Christ? And now you tell me to shut up..."
Harold was extremely embarrassed, and Mrs. Ribeiro was overcome with panic.
"Calm down, all of you!" he said.
"I’m leaving," I told them, exhausted, and stood up.
Geurtie looked at me sulkily.
"He’s going to pray at his temple. God won’t help him..."

I had a wild night. As soon as I was alone (I had wandered the streets for a long time, smoking endlessly and searching through all the native quarters, whose noise and bustle and language reminded me of my days with Maitreyi), and I undressed, the torment, which fatigue had somewhat lulled, surged over me again, this time without my being able to resist it at all. In vain I bit the pillow, in vain I struck myself to keep from screaming. I kept repeating: "Maitreyi, Maitreyi, Mai-treyi"... until I no longer understood anything of that girl’s name, its sounds evoked nothing for me, and I remained stunned, my face buried in the pillows, not knowing what had happened to me, what had broken inside me, what was going on. My thoughts raced from one event to another with no connection, I saw again Tamluk, Sadyia, countless other places I had known, without understanding anything. I was only afraid to think of anything that might evoke Maitreyi’s face on the evening of our parting, or Mr. Sen’s voice saying to me: "Good-bye, Allan!", or Mrs. Sen’s lingering look: "Take your tea!"... Whenever these scenes tried to come alive in my mind, I struggled. I could hear Harold snoring in the next room, I heard now and then the clock from the Protestant church counting the hours through the night. To calm myself, I thought of death. To drown myself in the Ganges and let Sen find out how pure my love for Maitreyi was. The next day, the newspapers would talk about this young European, who had killed himself for no reason, found at the edge of the city by the boatmen returning their skiffs. Maitreyi would faint upon hearing, Mrs.

Sen would have repented, for she too would have understood then how sincerely, how completely, I had loved Maitreyi. The thought of death was my only solace. I lingered voluptuously over every image, every gesture: how I write the letter to Mr. Sen, how I head toward the bridge and there I cry a little, but only a little, just a few tears, and then, leaning on the railing, I look down at the yellow waters flowing, thick with silt, I grow dizzy and then... I replayed the film, always from the beginning. That is how I fell asleep at dawn.

Harold woke me, to tell me someone was calling for me on the telephone. I ran like a madman into the hall, still in my pajamas. I recognized at once Maitreyi’s voice, which I drank in thirstily, though I was afraid to speak to her, lest Harold or some other boarder of Mrs. Ribeiro should hear me. She was telling me things I could only half guess, for she spoke softly, so as not to wake the others, probably, and kept breaking into sobs. Her voice seemed to come from prison, from a locked cell, so torn was her weeping, so longing for freedom her tone.

“Allan, do you still know me? It’s me, still me, I remain the same, Allan, whatever happens... Be a man and go on working, do not despair... I can’t anymore, Allan, forgive me... I can’t anymore. I would like to tell you...”
Her voice suddenly fell silent. Someone had come, probably Mrs. Sen. I called out in vain:
“Hello! Hello!”

No one answered anymore. I returned to my room, crushed by deathly dejection. I wanted to run away, the walls suffocated me, those things of mine tormented me, the straw mat on which Maitreyi had so often sat. Each of them evoked a scene, a word, and I was incapable of waking up, of putting an end to these memories of dreadful sadness, which had turned me from a man into something less than human in a single day.
“How is the engineer, Allan, has he had the operation?” Harold asked me.
“Not yet,” I replied in passing. “Perhaps today...”
“Poor man...”

I threw myself onto the bed, smoking again. By now I was almost inert, only my hands trembled, otherwise my face had frozen, expressionless, motionless, I could not even cry anymore, but lay there, under the fan, not knowing what I would do, what would happen.
Around ten, a messenger stopped in front of the house with a bicycle, asking for me. Mrs. Ribeiro brought me an envelope. The man did not wait for an answer. Sen was writing to me.
“Sir,
I now understand that you have neither respect nor honor. I thought you merely mad, but I see you act like a snake in the grass,

...which, if you do not crush its head when you must, turns around and bites you. Not even twenty-four hours have passed since you gave your word that you would not attempt to communicate with any member of my family, and you have broken it like a coward, causing suffering to a poor child upon whom, unfortunately, you have had some influence. If you try such things again, I will do everything in my power to have you expelled from the country. I believed you would have the decency to leave this city. By telephone, I have given orders for you to be dismissed today. The only thing left for you to do is to collect your salary and leave at once. Your ingratitude must have its limits.
Narendra Sen.

I read the letter, stunned. Not because I had been dismissed, for I myself had decided to leave; I could not have faced Sen again after what Khokha had told me. I was stunned because I understood that Maitreyi would make more and more such mistakes, from which she would suffer endlessly, and her suffering multiplied my own tenfold, for I knew I could be of no help to her and I tormented myself uselessly, alone, far away. I folded the envelope and left, taking only my helmet.
“Are you coming to lunch, Allan?” Mrs. Ribeiro asked me.
“Of course.”
“I’ve cooked your favorite dishes, Harold told me what they are, you’ll see... And don’t think about it anymore...”

I smiled and stepped out the gate, dazed, without any aim. I thought it would be wise to withdraw some money from the bank, if indeed I had to leave the city in a day or two. But I was not leaving at Sen’s command; his threats did not intimidate me. I was leaving because I knew all too well that only thus could I be of any use to Maitreyi: only thus could she forget me. I was thinking like an adolescent. I walked to the bank, though the distance from Royd Lane to Clive Street was quite great. After I had packed the banknotes securely in my wallet and distributed my silver coins among all my pockets, I set off further, toward the station. When I crossed the Howrah Bridge, I leaned over to look at the Ganges, dirty and crowded with boats, and the thought of suicide appeared to me suddenly in all its cowardice and absurdity. At the station I stopped to drink a glass of lemonade. It was already twelve o’clock. I went out and turned right, onto the ring road that leads to the villages around the city and passes through Belur. When I entered the shady road in earnest, I felt stronger, calmer, and I set out determinedly. I did not stop at all, not even to smoke, but walked on, with long, resolute strides. The cars running the Station-Hoogli route passed by on the road, and almost all of them stopped beside me, for it seemed strange to them to see a European walking on foot along a road outside the city.

I stopped only at a poor little shack, where an old woman was selling lemonade, pan, and peppers: I stopped to drink something cold. That encounter seemed to soothe me, for I spoke to the old woman in Bengali, not in Hindusthani, as would have been proper, and this language of Maitreyi’s was a true balm to me.

I reached Belur-Math around half past two, after walking two kilometers in the rain, my clothes soaked to the skin; I arrived spattered with mud, with a lost look in my eyes that frightened Swami Madhvananda, a monk I had met long ago, back when I used to come here in the engineer’s car. I went down to the bank of the Ganges to dry myself, and as I lay there on the grass, eyes turned to the sun, I recalled all our walks, side by side with Maitreyi, I saw myself again, happy and carefree. I could no longer restrain myself, and, since I could not cry, I took my notebook from my pocket and began to write, only for myself. (Today I reread those notes, written in blood, and they seem so cold to me, so ordinary. For example: “Why has it all passed? An immense emptiness within me. Nothing has meaning anymore. When I hear a Bengali song, up at the math, I feel like crying. Maitreyi, Maitreyi, Maitreyi. I will never see her again…” How incapable we are of rendering, even then, the substance of a joy or a pain too great. I have come to believe that only memory, only distance, can give them life. The journal is dry and insignificant.)

Swami tried to find out what was wrong with me, but when I told him I had walked from Calcutta and had not eaten, for I could eat nothing, he grew alarmed and begged me to leave at once, lest I fall ill, lest I catch malaria (he knew I had suffered from malaria the year before), and so on. His tone was commanding, and he probably despised me greatly, overwhelmed as I was by passion and pain. These Indian monks can never console you, for it seems to them unworthy of consolation, that soul enslaved by suffering, and their ideal of atrocious detachment has nothing to do with the human who suffers, with the misery of experience. These people live almost too divinely, whose ideal is supreme placidity.

Besides, since I had not come to the math for consolation, but only because there I could see my Maitreyi again, the one from memory, the true one, Swami’s words did not wound me too much; they only made me feel more alone. I left, thanking them for the fruits and sweets a brother had brought me. I did not take the road back, but set out further, along the same highway, toward Ranaghat. I reached Bally near sunset. I searched for the Ganges here as well, gazed at it for a long time, smoking idly, watched it flow smooth and vast toward our city. I sat on a stone, surrounded by a few children, who at first shouted at me in broken English: “White monkey!” Then, seeing that I was not offended, but looked at them pensively, with tears in my eyes, they drew nearer, embarrassed, until I began to speak to them in

Bengalis, and I hand out small coins. They escort me in a procession to the edge of the village. The evening is a little cooled by rain, yet clear and inviting for a journey. Soon I am left alone on the road. From time to time, cars pass by on their way to Calcutta, with large, blazing headlights. Now and then, a man or two, hurrying along. I wonder, in this way, how early people go to bed in India!... Then I remember Bhowanipore, and it is as if a warm wave rises in my throat. I quicken my pace. I only stop at a small shop to buy cigarettes. “Scissors,” the only ones I can find. An acetylene lamp was burning, and a few travelers were resting, smoking huka, with long, calm puffs. They all looked at me in wonder, and one even stepped out onto the road to watch me as I set off again, alone, into the darkness ahead.

I do not know until what hour I walked, nor through which village I passed. I was neither sleepy nor did I feel tired, but this march in the darkness had begun to enchant me, lulling my thoughts somewhat and flattering me a little, for I believed I was doing this out of too much suffering, I was doing it for Maitreyi. On the road, a few meters from the ditch, I found a well with a roof, and there I stopped to rest. I fell asleep without knowing it, my head resting on my helmet, directly on the stone slabs. The same dreams, of Maitreyi, which woke me at intervals and made me shiver with cold, with loneliness. People came to the well, and the noise woke me. (Strangely, despite all my pain, I was conscious that I was carrying five hundred rupees on me, and whenever people approached, I instinctively reached for my wallet.) They all looked at me in amazement, none daring to ask me anything, for although my clothes had been splashed with mud and my canvas shoes disfigured, it was still clear that I was a sahib, and a white sahib at that.

I refreshed my face and set off again, this time more quickly and more preoccupied, for the road was beginning to be more frequented now, at the break of dawn. I looked mostly down. I only stopped when, through the palm trees or at a bend in the road, I could catch a glimpse of the river. I do not know what comfort the Ganges gave me, knowing it flowed towards the place I had come from, towards the city of Maitreyi. I was almost no longer aware of the source of my pain. I did not wonder what Harold or Mrs. Ribeiro would say. I had only one joy: that perhaps Khokha would come, and, finding that I had left a day ago and had not returned, would tell the engineer. I wished Sen would believe I was dead, so that he might reflect a little on what he had done.
That day I ate at an inn near Ranaghat. I ate rice with carri* and boiled fish, and I ate with my hand, like an Indian, to the amazement and delight of the others.
* Curry (a powder of turmeric and other spices, or the dish prepared with this powder), transcribed in a way that approximates the pronunciation (kari) (editor’s note).

the villagers, who had already heard me, after all, speaking an elegant Bengali. Only my appearance gave them pause. I could sense that my face was haggard, my beard grown out, my hair flattened from sleep, my clothes dirty and my hands blackened.

I had begun to forget, to forget myself, and this gave me an even greater appetite for the road. I walked until sunset without coming across any more villages, encountering only ox carts and the occasional rattling truck. That day was one of dreadful heat, and I stopped at every well to drink and cool my face.

I lay down with the rising of the stars, beneath a huge mango tree, grown solitary at the edge of an abandoned pond. The mosquitoes tormented me for a long time, but in the end exhaustion overwhelmed me and I did not wake until late in the day, my limbs drained, scarcely aware of where I was...

I must have dreamed something terrifying, for I awoke sweating and trembling. I almost broke into a run along the road, pressing forward. It was a day of wandering without purpose, of which I remember nothing except that, as if in a dream, I asked a cart driver where I was and how I might reach a railway station. He directed me to a halt near Burdwan, which I found at nightfall. The first train would not come until dawn and did not stop here. I had to board a local train around midnight, in a third-class carriage (for I did not have the courage to enter any other compartment), and thus I reached Burdwan.

At first, the electric headlights in the stations dazzled and frightened me. I was like a sick man awakened by an alarm, almost dazed, not knowing at which window to buy my inter-class ticket (this time I was ashamed to squeeze in among the old women and ragged men at the third-class window; ashamed not for myself, but for the few Eurasians and Englishmen on the platform, who eyed my clothes with great suspicion). I waited, shivering, for the Lucknow express, sipping many teas and trying to reconstruct my escape from the beginning. There were gaps of hours, of nights, and this void in my memory obsessed me. Have I gone mad? I asked myself. I ordered myself not to think of anything. Everything will pass, everything passes, I told myself. (Since then I have learned this refrain, which later became a true leitmotif of my life.)

In Howrah I was once again nervous, as if I still expected to meet someone from Bhowanipore. (I remembered that there had been talk of a departure for Midnapur, and although this tormented me enough, for it took me even farther from Maitreyi, it also brought a kind of solace, since I was no longer in the same city as Sen and did not risk meeting him.) The car brought me home at the very hour when the police from Park Street had begun their search for me. Mrs. Ribeiro nearly fainted when she saw me getting out of the taxi, with my helmet broken, unshaven for four days, my clothes in tatters.

"Where have you been, for God's sake, where have you been? South 1144 kept calling for you, and that boy, Mr. Chatterjee, Khokha, as you call him there, kept coming to look for you... Oh Lord, oh Lord..."

I left her talking and went to wash myself. A bath was the only thing I still desired now. Harold called from the office to ask if there was any news, and when Mrs. Ribeiro told him I had come and how I had come, the boy took a car to see me as soon as possible.
"All right, man! All right, man!"
He was shaking my hands endlessly.
This emotion did me good, and I patted him on the shoulder.
He tried to console me.
"It's nothing, old man. This too shall pass. But what's with you? Where have you been until now?"
"I took a walk. Nothing serious. Just a simple walk."
I smiled.
"How are you?"

"The girls came yesterday, alarmed. We wanted to improvise something at 'China Town,' out of joy that you escaped from the idolaters' claws. All right, man. What's with you? That black fellow came looking for you. I think he got a bit upset. He bored me, so I told him to scram. 'Now he's a Christian again,' that's what I told him..."

Khokha called me right after lunch, from a bookstore on Asutosh Mukerjee Road, where he had friends. He told me hurriedly that serious things had happened and that he must come see me without fail. I asked him to take a car. I waited for him on the veranda.
"Where have you been?" he asked me.
"I'll tell you later," I replied a bit sharply. "Tell me what's new..."

A great many new things. They tried to marry off Maitreyi, but she screamed that she would confess to her husband, on the wedding night, that she had slept with me and would disgrace the whole family, for she would be thrown out with scandal, and the whole city would learn of her shame. The engineer, hearing this, struck her once across the face, knocking her to the ground in blood. But he immediately had an attack himself and was taken to the hospital. He can no longer see at all. They will operate on him in a day or two, if he calms down. But he is so agitated that even the doctors are afraid. Maitreyi has been locked in her room, after Mrs. Sen called the driver to beat her with rods before her eyes, until she fell unconscious. She asked Khokha to do the same, but he ran away. Chabù tried to kill herself, with creolin. She is also now in the hospital. Maitreyi sent me an envelope in which she barely had time to enclose a blooming oleander branch, and on a leaf she had written, with a heavy pencil: "Allan, the last gift from me"... She begs me not to leave for five days. She knew nothing of my flight, and it's better that she didn't know. She would have thought I killed myself, and who knows what foolish thing she might have done.

I listen to him as if in a dream, trying to convince myself of the gravity and consequences of the news brought by Khokha, but understanding almost nothing except that Maitreyi is suffering even more and that she is locked away. Khokha asks me for a few written lines for Maitreyi, but I remember my promise to Sen and I refuse him.
“What’s the use?” I tell him sadly. “What’s the use now? Let her forget me. She must forget me, for three or five years, until she is mine again...”
I find myself rambling. I start to cry, stupidly, then feel everything spinning around me and I say:
“If only I could love her, if only I could!... But I do not love her.”
Khokha looks at me, grinning.
“I wish I could love her,” I howl, “I wish I were able to love her...”
Mrs. Ribeiro comes in, surprised, and asks me what is wrong.
“I wish I could love Maitreyi,” I tell her, in tears. “Why can’t I love her? What have I done to her? What do they want from me? What do you all want from me?...”
Then I remember a telephone call from Maitreyi one morning.

“Goodbye, Allan, goodbye, my darling. In the next life we will meet again, my dear. Will you recognize me then? Will you wait for me? Wait for me, Allan, do not forget me. I will wait for you. No other will ever touch me...”
All I could say to her was:
“Maitreyi, Maitreyi...”

I left on the seventh day after my parting from Bhowanipore. I left after spending the last two nights hidden in front of their house, spying on the light in Maitreyi’s room. It was dark the whole time.
Chabù died that same day.
chapters.summary: Allan, overwhelmed by grief after leaving Bhowanipore, finds refuge in Calcutta, where Khokha brings heartbreaking news about Maitreyi’s suffering and Chabù’s remorse.

chapters.title: Himalayan Solitude
paragraphs: The months I spent in the Himalayas, in a bungalow between Almora and Ranikhet, are too sad and too serene for me to recount, as an unnatural consequence of my love and separation from Maitreyi.

I arrived here after fleeing, one after another, from Delhi, Simla, Naini-Tal, where I encountered too many people, and above all, too many whites. I was afraid of people, because I had to answer their greetings, to speak of things of no importance, to waste my time; and thus, I could not remain as alone

as much as I wished. Solitude was now both my comfort and my sustenance. Few modern men, I believe, have known a loneliness harsher and more desperate than mine. From October until February I saw only one person: the bungalow’s watchman. Only he was allowed to enter my wooden room, only with him did I speak, once or twice a day, when he brought me food or changed my water jug. I spent all my time in the forest, for the surroundings of Almora hold the most beautiful pine woods in all the Himalayas, and I wandered through them, back and forth, endlessly replaying the same inner film of my love for Maitreyi, imagining all sorts of happenings, each more fantastic than the last, through which the two of us would find happiness, meeting in an impenetrable solitude, or in that dead citadel of Fatehpur-Sikhri, or in some abandoned hut in the jungle.

All day long I witnessed the unfolding of the same fantastic dream, which isolated the two of us, myself and Maitreyi, from the rest of the world. Deeds long forgotten regained their freshness, and my imagination fulfilled them, deepened them, wove them together. Details I had not noticed at the time now changed the entire landscape of my inner vision. Wherever I went, I encountered her—among the pines and birches, on the rocks, along the paths. I lived so intensely with this marvelous story that any call from the outside world frightened me, almost caused me physical pain. I knew that Maitreyi, too, there in her cell in Bhowanipore, was thinking just as deeply of me, of our life together, and this communion in imagination seemed to bind us above the events, to bind us in spite of separation and death.

When the moon was out, I would walk through the forest down to the stream in the valley, and linger long on a rock, watching the water, calling out: “Maitreyi! Maitreyi!” until I grew tired and heard my voice growing fainter and fainter, almost a whisper. Then I would return home, along the same path, with an unspeakable peace in my soul, for it seemed to me that Maitreyi had heard my call, that my words had been carried by water and wind to her. I do not know whether I truly lived or not, in those many months of complete solitude, but this was my only means of survival. I was no longer the vigorous and optimistic young man, sure of what he wanted and what he could do, the European in love with technology and pioneering, who had once landed in India to civilize it. Everything seemed futile, meaningless. Everything, except those few months of my love and misfortune. For I did not suffer only because I was separated from Maitreyi; I suffered also for the crime committed against a benefactor of mine, against an incomparable mother, against the life of little Chabù, whom, without doubt, I had set on the path to death. All these certainties stifled me, kept me from breathing freely. I had to lull them to sleep, to numb them with an ever more powerful dream, in which there was neither death nor sin nor
Separation.

I kept rereading my journal, but I never had the courage to approach September 18. That day, in any case, was somewhat buried for me. In a thick envelope, I had sealed away a few of Maitreyi’s notes, the engineer’s letters, Chabù’s letter, the oleander branch, a hairpin, a few scraps of paper with Maitreyi’s handwriting (many from the days of our French lessons)—in short, all the traces of that definitive episode of my youth. (I opened the envelope only a few days ago, when I wrote the last chapters. How many disheartening things I could say about relics and memories!...) I especially liked to reread the preliminaries of my love, to mock my own naivety, my sentimental conceit, which had made me live so long in an illusion.

I neither received nor wrote letters. Once or twice a month, the bungalow’s watchman would go to Naini-Tal for certain supplies he could not find in the valley villages, and then I would send a few lines to the bank for money, or a telegram to Harold, so he would know I was still alive. As Christmas approached, I had a surprise that revealed to me just how deeply I was still bound to my past, and how dangerous a return to Calcutta would be. Khokha, inquiring at the bank, had found out my address in Naini-Tal (poste restante) and wrote to me. When I saw my name on the envelope brought by the watchman, I could hardly believe it was addressed to me. It seemed that that Allan no longer existed, that I had left him somewhere behind. I bolted the door and read Khokha’s letter, my heart pounding, as if I suddenly found myself face to face with Sen, or Maitreyi, or Mrs. Sen.

He wrote that the family had spent a month in Midnapur, from where even Maitreyi sent me a few lines scribbled on scraps of newspaper, on posters from the train station, alongside humble wildflowers, probably picked during her guarded walks at the edge of the village. I understood that Maitreyi had suffered too much to preserve my human, real, flesh-and-blood image. She had now created for herself another Allan, an entire mythology, splendid and inaccessible, which she ceaselessly nourished, to raise it ever higher, into pure unreality. She wrote to me: “How could I ever lose you, when you are my sun, when your rays warm me on this country road? How could I forget the sun?” On another scrap of paper, she called me “sun, air, flowers!” “Do I not kiss you now, along with the bouquet I press to my chest?” Or: “At night, you come to me, as I once came to you, in our love room in Bhowanipore. But I came as a woman, for you had made me a woman; whereas now you come as a god of gold and precious stones, and I adore you, for you are more than my love, you are my sun, my life!”
I thought then how strange was this withdrawal of hers into mythology, how painful for me this continual abstraction of myself, made from man into god, from lover

sun. I had discovered the dream, but a dream in which I met the same Maitreyi from Bhowanipore and held her just as manfully in my arms. My dream, however fantastic it might have been, continued the same life lived together and the same love, perfecting it, fulfilling it.
