But her mythology had long since transformed it into imagination, into an idea, and I could not find myself, as I would have wished, with my flaws and my passions, in her “sun,” in her “flowers.” I read the letter with a slight pang in my heart. Why was Maitreyi distancing herself from me? Why did she implore me to forget her, so that I might meet her in another life? What did I care for a future life and for all her gods?... I was thirsty for the concrete, for immediate life, for presence. What tormented me was precisely her carnal memory, precisely what was alive and immediate and irreplaceable in her being, and it was this Maitreyi, of soul and flesh, whom I desired, whom I met in the daily film of my mind. I did not want, at any price, to disappear in her love, to be replaced by an idea, by a myth. I did not want to console myself with an eternal and celestial love; my love demanded fulfillment, life on earth, not an angelic pair... Khokha gave me other news as well: the engineer’s operation had not gone very well, and his leave was extended by another six months. Mrs. Sen has turned white, her face now like that of a saint. Maitreyi has grown frighteningly thin and stubbornly refuses any proposal of marriage. Since she returned from Midnapur, she keeps asking about me on the phone, in Royd Lane, and believes she is being lied to, that I am again in Calcutta but do not wish to see her. Once, he—Khokha—went to my lodgings, and Mrs. Ribeiro complained that she no longer knew anything about me, that it had been agreed I would go for two or three weeks, and now, look, it has been three months since I have given any sign of life, except for the telegrams to Harold. As for Mantu, the engineer threw him out of the house because he had been insolent to Mrs. Sen, and now the poor boy is faring very badly, for he must pay the debts incurred with the wedding and lives apart from Lilu, she with her parents, and he in a student hostel, where he eats only bread and tea so as to pay off his debts more quickly and be able to be with Lilu again. Khokha ended his letter by asking me when I intended to return and imploring me not to ruin my career, nor to squander my youth for a mere episode of love. All men must go through such trials. And they must come out stronger, more powerful, not retreat to the depths of the mountains. This is not a solution, Khokha concluded. So, when would I return? That was what I asked myself as well. I could not reconcile myself to the thought of a new life in Calcutta. Besides, I did not even know what I could do there, for I no longer had work, I had obtained no certificates, and, at the office, to ask for them, it was beyond me to go. I had enough money saved to live in seclusion for another year. But after that? Would I start all over again, would I leave

farther away, toward Java, for example, and there I would have the courage to begin a new life… Yet these thoughts were merely thoughts. For I could not imagine myself separated from India, nor could I picture myself settling down to work again. Any activity, any ambition, any goal seemed to me so utterly futile that the mere memory of them saddened me to death.

I would sit on the veranda of the bungalow, once all the visitors had gone, and gaze at the pine forests, asking myself: could there be anything better? Could anything have more meaning than this forest, which no one asks why it grows or for whom it reveals its unparalleled beauty? I wished to be a log, floating lazily, serenely, drunkenly, on the waters of the Ganges. To feel nothing anymore, to remember nothing. Could there not be a meaning to existence in this return to the mineral, to the crystal, for instance? To be a crystal, to live and to share light like a crystal…

A host of foolish questions, with no connection to philosophy, passed through my mind then. I had not brought a single book with me, and I thought at random, whatever pleased me, whatever consoled me. Silent all the while, I spoke at length with people I imagined, all resembling myself, but much deeper, more manly, more free. I longed for freedom as I believe no prisoner has ever longed. I felt so bound on all sides. There were forbidden zones in my mind; for example, the zone on this side and the other side of September 13th…

At the beginning of February, in the dead of night, a stranger arrived, who woke the watchman, asking for a room, but in a language so incomprehensible that the man came to me for help. I went out wearing that fur-lined Himalayan cloak, which gives me the look of a Mongolian mountaineer. On a chaise-longue on the veranda, a woman had collapsed, exhausted, of whom at first I saw only her fair hair and hands—slightly too large—with which she clutched a shabby trench coat tightly around her body. She knew only a few words of Hindusthani, and her whole face lit up with joy when she caught sight of me. She was breathing heavily. In the courtyard, a young boy with the luggage. They had come on foot from Ranikhet, losing the path several times and having to cross the stream to climb up to the bungalow. She told me all this, trembling, for, as far as I could understand, she had had some unpleasant adventure in Ranikhet and had left after nightfall. Her name was Jenia Isaac, from Capetown, South Africa, and she had been in India for several months, wandering through the Himalayas in search of a monastery that would take her in. From the very start she struck me as a cold, lucid enthusiast, exalted more by disappointment than by a thirst for some other kind of truth. When the watchman lit the big lantern, I looked at her more closely; quite young, expressionless; her face

round face, blue eyes, the voice of a little girl, contrasting with her well-built body, tall, strong, with sturdy arms and a broad chest. She was dressed oddly, in a colonial travel outfit, very curiously adapted for a mountain journey. She was so frozen that the caretaker had to make a lot of tea, which she drank greedily, talking all the while, asking questions, suspecting me. This unwelcome visitor bored me somewhat, but I was reassured to learn that in two days at the latest she would leave for Maikhali, intending to reach Bhadrinath. The road to Bhadrinath is a good one, thirty days’ journey. I smiled as I listened to her, for the peaks were now completely frozen, the paths covered with snow, and besides, the road to Bhadrinath does not pass through Maikhali, but through Hardwar. I gave her all the necessary explanations, advising her to go to Kotwara, from where she could take the train to Hardwar. She asked if I was going anywhere, if I would stay here long. I detest any attempt to penetrate my soul, to know my present, to guess my past. I answered curtly and harshly that I did not know what I would do, but for now I would remain here, because this is a bungalow little visited by travelers, and the air of the pine forests suits me perfectly...

The next day I left at dawn, as was my habit. I skirted the mountain, bathed beneath the rock, ate my honey cakes, and returned at night. The caretaker told me that the memsahib was ill and had asked about me. How could he have guessed that? I amused myself, thinking of the smattering of Hindusthani that Jenia Isaac knew. I knocked at the door, and a voice altered by fever answered me. This annoyed me a little, for the thought that I would have to stay constantly near an invalid, and a white invalid at that, was unbearable to me. I found her feverish, trembling, but still quite spirited. She asked me to write a list of common Hindusthani words and to prepare her a cup of cocoa, since the caretaker did not know how. She was not at all impressed by the fact that she was ill here, in the heart of the mountains, alone, without knowing the language and without hoping for any help. She told me she had been suffering from fever for about three weeks, that she had lain near death in the house of a Bhutanese near Almora, but that she was not afraid. I asked her, just for the sake of it, what had brought her to India, and she blushed a little; then, suddenly:
— I want to find the absolute!...

A wild urge to laugh tempted me. This sense of humor, suddenly revived in the face of the stranger’s reply, saddened and unsettled me. I thought that no emotion and no ridicule could impress me anymore.

I thought I had become insensitive, that proportions or nuances could no longer stimulate my attention; I passed by them as one might pass by a stone. But the seriousness of Jenia, when she said “the absolute,” suddenly awakened me to a world of farce and folly, of trickery and sleep, of the ridiculous and the dramatic. The world in which
I too had lived for so long...

With great difficulty, I managed to change the subject, asking her what she thought about Gandhi and the Indian nationalist movement. It is something I always do when I want to keep someone at a distance. Jenia confided to me that, although a British subject, she belonged to a family of Finnish Jews who had settled at the end of the last century in South Africa; that she could not bear the hypocrisy of the whites; that she had come here determined to forget everything and enter an ashram, to seek truth, life, immortality. I listened, my face unchanged, listening to all her superstitions gathered about mystical and fakir India, all the inanities from the books of Ramacharaka, all the pseudo-culture circulating through Anglo-Saxon cities. I sensed she had spent much time alone and that she wanted to tell me everything, happy to have found someone who would listen and “understand” her. She did not cease her confessions, suddenly telling me she had four sisters, that she had been a cellist in the municipal orchestra of Capetown, that she had given concerts in Johannesburg, that she earned forty pounds sterling a month, but could not get along with her family (“bourgeois who wanted to marry her off!”), and so she withdrew to a nearby farm, where she would go every night after concerts, with a pony-cart she had bought with her own savings...

She would have continued her confessions, had I not excused myself, saying it was too late for me to linger in her room, and, after asking if she needed anything else, I withdrew, shaking her hand very soberly and wishing her a speedy recovery.

For a long time that night, I thought about the illusion of this “absolute” the poor musician was seeking, and I felt immense pity, reflecting that she had abandoned a home and freedom in civilization, only because she had read the books of that English charlatan with the pseudonym Ramacharaka. (I learned later that even the reading of these books—“which revealed to her another world beyond the senses”—had been full of adventures and mysteries. Once, she had dreamed the name of a bookstore she did not know; the very next day, her car had an accident on one of the less populated streets, and when she looked up, she found herself in front of the bookstore from her dream! She went in and found, on a shelf, a number of books on theosophy, occultism, and yoga; but she bought only Ramacharaka’s books, through which she had her “revelation of India.”)

For two days I could not take my long walks, could not dream and meditate as I had for so many months, because Jenia was still ill and needed me almost every hour. She too, in the end, sensed that she was beginning to bore me a little, but she was so alone and so unhappy that she swallowed her pride and kept sending for me, inventing pretexts. In those hours of companionship, she continued her confessions, as if it were impossible for her to communicate with me on a spiritual level before telling me her entire life and illuminating all the hidden recesses of her soul, which she wanted to be different from others...

the other moderns, when, like any other, she too lived in a state of permanent bovarism, nourishing herself with grand ideas and truths with a capital T. Thus, Jenia confided to me her entire disgust with the world, with society, with family and with love, her endless sufferings, until she found her freedom again by renouncing everything. Only the separation from music, from art, was more difficult. About love, she had too rudimentary a notion for it to trouble her thoughts. She had never fallen in love, and the one she had once believed she loved became engaged to another. Then she understood that it had only seemed to her that she loved. She would have liked very much to know the experience of complete love before renouncing this ephemeral life, in order to seek the absolute. So, two weeks before leaving Africa, she gave herself to a comrade, a pleasant German, an excellent dancer, who had courted her for some time and who refused to believe her when she told him she was a virgin. That friend, either brutal or clumsy, made her feel a definitive disgust for the carnal closeness of men. She was even delighted that the life she was preparing for herself would prevent her from loving and being loved. She had come to believe that every man is a brute, a pig, or an imbecile, and that the only males worthy of any consideration are those who renounce the “pleasures” of the world, that is, hermits, philosophers, mystics. In Jenia’s head, a jumble of inconsistent ideas clashed, alongside sentimental disappointments and feminine superstitions (the cult of the “superior man,” of the “solitary man,” isolation, adventure, renunciation).

I was almost horrified listening to her, for since I had withdrawn here, I had come to think a thing through to the end, to examine an idea in all its implications, and she made me, against my will, suffer the hybrid and incongruent substance of this young girl’s consciousness in search of the absolute.

Whenever I returned to my room, I would note in my journal judgments and impressions, for it seemed to me that Jenia’s presence was more than a mere happenstance; it was my very contact with a world and a way of thinking from which I had once torn myself away. A week after her arrival, during which time Jenia had had time to recover and regain her strength, but had not yet left, I had completely changed my attitude toward her. Whereas at first she bored and irritated me, now she interested me as a spectacle, as a verification. The first verification I made concerned our white, European world, which I had left and to which I would have to return, sooner or later. The second, and much more serious, was regarding my own life and youth.

I must say that I was almost frightened when, once surprising Jenia half-naked in her room, I felt not the slightest stir and looked at her as at any other object. I thought a great deal that night, asking myself whether perhaps my too great love for Maitreyi, and the harsh shock of our separation, and solitude, had not contributed to neutralize me sexually, had not made of me a sentimental and

cowardly; if perhaps I live far from the world because I cannot face it, and I have decided to renounce love and women, because neither can tempt me any longer. I have passed through hours of dreadful terror, thinking that I might be nothing but a mere wreck, reacting automatically and bearing all my life the mark of my first defeat. I admit, the world—with its women and illusions, with its realities and struggles—no longer interested me. But with an unquenchable thirst I wanted to know if all these things could still interest me. Is it not possible that I withdraw and feel disgusted only because I must do so? What if I am no longer free to choose?

I looked again at Jenia, and I felt for her neither disturbance nor passionate thought, not even mental freedom, and then I tried to probe her, to force her to be feminine, as, without doubt, she had been before leaving Capetown; I thought that perhaps in this way she might succeed in tempting me. And if she had proved to me that the man within me was not dead, that I had remained the same, with my sins, my smallness, my passions, then I could have withdrawn from the world, I would have been free to choose the path I had set for myself, I would have been free to do anything, precisely because I could do the opposite. It is true that Jenia sometimes showed herself to be very feminine with me. Whereas, usually, she would lecture me on theosophy and the "secrets from the heart of Tibet" (for she had a host of myths in which she blindly believed), speaking with her eyes half-closed, in a slightly veiled, mysterious voice, sometimes, on the contrary, she laughed a lot, served me a cup of chocolate in a very charming manner, powdered herself (she had given up powder and rouge as soon as she arrived in the Himalayas), and kept trying to make me tell her how I had come to solitude and what was the meaning of the ring with the black stone that I wore.

It is strange how much I thought of Maitreyi while looking at and speaking with Jenia. I had her always in my mind, her alone, and often, imagining myself embracing some woman, Jenia, for instance, I was bewildered by the impossibility of this image, by the unreality of any amorous eventuality. Decidedly, I loved Maitreyi so madly, and her memory so completely annulled any foreign presence, that I even wondered if this living in a vivid past was not degrading. I caught myself, asking myself in terror what I would do for the rest of my life, if I would not repeat the story of Abelard and Heloise. I would have liked to feel free again, to verify my freedom, so that I could love Maitreyi without fear that I was withdrawing from life. It is very difficult for me to clarify here all those obscure feelings that then urged me toward a release, toward a new experience. Perhaps I do not understand them myself. Perhaps.
Jenia had decided to leave on a Monday morning and had even sent word to Ranikhet for a porter. Three days before, she had become very insinuating, taking advantage of many innocent words

hers, so that she would laugh knowingly, complaining that she was giving up a life she did not know, that she wanted only a single experience, for nothing deserved to be repeated in love, and so on. All these returns to femininity delighted me immensely. And because that evening the moon was wonderful, and because I felt like talking, like understanding what was happening to me, why I was so silent and why I was hiding, we both stayed on the veranda and I told her, in every detail, the story of Maitreyi.

Close to midnight, it grew cold outside, and we went into her room to finish the story and drink a cup of tea. When I had told her everything and summarized Khokha’s letter, and confessed my decision to forget her so as not to make her suffer (I did not understand what this might mean, but it was a phrase that sounded beautiful, and I said it; especially since, surprising for my sincerity, which was most often foolish, that evening I had even played a little theater), Jenia remained sad, silent, with a tear at the corner of her lashes. I asked her, almost absentmindedly, why she was crying. She did not answer. I went closer to her, took her hands, asked her again, squeezed her arm. She kept silent. And then I brought my face closer, my breath almost at her lips, asking her ever more softly, more insinuatingly. She sighed deeply, closed her eyes, and wound her arms around my shoulders, kissing me on the lips, biting, wild. I felt a strange joy when I went to bolt the door.

It might seem that what I have written in these last pages no longer concerns Maitreyi’s story. And yet, it is nothing but a continuation of it. I thought of Maitreyi as I embraced that fair and robust body of the Finnish Jewish woman; I sought Maitreyi in the kiss, it was her I wanted to rid myself of, her I wanted to forget. I sought her and I banished her. I begged for a single detail that might remind me of her; and at the same time I knew it would have shaken and disgusted me to find it, somewhere, along this white body over which love had passed without stopping.

...Did I truly want to forget her, or did I want to prove to myself that I had loved only her, and that any other love would be in vain? I did not know whether this was a simple test or my first flight, my first halt in the mud. I could not believe that such things could ever be forgotten. I could not believe that I too was like the other thousands of unhappy mortals, who love and forget, and die without considering anything eternal, anything definitive. Only a few weeks before, I had felt so bound and so certain in my love for Maitreyi. Could it be, then, that all life is such a farce?...
I asked myself such foolish questions because I was afraid to admit the immense strength of my love for Maitreyi. Without a doubt, Jenia’s embraces had deeply disgusted me. For

now I am certain that a long time will pass before I will again have the courage to approach a woman, and that only if circumstances change. I love Maitreyi, only her! And I clenched my teeth, inventing all sorts of caresses that killed the innocent Jenia, but only made me more restless, for they failed to brutalize me as much as I would have wished, they failed to erase from the living memory of my senses the other, the only one, Maitreyi.
I asked:
"Why did you fall into my arms then?"
"I wanted you to love me too, like you love Maitreyi," she said, looking at me with her blue, expressionless eyes.
I was speechless. Is it possible to have such a thirst for illusion, such a longing for love?
"You used to tell me how you loved Maitreyi, and I thought about myself, how lonely and unhappy I have been, and I felt like crying..."

I think she understood that I could never love her; not even physically. I left her room at dawn, exhausted, inhumanly lucid, and she remained on the bed, ravaged by the spasm of all attempts to forget Maitreyi.
...On Monday, I walked her as far as the brook that runs through the pine forest. Why did God bring her before me? Jenia Isaac, will we ever meet again?

I was alone again; disgusted, dazed, trying to understand what would become of me, trying to return to my sweet sleep beside Maitreyi. I will never be able to write all that passed through my mind then, in the long weeks that followed Jenia’s departure. I vaguely remember my insomnia, the futility of the days.

And it is as if everything passed in a single instant, waking up one morning a little earlier, looking surprised straight at the sun, the light, the greenery. I had escaped something heavy, something deadly. I felt like singing, like running. I do not know how this happened. Something had descended into me, something had overwhelmed me.
And then I turned back.
chapters.summary: Allan isolates himself in a Himalayan bungalow, haunted by memories of Maitreyi and tormented by loneliness.

chapters.title: Letters Unanswered
paragraphs: All day I search for work at the offices on the quay. B.’s promise that he would find me a position as a translator from

In French, at the consulate, nothing is happening. I have about a hundred rupees left, though many people here owe me money. Harold is behaving very badly. I asked him to share his room with me, since from the 15th of the month I am forced to move, and he refuses for a stupid reason: that I am no longer a Christian! That he cannot sleep with an idolater!

The truth is that he knows everything by now, he knows I have no more money, nor any hope for a good salary. Mrs. Ribeiro, who sees my dirty shirt, has now forgotten all the good I did for her, despite my own poverty. She barely gives me a cup of tea when I go to see Harold. I have nothing left to sell. I am left with about six or seven shirts. A depressing day; many, too many annoyances.

...Meeting with Khokha. He brings me yet another letter from Maitreyi. I refuse to accept it; I tell him I gave my word (but did I really? Even now I do not know) to the engineer. Khokha insists that Maitreyi begs me to meet her just once, either in Bhowanipore Park or at a cinema; or to let her call me on the telephone. I refuse everything, flatly, stubbornly, suffering terribly. What is the use of starting over, when everything will end up in the same place, in tears, in madness?
"Tell her to forget me! Allan is dead! Who is she waiting for now?"

I wonder if there is some madness by which, if I accomplished it, Maitreyi would become mine again, forever. But I find nothing, I can imagine nothing. To run away with her into the world... But how to steal her, how to penetrate again into that Bhowanipore guarded by Sen?... And perhaps there is something else; perhaps I no longer deserve her. I know nothing, nothing. I wish she would forget me, that she would no longer suffer. Our love has stopped here.

...Since yesterday morning, phone calls every hour. "Where is Allan? I want to speak to Allan! Tell him it is something urgent from Maitreyi, from his beloved!" Mrs. Mctyre ends up rebelling. She tells me:
"Allan, come and finish once and for all with that black brute!"
I feel like slapping her across the mouth, but I smile savagely. Yes, yes, more, more cruelly, until I fall to my knees and scream: God, I have had enough...
...Evening, at Geurtie’s. She is a good girl, admirable, this Geurtie of mine. I tell her:
"Girl, I am doing terribly. I have no work..."
And she slips me a ten-rupee note under the table.
"Come on, Allan," she laughs, "how many of these have you spent on me!... What do you want to drink?"
"Whisky," I ask, "whisky, because only then do you begin to forget..."

— Forget what? she frowned. Poverty or love? — It makes you forget the day, Geurtie; it’s terrible to live only in the day, never to meet the night again, never to sleep again. What a long day, Geurtie, what an endless day...

...I hadn’t expected this, too. Here I am, loved and, dear God, dear God! loving Geurtie. It’s given to me just like that, all of a sudden, when I had come to her for a proper dinner and to borrow a pair of pajamas. For so long I’ve been sleeping in borrowed pajamas. And now I find myself sleeping in her bed. Truly, this life is a miracle!

— You are my dear boy! she caresses me. I am unmoved. It’s as if she had said: you smell of cologne. It seems just as insignificant to me. But, since I have become a coward lately, ever since I’ve been hungry, I say nothing, but caress her too: “You little rascal, you little rascal!” I say, and this delights her immensely. She leaves for work at ten, but only after giving me breakfast and buying me “State Express 555” cigarettes! How long it’s been since I smoked such a good cigarette... I want to go home, I tell her how awkward things are with my landlady, and she invites me to live with her.
— What do I care about the world? she sneers.

I hadn’t expected such courage from a Eurasian woman. I, who thought she cared only about money. (Besides, I know she has two rich suitors, two bara-sahibs!) She confesses that she has been in love with me since the very first evening. And I, who knew nothing!
...Today I had just finished a telephone conversation with B. when I hear and, with what dread, recognize Maitreyi’s voice:
— Allan! Why won’t you let me speak to you?! Allan, have you forgotten...

I hang up and, almost clutching at the furniture, drag myself to my room. Lord, why can’t I forget? Why won’t this senseless, fruitless fire finally die out? I wish I could do something to make Maitreyi disgusted with me, to force her to forget me. For we could never belong to each other. I will go live with Geurtie and send Khokha to tell Maitreyi everything.

...Negotiations with “Burma Oil Company.” They need a river agent. I think I can handle that too. I must. I spent the afternoon at the Technical Institute Library, trying to find out what a river agent actually does. Twice now the police have inquired about me. They are always deporting the unemployed, over there, to Europe. That would be the most crushing defeat for me; to be expatriated... Geurtie gave me another twenty rupees; poor thing, with tears in her eyes.

...Today I rummage through my older papers and come across the letter sent to Maitreyi on her birthday by an unknown admirer, together with those magnificent flowers. I am seized by a wild desire to know what is written there, and, since my Bengali is now quite uncertain, I beg a pharmacist nearby to translate it for me. Here it is: “My unforgettable light, I cannot come to see you today, for I can only see you alone, only for myself, as I once had you, in my arms, and that day…”

I can write no more. I am suffering from a mad, inhuman jealousy. I felt like biting into the wood of the table. I wished Maitreyi would call me on the telephone at that very moment. My God, when am I deceiving myself? Where am I deceiving myself? Or is it that the whole world is always right?...

…I have not written in my journal for a long time. I hope to finish with India soon. I have solid promises, though without an advance contract, in Singapore. I do not yet know what I am to do there, but I see that travel money is being arranged for me. I have told no one. I have boasted too much already that I would find a position.

With Harold, I have broken off definitively. If Clara had not been there, I would have knocked him to the ground. I have a terrible craving for a fight. Because of this incident, Geurtie quarreled with Clara. Since I moved in with Geurtie into the same room, people believe us to be the happiest “couple” (for I do not know who put it into their heads that we are secretly married). The truth is that Geurtie knows: that I am madly in love with Maitreyi and that I moved in with her only to take my revenge. (All these are stories: I moved because I had nothing left to eat.)

Khokha has sought me out countless times. I have left word not to let him in. He sends me letters which I read only halfway, for they are written in miserable English. He keeps telling me that Maitreyi has decided to do something mad so that she will be thrown out of the house and can come after me. I tremble every time I try to think about it, and so I stubbornly avoid any thought that might bring me closer to Maitreyi. Khokha tells me that she would be capable of giving herself to a stranger, just to be cast out into the streets and thus be able to come back to me. Literature.

…I meet J., Mrs. Sen’s nephew, who has come here for a position at a large printing house. Joy, embraces, memories. He is the first acquaintance I see in Singapore. I invite him to dinner, and after the third cigarette, he looks me in the eye, seriously, and says:
“Allan, do you know that Maitreyi loved you very much? The whole world found out about that love…”
I try to stop him, for though I sometimes enjoy meeting people from those places, I cannot bear to…

either pitying me or commenting on our love. I know, now, that much has come to light. But what good is it, if it has? “No, no,” he insisted, “I have to tell you sad things.” “She hasn’t died, has she?” I asked, frightened. (Though I could not believe in her death, for I know I would feel that moment, if it should happen that Maitreyi dies before me.) “It would have been better if she had died,” J. added, superstitiously. “But she did a shameful thing. She gave herself to the fruit seller…” I felt like screaming, like laughing. I sensed that if I did not grip the table tightly, I would lose consciousness. J. noticed my change and tried to console me. “It was a heavy blow for all of us. Maika is almost mad with grief. Maitreyi left for Midnapur, supposedly to give birth in secret, but everyone found out. They tried to buy off that wretch, but now they’re in court…” I understood nothing anymore. And I still do not understand. Who is in court? I asked him if they had thrown Maitreyi out. “Sen absolutely refuses to cast her out. He said he would rather kill her with his own hand than drive her away. Perhaps they want to make her a philosopher, who knows… They were keeping her for a good match, but now almost everything is known… Who will take her now? And yet, they will not drive her out. Maitreyi keeps screaming: ‘Why don’t you throw me to the dogs? Why don’t you cast me into the street?!’ I think she has gone mad. Otherwise, who would have done such a thing?...” It has been hours since I started thinking. And I can do nothing. Should I telegraph Sen? Should I write to Maitreyi? I feel she did this because of me. If only I had read the letters brought by Khokha… Perhaps she had planned something. I am very confused now, very confused. And yet I want to write here everything, everything. …And what if it is nothing but a cruel trick of my love? Why should I believe it? How do I know? I would like to look into Maitreyi’s eyes. January–February 1933.
chapters.summary: Allan struggles with poverty, rejection, and emotional turmoil as he refuses Maitreyi's desperate attempts to contact him, finds solace with Geurtie.
